case_information: Previously healthy 20-year-old male presenting after multiple gunshot wounds to the left upper and lower extremities. Vascular exam showed diminished left radial pulse. CT imaging demonstrated left axillo-subclavian vascular injury with associated lung contusion and nondisplaced humerus fracture. CT angiography showed arterial injury with active contrast extravasation, a large contrast pool in the axillary region, and an expanding hematoma; no vascular injury identified in the lower extremity. Underwent emergent endovascular repair via common femoral artery access with deployment of covered stents to the distal/proximal subclavian and axillary segments; completion angiography confirmed no endoleak and good distal runoff. Postoperatively had palpable left brachial and radial pulses; managed in ICU then surgical floor; discharged home POD#5. Follow-up showed patent stent graft without endoleak.
diagnosis: Traumatic injury of left subclavian artery

case_information: A 75-year-old female presented with dyspnea, orthopnea, lower extremities swelling, and palpitations. Past history includes 3 years of atrial fibrillation and 1 year of chronic heart failure (NYHA class II). Exam: irregular pulse 80/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, bibasal crackles, peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, and a grade IV pansystolic murmur along the left sternal border. She reported right upper quadrant abdominal pain worsened by palpation; liver edge was tender and enlarged (6 cm below costal margin) with smooth surface; spleen not palpable. EKG: atrial fibrillation (80/min), right bundle branch block, inferolateral ischemic changes. Abdominal ultrasound: homogeneous hepatomegaly with dilated hepatic veins and dilated inferior vena cava (30 mm) without respiratory variation.

A 46-year-old woman with a genetically confirmed connective tissue disorder and prior major aortic surgeries (including repair of descending and ascending aortic dissections) underwent routine CT imaging in 2016 that showed a newly developed circumscript 4.1 x 3.3 cm aneurysmal dilation of the left subclavian artery in the retroclavicular intrathoracic space. She reported recent onset pulsatile sensation in the left supraclavicular fossa and progressively increasing hoarseness; exam found a palpable swelling in the retroclavicular space. Because of limited mobility after prior thoracotomies and restricted lung function, she declined open resection and chose a percutaneous endovascular approach. A flexible self-expanding stent-graft (9 x 100 mm) was deployed across the lesion with ~3 cm landing zones while preserving flow to the left vertebral and internal mammary arteries. Completion angiography showed correct position and no endoleak; follow-up CT angiography before discharge confirmed complete exclusion. She was discharged on aspirin, bisoprolol, and losartan. At 1-year follow-up CT, there was no endoleak, the treated segment was completely thrombosed, and the aneurysmal sac had resolved.

A 69-year-old male admitted with acute respiratory failure and septic shock after severe pneumonia; history of Down syndrome, heart failure, hepatitis B with liver cirrhosis, and prior trans-aortic valve insertion. On admission: hemodynamic instability requiring noradrenaline and hydrocortisone; elevated inflammatory markers and lactate; mild acute kidney insufficiency with preserved diuresis; signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Treated empirically with piperacillin/tazobactam; escalated due to poor response and purulent tracheal secretions; blood cultures grew Streptococcus dysgalactiae and antibiotics adjusted.

After respiratory status improved, persistent mild respiratory insufficiency led to suspected COPD; receiving inhaled bronchodilators (ipratropium/fenoterol, salbutamol), IV morphine, intermittent IV furosemide, and required constant parenteral potassium replacement. A planned IV methylprednisolone dose was mistakenly replaced by an IV administration of 1 mL of salbutamol solution 5 mg/mL, followed immediately by severe tachycardia and hemodynamic collapse: atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 170–200/min, acute hypotension requiring fluids and escalating noradrenaline; somnolence and acute hypercapnic respiratory distress; elevated lactate and worsening hypokalemia.

Management included intubation and mechanical ventilation; attempts to control tachycardia with IV landiolol worsened hypotension without rate control; electrical cardioversion unsuccessful; potassium chloride given. Because of persistent life-threatening shock and refractory tachyarrhythmia, hemodialysis was initiated; ~30 minutes after starting dialysis, rhythm converted to sinus (~80/min) without rebound tachycardia, though hypotension persisted due to ongoing septic shock. Glucose was elevated. Despite ongoing intensive care and infection management, he remained febrile and hypotensive with abundant purulent tracheal secretions and died 9 days after MICU admission from septic shock with multiorgan failure.

Male infant born at 37+1 weeks, birth weight 1,211 g; Apgar 8 and 9. Multiple minor anomalies (prominent occiput, micrognathia, short sternum). Chromosome analysis: 47,XY,+18. Transthoracic echocardiography: large inlet-type ventricular septal defect (4 mm) and patent ductus arteriosus. Resting heart rate 60–70 bpm. ECG: second-degree or higher atrioventricular block (transiently 3:1) with QT interval prolongation; nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. Parents declined aggressive treatments (pacemaker, VSD surgery). Progressive heart failure leading to death at 85 days. Genetic testing of long-QT candidate genes identified SCN5A R1193Q variant.

A four-year-old female presented with dysphagia and regurgitation of solid food. Chest contrast-enhanced CT showed an anomalous origin of the right subclavian artery arising from the medial wall of the descending thoracic aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery, coursing posterior to the esophagus and crossing to the right at the level of T4 with posterior esophageal compression. Additional imaging finding: common origin of the right and left common carotid arteries; left-sided arch with left descending thoracic aorta. Echocardiogram showed a large ostium secundum atrial septal defect (~20 mm) with dilated right atrium and right ventricle. Surgical management via median sternotomy included division of the anomalous vessel at its origin with oversewn aortic stump, mobilization anterior to the esophagus, and reimplantation end-to-side to the right common carotid artery; pericardial patch closure of the atrial septal defect under cardiopulmonary bypass. Postoperatively symptoms resolved.

An 80-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and atherosclerotic heart disease on amlodipine/atorvastatin, metformin/vildagliptin, and daily aspirin. No history over the past 10 years of episodes suggestive of transient cerebral ischemia (no limb numbness, paralysis, or visual disturbance). For 2 years she has had recurrent dizziness with bilateral tinnitus, hearing impairment, and headaches; prior evaluations (cardiology/ENT/neurology) labeled as central vertigo and treated with piracetam with minimal benefit. On examination, arm blood pressure measurements showed a marked systolic BP discrepancy of 53 mmHg between right and left arms. Chest CTA (12/26/2018) demonstrated atherosclerotic stenosis of the left subclavian artery. She declined endovascular stenting due to age and chose conservative management with ongoing follow-up; symptoms persisted initially and later dizziness decreased during subsequent conservative therapy, with serial measurements showing reduction in the inter-arm systolic BP difference over time.

A 14-year-old girl presented with aortocoronary fistula causing decreased coronary flow during diastole, with clinical worsening during exercise. Right three-port (3 mm) thoracoscopy was performed in an upright position. An abnormal vascular tract was identified and dissected on arrival at the right atrium. Fluorescence imaging with immediate indocyanine green injection (0.2 mg/kg) confirmed the vascular anomaly and aided visualization for secure ligature.

61-year-old man presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath. Past medical history includes congestive heart failure, prior coronary artery bypass graft surgery, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Three months earlier he had complete removal of a left chest wall device and leads due to bacterial endocarditis with vegetations on the atrial portion of the ventricular lead, followed by placement of a new right chest wall device with new leads.

On presentation: hypertensive (156/108 mmHg) and tachycardic (132/min) with regular rhythm; exam notable for jugular venous distention, bilateral lower-extremity pitting edema, and bilateral rales. Labs showed leukocytosis, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, elevated BNP, and normal troponins. Chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema pattern, with right chest wall device leads in expected position.

CT chest performed for concern for pulmonary embolism showed bilateral perihilar/basilar ground-glass opacities consistent with pulmonary edema and no acute pulmonary embolism. CT also demonstrated a calcified fibrin sheath in the left brachiocephalic vein and new linear calcified opacities within the right interlobar and left lower lobe segmental pulmonary arteries, not seen on a CT 9 months earlier. The patient improved with diuretics and was discharged after 2 days.

An 83-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain radiating into both lower limbs for 1 hour. History of hypertension and dyslipidemia. CTA showed an abdominal aortic aneurysmal dilation extending from just below the superior mesenteric artery to the aortic bifurcation (length 10.8 cm; maximum sac diameter 7.4 cm) with fusiform dilation of both common iliac arteries (right 1.1 cm, left 1.5 cm). Infrarenal neck length 22 mm with severe tortuosity/angulation (90°). Managed with endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) via bilateral femoral surgical cutdown, requiring stiff-wire alignment of the proximal neck, deployment of a bifurcated stent graft with bilateral iliac limb extensions; intra-procedural proximal endoleak required ballooning and placement of an additional proximal cuff with resolution on final angiography. Discharged well; 3-month follow-up CTA showed good stent position/expansion without migration and no endoleak.

A 19-month-old girl sustained a puncture injury to the right cheek from a glass bottle with pain and bleeding. She underwent local anesthesia, debridement, and suturing. One week later the sutures were removed. One week after suture removal, she developed increasing redness and swelling of the right cheek wound for 3 days. Exam: right cheek erythema and swelling with increased skin temperature; central black necrotic area ~0.5 cm; palpable throbbing; pain and purulent drainage when squeezed; systolic murmur on auscultation. CT head/face (plain): short "U"-shaped high-density foreign body in the right cheek space (~1.8 cm) with local hematoma. Ultrasound: irregular hypoechoic area with "C"-type strong echo and no flow on CDFI; adjacent "C"-type strong echo; deep round cystic mass ~1.7 × 1.7 cm with clear boundary and obvious pulsation; CDFI demonstrated "yin-yang" flow pattern continuous with a branch of the facial artery; PW Doppler showed biphasic bidirectional arterial flow at a breach. Surgery: removal of ring-shaped glass fragment (~1.2 cm long, 0.5 cm diameter) and three small glass pieces; adjacent pulsatile mass on deep side ~1.8 cm was ligated and excised. Pathology: wall composed of mixed thrombus with organization. Post-op follow-up: wound healed well.

A 17-year-old man was admitted to intensive care after a drowning event. Initial cranium/chest/abdomen CT was negative. Arterial blood gas showed hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis. He required mechanical ventilation; acidosis worsened and he was intubated. After about 1 day, he developed hypotension (79/40 mmHg), tachyarrhythmia (HR 128 bpm), and hypoxemia (PaO2 < 79%). He died about 36 hours after admission. Toxicology was negative. Autopsy: focal sub-meningeal hemorrhage; external inspection of neck/chest/abdomen negative. Lungs congested with subpleural Tardieu’s spots. Heart silhouette preserved and coronaries not occluded; ventricular wall thickness increased (LV 2.3 cm, RV 1.3 cm, septum 1 cm) with a large intracavitary blood clot; after clot removal, papillary whitish multifocal lesions based in the ventricular wall. Histology of myocardium showed increased muscle cells with interposed fibrous tissue consistent with cardiac hypertrophy. Papillary lesion histology showed extracellular fibrous matrix with elastic component and few cells, covered by a single cell layer; special stains showed mainly collagen and elastic fibers; immunohistochemistry positive for CD34 and S-100 throughout, FVIII on the surface, and focal actin positivity. Lung histology showed irregular emphysema, congested vessels, pleural hemorrhagic spots, alveoli filled with proteinaceous exudates with eosinophilic granulocytes and erythrocyte extravasation. Brain, liver, and other organs showed edema, congestion, and erythrocyte extravasation.

36-year-old pregnant woman had routine prenatal exam at 26 weeks. Fetal echocardiography showed severe pulmonary valve obstruction with intact ventricular septum and moderate tricuspid regurgitation (TR jet 4.7 m/s). At 30 weeks: TR jet decreased to 2.56 m/s; persistent pulmonary stenosis; reversed flow in ductus arteriosus. Serial fetal echocardiography every 2–3 weeks: right ventricular hypoplasia did not worsen; did not meet criteria for intrauterine intervention; TR degree/velocity decreased significantly.

Female infant delivered at 38 weeks (3100 g). Initial vitals: HR 128/min, RR 45/min, SpO2 93%. Postnatal echocardiogram: small right ventricular cavity; foramen ovale 6.4 mm; pulmonary valve annulus 7.6 mm; no obvious systolic flow across pulmonary valve; patent ductus arteriosus 4.3 mm supplying pulmonary circulation; tricuspid annulus 10 mm (Z score −1.13) with mild systolic regurgitation and slight diastolic flow; aorta and pulmonary artery morphology normal.

Day 1: SpO2 fell to 85% with ductus trending toward closure; prostaglandin E1 infusion started (1–3 ng/kg/min) with SpO2 ~92%. Preoperative reassessments: no severe tricuspid valve malformation (not Ebstein); TR jet ~2.0 m/s; no myocardial sinusoids; coronary arteries normal. Planned catheter-based relief of pulmonary outflow obstruction (balloon dilation considered).
diagnosis: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

case_information: A 79-year-old man with controlled hypertension was involved in an altercation at a restaurant and sustained a single strong blow to the center of the chest, followed by a fall. He had mild alcohol intoxication and could not recall details; an eyewitness confirmed the mechanism. About 30 minutes later he developed nausea and called emergency services. In the emergency department he was alert and oriented with near-normal vital signs except relatively low blood pressure (92/68 mmHg). He denied chest or back pain and had no other associated symptoms. Physical examination showed no obvious external wounds. Labs showed mildly elevated D-dimer (2.7 microg/mL) with otherwise near-normal results. Non-contrast head CT was normal; chest CT showed massive pericardial effusion and suspected ascending aortic pathology. He was transferred for further evaluation. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated pathology localized to the ascending aorta with massive pericardial effusion; 3D reconstruction showed a dissected/dilated ascending aorta with maximal diameter 44 mm. Emergent surgery found massive hemorrhagic pericardial effusion and hematoma adjacent to the ascending aorta on the pulmonary artery side, with no obvious adventitial laceration; intimal tears were present on the noncoronary sinus of Valsalva and distal ascending aorta at the lesser curvature, with intact coronary ostia. Ascending aortic replacement with a single-branched Dacron graft was performed using cardiopulmonary bypass, hypothermia, retrograde cardioplegia, and antegrade cerebral perfusion. Postoperative CT showed no residual pathology at anastomoses; pathology of the ascending aortic wall showed hemorrhage and fibrosis in the adventitia with no media abnormality. Recovery was uncomplicated and he was discharged home on postoperative day 24 with in-home nursing care services.

A 30-year-old male with recurrent episodes of moderate abdominal and back pain predominantly in the left lumbar region and left flank for about 1 year. Pain began suddenly, worsened over 1 day, rated 3–4/10, nonradiating, with no clear aggravating or relieving factors. No nausea, vomiting, or bowel habit changes. Unintentional weight loss of ~10 kg over the past year with reduced appetite and occasional abdominal fullness. No hematuria or testicular pain; no relevant family history. Exam: vitals normal; tenderness on deep palpation of left lumbar and flank; no peritoneal signs; no renal angle tenderness. Labs: normal renal function, normal urinalysis (no proteinuria/hematuria), and normal routine blood tests. CT: compression of the left renal vein below the superior mesenteric artery origin with left renal vein dilatation and splenorenal shunting/collaterals; no duodenal or bowel compression. Managed conservatively with complete pain resolution; referred for vascular surgery follow-up.

A 67-year-old woman with hypertension presented with acute chest pain. CT demonstrated a type A aortic dissection with a large intramural hematoma in the ascending aorta. She underwent urgent Bentall procedure with composite graft and biological aortic valve and coronary reimplantation using extracorporeal circulation, hypothermia, circulatory arrest, and retrograde cerebral perfusion. Postoperatively she had signs of right heart failure; extracorporeal perfusion was restarted and a 14F venting catheter was placed through the left ventricular apex, later removed and the apical hole closed with suture. Recovery was uncomplicated except for pacemaker implantation for second-degree atrioventricular block. Follow-up CT at 1 and 2 months showed a slowly enlarging 4.5 × 2.5 cm outpouching arising from the left ventricular apex and a small septal defect; echocardiography confirmed these findings. Additional CT noted a minor leak from the aortic graft suture into the false lumen. Because redo surgery was expected to be technically difficult in an otherwise stable patient, percutaneous endovascular closure was attempted via right common femoral arterial access, catheterization across the aortic valve into the left ventricle, and deployment of an Amplatzer septal occluder; transient ventricular arrhythmias occurred during catheter manipulation but were controlled by the pacemaker. Post-procedure CT 10 days later showed no contrast filling of the treated lesion but revealed a second similar outpouching near the base of the apex, which was then closed in a second procedure with another Amplatzer device. Subsequent CT at 3 weeks and 3 months showed complete exclusion of both lesions and the patient remained well.

A 50-year-old white male was referred for skin cancer screening. Physical exam revealed a 3 cm blackened macule on the right calf with irregular borders and multiple colors. The lesion appeared about 10 years ago with progressive growth in recent months. Positive family history of melanoma. Dermoscopy showed a peripheral atypical pigmented network (more marked on the right), brownish streaks centrally and in the right periphery, a peripheral black blotch with some globular structures, an amorphous area with pseudofollicular opening and pseudocysts on the left, and a central veil. Because the lesion had some clinical aspects of seborrheic keratosis but suspicious dermoscopic findings were localized, an incisional punch biopsy (4 mm) was taken from the streaked area. Histology demonstrated confluent atypical melanocytes in part of the epidermis extending into the superficial dermis, several mitotic figures, and an inflammatory dermal reaction (reported Breslow thickness 0.37 mm). The lesion was subsequently excised with 1 cm margins; the excision specimen showed only residual inflammatory reaction without additional malignant features. The dermoscopic blotch corresponded histologically to acanthosis, papillomatosis, and extensive dermal melanin deposition consistent with partial regression.

An 82-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 3.5 cm brownish skin nodule on the scalp; excisional biopsy performed. Histopathology showed an exophytic, extensively ulcerated tumor diffusely infiltrating superficial and deep dermis with abundant necrosis. The lesion comprised two intimately intermingled cell populations: (1) atypical squamous cells in nests and cords with true keratinization, dyskeratinocytes, horny pearl formation and focal clear cell change; (2) epithelioid (less often spindle-shaped) pigmented cells with markedly atypical nuclei, prominent nucleoli and eosinophilic cytoplasm, with significant melanin deposition. Focal epidermal connection at lesion edges, without an in-situ component. Brisk mitotic activity in both populations (up to 15 mitoses/mm2) including atypical mitoses. Thickness measured 10 mm with focal vascular invasion. No brisk tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes or regression; multiple plasma cell aggregates and severe solar elastosis in surrounding dermis. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated a dichotomous pattern: one component positive for CK-AE1/AE3; the pigmented component positive for Melan-A and PRAME; strong nuclear p53 in the pigmented component. BRAF V600E and p16 negative in both components.

28-year-old female with several years of patchy non-scarring hair loss involving the scalp with loss of eyebrows and eyelashes. Also has persistent inflammation around the fingernail with ridging and pitting of the right 4th digit and associated nail dystrophy. Periungual inflammation improved after 8 weeks of topical tacrolimus ointment, triamcinolone lotion, clobetasol ointment and oral fluconazole, but nail dystrophy did not. Shave biopsy of the right 3rd digit performed to rule out psoriasis showed spongiotic dermatitis. Started on baricitinib 4 mg daily; after 4 months had significant eyelash and eyebrow regrowth with mild improvement in nail dystrophy. By 11 months of therapy, the nail normalized in appearance and texture; continued overall improvement in hair loss with ongoing baricitinib treatment.

70-year-old white man born in Buenos Aires with a localized swelling on the tip of the nose and an external orifice with serosanguineous discharge. Had rural/wooded exposure; initially treated empirically with ivermectin twice one week apart without improvement over 2 months. Lesion persisted with an orifice producing sebaceous-like secretion; excisional biopsy with curettage performed. Histopathology: follicular hyperkeratosis; prominent sebaceous glands; telangiectatic capillaries; diffuse mononuclear dermal inflammation; cystically dilated infundibular structure with squamous proliferation showing wide eosinophilic cytoplasm, pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, extensive dyskeratosis, and areas of necrosis; interpreted as adnexal neoplasia with pilar differentiation / possible proliferating epidermoid cyst. Lesion recurred 45 days later; repeat surgery with partial removal of alar cartilage and reconstruction with dorsal nasal flap; histopathology confirmed complete excision; no recurrence on follow-up.

A 54-year-old Caucasian woman was referred by her oncologist to dermatology with a 2-month history of diffuse painful and pruritic skin tightening that began on the distal extremities and gradually involved the trunk and abdomen. No history suggestive of Raynaud phenomenon, dysphagia, or gastro-oesophageal reflux; no prior skin problems or autoimmune disease. Past history includes extra-skeletal osteosarcoma of the left leg (fully excised, treated with radiotherapy). She had triple negative right breast carcinoma treated with neoadjuvant carboplatin-paclitaxel with an immune checkpoint inhibitor, then surgery and radiotherapy to the right breast/axillary nodes, followed by additional cycles of the immune checkpoint inhibitor; after cycle 9 she developed an erythematous rash with hardness and swelling confined to the prior radiotherapy field that improved with topical hydrocortisone and therapy was continued. Three months after the final cycle, she developed persistent pruritus and erythema starting on extremities and later involving the trunk, with progressively worsening skin induration and discomfort; low-dose oral prednisolone and topical betamethasone provided minimal benefit. Exam showed diffuse skin sclerosis with induration, thickening, and erythema; telangiectasia only on the previously irradiated right chest; digits spared with no swelling, ischaemia, or calcinosis. Laboratory workup including CBC, ANA, rheumatoid factor, ENA, ANCA, anti-CCP, RNA polymerase III, anti-topoisomerase I, anti-centromere, anti-Ro52, and anti-RNP antibodies was unremarkable. Biopsies from left forearm and right upper abdomen showed thickened dermis with hyalinised sclerotic collagen bundles extending into subcutis in thick bands, mild blood vessel wall thickening, and very focal scant mucin on Hale’s colloidal iron stain. PUVA produced minimal improvement; methotrexate led to gradual improvement in pain/erythema though stiffness persisted, managed with physiotherapy; fibrosis improved but remained noticeable, especially over the right upper limb.

A 3-year-old girl with severe atopic dermatitis not responsive to emollients, topical hydrocortisone, and topical triamcinolone was started on dupilumab 300 mg/2 mL every 4 weeks. She had rapid improvement of skin symptoms within 9 days. Sixteen days after the injection she developed left leg pain and a limp, followed within 12 hours by red urticarial plaques around the injection site that rapidly generalized over the next 8 hours to the face, both legs, arms, abdomen, and buttocks. She presented to the emergency department with low-grade fever (102°F), injected conjunctivae, worsening rash, severe arthralgias causing inability to walk, and no lymphadenopathy. Labs showed elevated ESR (40 mm/h) and CRP (5.22 mg/L) with normal complement C3/C4, negative urinalysis for proteinuria, and no eosinophilia on WBC differential. Symptoms resolved within 2 days after starting prednisolone 18 mg twice daily for 7 days.

A 42-year-old female presented with a traumatic depressed scar (~8x1 cm) over the right cheek extending from the lower eyelid to the nasolabial fold. The scar developed after a road traffic accident 20 years prior. It caused significant psychological distress, and she sought multiple consultations for reconstruction but preferred a non-surgical approach. After counseling, she underwent correction using dermal fillers: total 2.0 mL hyaluronic acid injected with a flexible 24G blunt cannula (1.0 mL injected deep into the scar tissue and 1.0 mL injected more superficially into wrinkled atrophic scar tissue). Immediate improvement was visible with the scar filled to the level of adjacent skin; no erythema, pain/tenderness, lumps/bumps, swelling, bruising, or bleeding; improved facial symmetry. Follow-up at 2 weeks and sustained improvement at 6 months; no complications.

A 41-year-old male developed shooting back pain radiating to the front with vesicular skin lesions over the trunk and was treated with oral acyclovir, mecobalamin, folic acid, and carbamazepine. The initial lesions subsided within 5 days, but on day 7 he developed new reddish skin lesions over the trunk; he stopped all medications and the new lesions resolved within 2 days. Due to persistent shooting pain, he was later prescribed carbamazepine again along with fexofenadine, clonazepam, and aceclofenac. After 9 days, reddish lesions recurred and spread over the trunk to upper and lower limbs. Exam showed flat, reddish, well-demarcated lesions over the body. Labs: Hb 13.4 g%, TLC 5300/mm3 (neutrophils 86%, lymphocytes 9%), RBS 128 mg%, urea 21 mg%, creatinine 0.9 mg%, SGPT 50 IU/L (borderline high), SGOT 23 IU/L, bilirubin 0.6 mg%. Medication suspected was stopped and he was treated with intramuscular dexamethasone 8 mg and pheniramine 4 mg daily for 3 days; lesions subsided within 4 days and liver enzymes normalized.

42-year-old Caucasian man referred to dermatology with 6 months of multiple itchy, scaly, red-gray plaques covering nearly the entire body (scalp, arms, trunk, thighs), severity measures PASI 18.5 and BSA 45%, with 10-year course of similar skin disease and positive family history (mother and sister affected). Also has 10-year history of inflammatory peripheral joint involvement with dactylitis. Additionally developed moderate chronic recurrent inflammatory lesions in the groin area in the prior year, Hurley stage II, IHS4 score 10. Marked quality-of-life impairment (DLQI 25). Prior systemic/biologic therapies included cyclosporine for 2 years stopped due to elevated urea/creatinine (resolved after stopping), methotrexate and golimumab for 3 years with improvement mainly in joint symptoms, and adalimumab, ustekinumab, and secukinumab with only partial response. Normal laboratory workup. Started brodalumab 210 mg at weeks 0, 1, 2 then every 2 weeks, with marked improvement in skin and joint symptoms by week 8 and groin disease by week 16; PASI 1.5, BSA 8%, IHS4 3; continued for 1 year with DLQI improved to 1 by 3 months.

An immune-mediated mucocutaneous/subepithelial blistering disorder predominantly affecting the oral mucosa (most often gingivae), sometimes with skin involvement. Common presentation includes desquamative gingivitis that may be the only manifestation, and oral blood-filled blisters from bleeding into bullae. More frequent in females and typically in patients older than 50 years. Managed with topical or systemic corticosteroids; if ocular involvement is present, dapsone is recommended.

A 6 month-old female presented with multiple painless swellings over the left knee for 4 months, insidious onset and gradually progressive. Illness began after an insect bite 4 months prior, followed by erythematous nodules that gradually progressed with ulceration; associated low-grade fever for the first 10 days. Exam: multiple nodules over the extensor aspect of the left thigh and a single well-defined erythematous indurated non-tender nodule (3 cm x 4 cm) with central ulceration and eschar over the left knee; firm, smooth rounded edges, freely mobile over underlying structures. Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Labs: Hb 13.7 g%, TLC 9,900/cu.mm, differential N 55% L 40% E 4% M 1%, platelets 1.76 lakhs/cu.mm; urinalysis essentially unremarkable; HIV 1/2 non-reactive; LFT normal. X-ray left thigh: soft-tissue swelling. Tissue microscopy with 10% KOH: fungal elements with broad aseptate hyphae. Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 30°C: flat creamy-brown furrowed colonies with pale reverse by 3 days, later brown with satellite colonies. Lactophenol cotton blue mount: aseptate hyphae and smooth-walled zygospores with conjugation beaks; identified as Basidiobolus ranarum. Histopathology: subcutaneous granulomatous inflammation with dense eosinophilic infiltrate, polymorphs, histiocytes, plasma cells, lymphocytes, multinucleated giant cells; central fragments with aseptate hyphae. Treated with saturated solution of oral potassium iodide with gradual dose escalation then taper; complete lesion resolution by 8 weeks.

55-year-old female with hypertension, obesity, and prior tobacco use developed an acute dark, circular, tender lesion on the right palm noted the same morning. Six days earlier she was discharged from the ED after evaluation for right-sided branch retinal artery occlusion and started on aspirin 81 mg daily and high-dose atorvastatin 80 mg daily (LDL 190 mg/dL; MRI brain mild chronic small-vessel ischemic changes; MRA neck/brain, echocardiogram with bubble study, EKG normal; ESR/CRP normal). At primary care visit five days after discharge: afebrile and stable vitals; exam showed a single 2×3 cm hyperpigmented targetoid lesion with central clearing on the palmar aspect of the right hand, mildly tender; no other skin lesions and no mucous membrane involvement. Medications: amlodipine, aspirin, and atorvastatin. High-dose atorvastatin was stopped and the lesion resolved within four days.

A 69-year-old postmenopausal woman with early-stage invasive lobular breast carcinoma (pT1cN0; ER 95%, PR negative, HER2 negative, Ki-67 15%) underwent breast-conserving surgery and sentinel lymph node biopsy and then began adjuvant endocrine therapy with letrozole 2.5 mg daily. Three months after starting letrozole, she developed sudden fever to 39°C and an exuberant, painful, expanding erythema with burning sensation on the left trunk, without arthralgia, myalgia, headache, malaise, or recent respiratory/gastrointestinal viral infection. Exam showed painful, brightly erythematous papules, some coalescing into plaques, asymmetrically distributed over the neck, left trunk, back, and upper extremities. Labs showed no inflammatory signs: WBC 4,800/mm3 (69% neutrophils), hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, normal liver/kidney function, normal CRP; blood cultures negative; no evidence of malignancy recurrence. Dermatology evaluation with skin biopsy showed dermal oedema and a dense diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Letrozole was stopped and systemic corticosteroid therapy with prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day was started with rapid improvement within 24 hours, then tapered over 7 weeks; letrozole was not restarted and tamoxifen was initiated. No recurrence of the dermatologic episode over 4 years.

38-year-old female referred to a skin fragility center with a 10-year history of progressive skin fragility beginning after her second pregnancy (2008). Chronic blistering and scarring with severe involvement of skin and multiple mucous membranes (ocular, oral, esophageal, genital), as well as nails and hair. Prior autoimmune diagnostic testing was inconclusive; differential diagnoses considered for years. Previous systemic treatments by dermatologists (systemic glucocorticoids with chloroquine, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil) were unsuccessful. Family history unremarkable; otherwise healthy and not taking medications. Treated with intensive topical care plus rituximab (2×1000 mg) followed by monthly IVIG, leading to stabilization with less blistering and reduced dressing needs, enabling occupational reintegration and improved daily functioning.

A 64-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presented with a 20-month history of nonpruritic erythematous ulcerated lesions on both legs. Exam showed a large oval erythematoviolaceous plaque covering more than half of the right pretibial region with slightly elevated, indurated, infiltrative border and a center with small necrotic/crusted ulcers and small atrophic areas; smaller similar plaques were present on the left leg. No regional lymphadenopathy, no history of trauma or insect bite, and no fever or other systemic symptoms. Blood count, routine biochemistry, urinalysis, and chest radiography were normal except hyperglycemia (11.8 mmol/L). Bacteriological tests were negative. Skin biopsy revealed dense lymphocytic infiltrate throughout the dermis with multiple non-necrotizing granulomas containing epithelioid cells, histiocytes, and multinucleated giant cells, outlined by dense lymphocytes. Giemsa stain showed intracellular basophilic regular structures consistent with amastigotes. Treated with intramuscular meglumine antimoniate 20 mg/kg/day for 15 days with ulcer healing and residual atrophic scarring.

A 58-year-old uncircumcised male with 36-year history beginning at age 22 of severe dysesthesia of the glans penis with concurrent distal foreskin swelling, causing major quality-of-life impairment and depression. Infectious causes (including herpes and other sexually transmitted infections) were ruled out by swab testing and clinical correlation. Multiple specialist reviews over years; a skin biopsy showed compact hyperkeratosis, oedematous collagen in the superficial papillary dermis, prominent/dilated superficial vessels, and a light lymphocytic infiltrate. Long-term self-treatment with potent topical corticosteroid (betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% ointment) and topical lidocaine gel for ~15 years with symptomatic relief, then switched by family doctor to mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment for ~10 years. On later review he reported recurrent glans ulcers and mild dyspareunia. Exam: diffuse erythema of the glans, minor adhesions across the coronal sulcus laterally, some telangiectasia, mild foreskin swelling without phimosis; no erosions or ulcers at the visit. Erythema was thought secondary to chronic topical corticosteroid use rather than ongoing active disease. Advised to stop mometasone and use 1% hydrocortisone twice daily plus regular emollient; stopped topical steroids 1 year ago with no withdrawal symptoms and no further dysesthesia, pain, or swelling.

A 56-year-old male presented with 2 months of unilateral nasal obstruction unresponsive to amoxicillin/clavulanate and daily fluticasone, progressing over the next month to near-daily epistaxis, persistent left-sided periorbital pain, and epiphora. He also reported unilateral V2 distribution hypoesthesia and maxillary pressure, with mild left eye exophthalmos without diplopia; denied visual changes or dental pain. Past history notable for alcoholic liver cirrhosis with thrombocytopenia (platelets 75 x 10^3/uL) and mildly elevated PT/INR (15.9/1.3); reported isolated epistaxis without hematemesis or melena. CT showed a large heterogeneous-density left maxillary sinus mass with smooth bony destruction of medial and lateral maxillary sinus walls, extension into the nasal cavity, and erosion of the left inferior orbital wall. MRI with gadolinium showed a heterogeneously enhancing mass with foci of high T1 and low T2 signal suggesting blood products. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated total obstruction of the left nasal cavity. Biopsy of an encapsulated mass caused profound bleeding requiring nasal packing and 24-hour inpatient observation; pathology showed inflamed respiratory mucosa with organizing thrombus. Endoscopic medial maxillectomy and tumor debulking were performed; final pathology demonstrated inflamed respiratory-type mucosa with hemorrhage, fibrin, and organizing thrombus with CD31 positivity along small vessels. Postoperatively, symptoms resolved with no recurrence at 1-year surveillance.

A 50-year-old man with 6 months of sore throat and neck swellings; no dyspnea or weight loss. Heavy smoking history (60 pack-years), no alcohol use. Flexible laryngoscopy showed bilateral intense arytenoid edema and fullness of the right pyriform sinus; multiple palpable right cervical lymph nodes. Initially declined further workup and left hospital; returned one month later with severe respiratory distress requiring emergent tracheotomy. Direct laryngoscopy revealed an ulcerovegetant tumor originating from the medial wall of the right pyriform sinus, filling the sinus; biopsies taken; surrounding laryngeal structures markedly edematous. Contrast CT/MRI demonstrated a right pyriform sinus mass with extralaryngeal extension, thyroid cartilage destruction, and prevertebral involvement; multiple pathologic right cervical lymphadenopathies. Thorax CT showed multiple metastatic nodules in both lungs; no other distant metastases. Biopsy showed small hyperchromatic cells in nests/sheets with necrosis, nuclear molding, crush artifact; immunoreactive for pancytokeratin, CD56, focal synaptophysin, and TTF-1; negative for CD20, leukocyte common antigen, and S100; Ki-67 >70%. Treated with cisplatin/etoposide chemotherapy with complete response at primary site, neck, and lungs; radiotherapy to primary and right neck started but stopped early by patient; follow-up showed no residual disease and disease-free status for 15 months.
diagnosis: Small cell carcinoma of the hypopharynx

case_information: A 49-year-old female with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging large swelling with discomfort on the left side of the neck just below the lower jaw. No tenderness, discharge, dysphagia, or similar lesions elsewhere. Exam: nontender, soft-to-firm, diffuse mass not fixed to surrounding tissues with normal overlying skin; approx. 10 × 8 × 6 cm, extending posteriorly to the sternocleidomastoid, crossing the midline anteriorly, overlapping the lower border of the mandible superiorly, and reaching the level of the cricoid inferiorly. No palpable regional lymphadenopathy. Fluctuant only at the most prominent point; lesion sagging inferiorly. Intraoral exam (dentition, tongue, floor of mouth, vestibule, salivary flow/duct opening) unremarkable; bimanual palpation and illumination tests negative. Needle aspiration yielded thick dirty cheesy white material; histopathology showed ductal elements, epidermoid cells, and keratin without dysplasia/atypia. CECT and MRI showed a well-capsulated benign-appearing cystic lesion in the submandibular region with a maintained outer fatty layer. Surgical excision performed; intraoperative frozen section indicated malignant transformation without regional lymph node involvement; further surgical clearance including modified supraomohyoid neck dissection. Definitive pathology showed malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma. One-year follow-up uneventful with no recurrence.
diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of submandibular gland

case_information: A 21-year-old nonsmoking nullipara at 39 weeks’ gestation had an unremarkable prenatal course with normal routine labs and no history of ear infections, ear surgery, baseline hearing deficits, or barometric pressure–related activities. She had a rapid labor without oxytocin augmentation, neuraxial anesthesia, or IV narcotics, and performed closed-glottis pushing. She delivered a healthy male infant after a 32-minute second stage; placenta delivered intact; mediolateral episiotomy repaired; estimated blood loss ~300 mL. About one hour postpartum, she was noted to have new facial petechiae and blood in the left ear; the right ear appeared normal and she denied inserting anything into the ear. Otoscopic exam showed minimal dark blood and a superficial thrombus obscuring the eardrum without active bleeding; she was afebrile, had no ear pain, and denied hearing reduction. Gentle clot removal revealed a 2–3 mm defect in the inferior aspect of the left eardrum; contralateral eardrum was intact. No otic lavage was performed; cotton packing was placed; no antibiotics were given. At 6-week follow-up she had no further ear bleeding, pain, or hearing deficit, and the left eardrum appeared grossly normal.

Following informed consent, an oral surgery procedure was performed under local anesthesia (articaine 4% with epinephrine 1:100,000). A full-thickness flap was elevated from 2.3 to distal 2.6 with a distal vertical release incision. Tooth 2.4 and an implant at 2.6 were removed due to severe bone loss and mobility. Granulation/infected tissue was curetted. An implant surface was debrided/decontaminated using an air-powder device with erythritol/amorphous silica/0.3% chlorhexidine for ~3 minutes circumferentially at <1 cm distance. A bone substitute (deproteinized bovine bone matrix) mixed with pure platelet-rich plasma was placed as grafting material around the 2.5 implant. Two resorbable collagen membranes were placed: one to isolate a communication with the Schneiderian membrane created after removal of the 2.6 implant, and one to cover the graft.

47-year-old female with swelling in the right posterior maxilla/upper back jaw region for 2 months; history of tooth extraction in the same region 7 months prior. Intraoral swelling extending from right premolar region to tuberosity with expansion of both cortical plates; sinus opening related to the extraction socket of the maxillary right first molar. Radiograph: well-defined unilocular radiolucency in the right posterior maxilla. Lesion enucleated with associated tooth extraction. Gross: cystic grayish soft tissue with irregular borders, rough surface, soft consistency. Microscopy: thin nonkeratinized epithelial lining with papillary projections and intraepithelial crypts (empty or mucin-filled); lining of cuboidal cells resembling reduced enamel epithelium; focal continuity with sinus lining; numerous mucous cells, clear cells, and few epidermoid-like cells; focal epithelial thickening/plaque formation; mucin-filled cystic spaces in fibrous capsule. Special stains: mucin positive on mucicarmine; mucous cells/pooling positive with PAS and alcian blue (acidic mucin); clear cells PAS positive without diastase and negative with diastase (glycogen). Follow-up 5 years without recurrence.

A 21-year-old male with swelling and pain on the left side of the face for 1 month. Pain decreased with medications but swelling persisted. Pus discharge for 2 days. Intraoral exam: 3 × 3 cm swelling in the left anterior maxillary region with ill-defined borders; soft on palpation; no lymph node involvement. Imaging: upper occlusal radiograph showed an osteolytic lesion with irregular margins; CT demonstrated a soft tissue mass perforating the anterior wall of the maxilla and palate. Incisional biopsy: grossly four brownish soft tissue bits (one 3 × 1.5 cm and three ~1 × 1 cm). Microscopy: connective tissue proliferation predominantly of fibroblastic cells with moderate collagen; arrangement in sheets/storiform and partly fascicular; large oval fibroblastic cells with abundant pleomorphism (including giant-cell–like elongated nuclei), moderate to abundant cytoplasm; focal spindle/wavy areas; blood vessels appeared constricted by proliferating cells; nuclear membrane generally clear with focal chromatin condensation and two or more nucleoli; mitotic figures present but not uniform.

21-year-old male with congenital bilateral cleft lip and severe nasal deformity (short nasal bridge, flat nasal tip). Under general anesthesia underwent nasal reconstruction using septal cartilage and upper-lip reconstruction using a lower-lip switch flap based on left inferior labial artery and vein (approximately 10 mm wide, 17 mm long) transferred to the upper lip. Initial flap color was good, but at 6 hours developed marked swelling with venous congestion; suture release around the pedicle did not improve perfusion and congestion worsened with concern for flap necrosis. At 8 hours post-op, flap was taken down, hematoma evacuated/irrigated, and flap returned to the lower lip donor site to restore circulation; postoperative heparinized saline gauze used. Congestion improved within hours and flap largely recovered by 1 week; later re-transferred with more tissue around the pedicle under local anesthesia with good engraftment and division at 9 days. At 2-year follow-up, reconstruction outcome was favorable.

43-year-old female admitted with a large left oro-antral communication. Symptoms: persistent pressure in the left maxillo-malar area, nasal regurgitation of fluids, whistling sound during phonation, and oral secretion discharge at the defect site. History of multiple dental/sinus-related surgeries over ~1 year for missing lateral teeth including sinus lift, implant placement, and bone augmentation; implants displaced into the sinus cavity with failed augmentation. Multiple prior unsuccessful surgical closure attempts (two buccal advancement flaps 2 months apart; later sinus irrigation with antibiotic solutions plus collagen membrane and compromised buccal flap as second layer). Exam: slight erythema of gingival mucosa in the lateral region; two fistulous openings on buccal mucosa adjacent to teeth region 2.5/2.6 with surrounding granulation tissue; probing reveals large bony defect communicating with left paranasal sinus. CBCT confirms a considerable oro-antral defect. Chronic course with symptoms leading to decision for radical antrostomy (Caldwell-Luc) and closure under general anesthesia using an autologous pedicled buccal fat pad flap. Intraoperative finding of ~1.5 cm communication with granulation tissue and sinus polyps; sinus cleaned and drained; buccal fat pad mobilized and sutured to palatal margins with partial coverage by buccal flap. Postoperative antibiotics and daily oral wound hygiene; uncomplicated healing with complete epithelialization.

A 46-year-old female presented to the emergency department with onset of painful swallowing after ingesting a fish bone a day earlier. No other local or systemic symptoms were present. Lateral neck radiograph showed a foreign body in the retropharyngeal space, which was removed by otolaryngology. She was discharged on oral antibiotics but returned one week later with worsening odynophagia, fever, and central painful neck fullness. Repeat radiograph showed a large collection requiring urgent incision and drainage. Culture grew Gram-positive alpha-hemolytic streptococci. Treated with intravenous antibiotics with in-hospital observation for 2 days, then discharged on oral antibiotics.

Caucasian female in her late 50s with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, refractory to oral and local corticosteroids, with prior functional endoscopic sinus surgery 5 years earlier for obstructive nasal polyps. Nasal endoscopy showed grade 3 polyposis bilaterally; SNOT-22 score 45/110. Blood eosinophils normal (120/mm3, 1.6%) with increased total serum IgE (baseline 464 kU/L). Planned for functional sinus surgery followed by monthly omalizumab starting 5 months post-surgery; followed clinically/endoscopically up to 1 year after surgery and 7 months after omalizumab initiation. Polyp pathology described as eosinophilic. Nasal brushing of middle turbinate performed (no local anesthesia) and ciliary function assessed by digital high-speed video microscopy at 500 Hz and 37°C, including ciliary beat frequency measurements and classification of ciliary beat pattern as normal vs abnormal.

A 75-year-old male presented to a prosthodontics specialty clinic requesting construction of a new denture due to a loose lower denture. Both upper and lower dentures were 25 years old; he was satisfied with the upper denture. Medical history included diabetes and hypertension controlled with oral medications (metformin and bisoprolol). Oral exam showed papillary proliferations on the labial mucosa of the premaxilla, described as mucosal lesions resembling denture-related inflammatory changes/papillary overgrowth. The patient did not return for further visits due to serious illness, so no follow-up was available.

A 26-year-old male presented with an orthopantomogram for implant (bone plates and screws) removal. Orthopantomogram and cone beam CT incidentally showed an impacted ectopic maxillary tooth in the second quadrant. The tooth was inverted, with the most superior cusp tip about 18 mm above and located distal to the root apex of the second molar. No associated cystic pathology was evident. All third molars were missing, and the ectopic tooth morphology did not match the size and shape of a third molar. Patient was informed of consequences and advised follow-up.

A 23-year-old male presented with 10 days of asymptomatic swelling and pus discharge from the left posterior maxilla. No significant past medical history. Extra-oral exam unremarkable. Intra-oral exam: partially edentulous; missing teeth 13, 14, 18, 27, 28, 37, 47; slight buccal cortical plate expansion in left posterior maxilla; on pressure, white creamy exudate expressed between 23 and 24; no tenderness or bleeding. Panoramic radiograph showed multiple well-defined radiolucencies in all four quadrants; left maxillary lesion associated with multiple impacted teeth and retained deciduous teeth; mandibular radiolucencies associated with missing 37 and 47 mimicking dentigerous cysts. Chest and skull radiographs unremarkable; dermatology exam without cutaneous abnormalities; hematologic investigations normal. Multiple cystic lesions were enucleated under general anesthesia and the surgical bed treated with Carnoy’s solution; one small cystic lesion distal to tooth 36 was observed. Histopathology from three lesions showed parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelial lining of uniform 6–8 cell thickness with palisaded columnar basal cells and polarized nuclei; satellite cysts and epithelial remnants in the connective tissue capsule; one separate lesion associated with an impacted right maxillary canine showed a dentigerous-type cyst lining.

A 5-year-old girl with swelling on the left side of the face since birth, with no pain or pus discharge and no change in size. Clinical exam: diffuse swelling over the left cheek extending from infraorbital rim to lower border of mandible and from angle of mouth to ~2 cm anterior to tragus; no clinically palpable lymph nodes. Intraoral: minor enlargement of left alveolar process, early eruption of 23, 24, 26, and early exfoliation of 63 and 64. MRI: poorly defined lipomatous lesion on the left cheek in the subcutaneous plane and buccal fat pad, with secondary hypertrophy of maxillary alveolus and hyperplasia of left maxillary sinus; no fatty infiltration of muscles. Incisional biopsy: soft tissue 1.5 × 0.8 × 0.4 cm, light brown, soft, irregular; histology showed collection of adipocytes with scanty fibrous tissue. Managed with regular follow-up; no treatment given due to young age.

30-year-old woman with a 6-year history of painless swelling in the left submandibular region, enlarging over the last 3 months to the root of the neck. Exam: ~12 cm × 6 cm cystic, non-tender mass in the left anterior cervical region; no swelling in the floor of the mouth. Color Doppler ultrasound: well-defined anechoic, loculated fluid collection in the left superficial anterior cervical region extending from mandibular angle to suprasternal fossa (~10.98 × 1.49 × 4.92 cm), poor internal sound transmission, internal septations, no obvious blood-flow signal. Contrast-enhanced CT used to confirm lesion extent. Fine-needle aspiration yielded egg white-like fluid. Under general anesthesia via transoral approach: excision of enlarged left sublingual gland and aspiration of mucus; blunt dissection toward anterior submandibular gland margin without significant cystic fluid; left submandibular region compressed 3 days. Histopathology: dilated ducts with mucous pool due to partial acinar rupture and mucous overflow. One week post-op: persistent left anterior cervical swelling similar to pre-op; aspiration from left carotid triangle yielded 15 mL light red clear fluid (not mucus). Swelling gradually resolved without intervention; no recurrence at 6-month follow-up.

Family growth/puberty history: father 169 cm with voice change at 14 years; mother 163 cm with menarche at 12 years; target height 159.5 cm; grandfather 167 cm; grandmother 147 cm with early menarche at 9 years. Genetic testing identified a novel heterozygous MKRN3 exon 1 point variant c.G277A causing p.Gly93Ser; the same variant was present in the father and absent in the mother. In silico predictions were mixed (PolyPhen-2 probably damaging; SIFT neutral; MutationTaster polymorphism). Functional studies showed reduced auto-ubiquitination for the p.G93S variant compared with wild-type and increased protein stability. Reporter assays using human GNRH1, KISS1, and TAC3 promoters showed weaker transcriptional suppression by the p.G93S variant than wild-type; in GT1-7 hypothalamic GnRH neuron-derived cells, wild-type reduced GnRH1 protein while the p.G93S variant did not.

59-year-old Caucasian female incidentally found to have persistent hypercalcemia over 6 months (11.4–14.0 mg/dL) and new severe hypertension. Largely asymptomatic; drinks 32–44 oz water daily by habit; no polyuria/polydipsia. Unintentional 25-lb weight loss over 6 months. Remote nephrolithiasis; occasional bilateral hip pain. Prior benign skin lesion removed. No supplements/medications; no tobacco/alcohol/drugs; no family endocrine history. Exam: initially BP 210/98 improving with treatment; low-grade temp 99.4°F; systolic ejection murmur; otherwise normal. Labs: normocytic normochromic anemia (Hgb 9.9 g/dL); impaired renal function (creatinine 1.7–2.4 mg/dL, BUN 26–32 mg/dL); elevated 24-hr urine calcium (448 and 587 mg/24h); serum phosphate and 25-hydroxyvitamin D normal; PTH suppressed; PTH-related peptide elevated; ACE elevated. Malignancy evaluation negative (chest/spine X-rays, mammogram, bone marrow biopsy, bone scan). CT chest showed borderline mediastinal adenopathy (paraaortic, pretracheal, subcarinal). Lymph node biopsy performed. Hypercalcemia and renal function improved after steroid therapy (calcium 9.2 mg/dL; creatinine 0.8 mg/dL).

45-day-old infant referred for jitteriness, poor sleep, poor weight gain despite voracious appetite, sleeping with eyes open, and ~10 bowel movements/day. Exam: thin, alert/irritable, moderately dehydrated; weight 3920 g with low daily weight gain; tachycardia (pulse 182/min); staring look with mild proptosis; diffusely enlarged thyroid; otherwise unremarkable. Labs: markedly elevated free/total T4 (>24.9 with reference 7–13.5), suppressed/undetectable TSH (ref 0.45–5.5), elevated thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin index (6.2; ref <1.9). Treated with antithyroid medication, beta-blocker, and iodide due to concern for heart failure; improved and therapy later discontinued with close monitoring.

A 72-year-old female with past medical history of tobacco use, stage II chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism and depression presented with two weeks of worsening dizziness, non-bloody non-bilious emesis and diarrhea after a hospitalization two weeks earlier. Two months prior she received amoxicillin for a dental procedure, after which she developed loose non-bloody, non-mucoid stools that progressed to watery bowel movements about three times daily, later accompanied by nausea and vomiting after every meal and cramping periumbilical abdominal pain. She completed a 7-day course of metronidazole and cefuroxime after being diagnosed with duodenitis on EGD at an outside hospital, but symptoms persisted. She denied blood in stool; prior colonoscopy four years earlier reportedly normal. She had an unintentional 20-lb weight loss over the last month. On arrival she was hemodynamically stable and afebrile; exam showed diffuse deep periumbilical tenderness without peritonitis, normoactive bowel sounds, no organomegaly; thickened shiny skin overlying the cheek bones. Labs showed hyperkalemia, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, and acute kidney injury; orthostatic hypotension was found. CT abdomen/pelvis without contrast showed mesenteric panniculitis without other acute findings. Extensive infectious diarrhea workup (stool cultures, ova/parasites, stool electrolytes and pH, C. difficile, Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Vibrio) was unremarkable. Repeat EGD showed small hiatal hernia, mild inactive gastritis negative for H. pylori, non-bleeding gastric angioectasia, and gastric mucosal atrophy. Colonoscopy showed small tubular adenomas and internal hemorrhoids but was otherwise unremarkable. She developed acute encephalopathy with visual hallucinations over three days after EGD; CT head was unremarkable; Mini-Mental score 21. Persistent diarrhea with persistent hypotension and hyperkalemia prompted endocrine evaluation; anti-adrenal antibodies were negative and repeat CT abdomen showed normal-size adrenal glands. Treatment with fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone led to normalization of stool consistency, resolution of vomiting, improvement in mentation, and normalization of laboratory values and vital signs.

Gene panel evaluation of a duplication at 4q28.1–4q32.1 in a child with short stature/growth retardation, speech delay, microcephaly, and genitourinary/renal malformations. Within the duplicated region, LRBA and RAB33B were excluded as not fitting the phenotype. Remaining short-stature candidates included INTU, NAA15, and PLK4; INTU-associated conditions were not consistent with the child’s presentation, and duplication of NAA15 had the highest PPV for short stature (0.80). For speech delay, MFSD8 was excluded; INTU and NAA15 were possible contributors, but GRIA2 had the highest PPV (0.90). For microcephaly, PLK4 was the only gene in the region with an OMIM microcephaly association and had PPV 0.50. No candidate gene was identified for the genitourinary/renal malformations.

A 53-year-old woman was referred for investigation of hypercortisolism after a two-year history of easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, and poor wound healing following surgery for diverticulitis and a vaginal fistula 15 months earlier. Surgical course was complicated by deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Additional symptoms included insomnia, depression, obesity, and hypertension. Physical examination showed facial plethora, supraclavicular and dorsocervical fat pads, and mild proximal myopathy. Endocrine investigations including inferior petrosal sinus sampling supported an ACTH-dependent source localized to the pituitary. She underwent transsphenoidal resection; pathology confirmed a corticotroph adenoma.

A 65-year-old woman, 9 days after right hip replacement surgery, developed nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain with paralytic ileus, urinary retention, and upper limb paresthesia. Labs showed hypokalemia and severe hyponatremia, normochromic anemia, low-range platelets, prolonged partial thromboplastin time, elevated C-reactive protein and procalcitonin. Chest X-ray showed focal pneumonia with bilateral pleural effusion; she received antibiotics plus hemin and glucose.

Despite therapy, severe hyponatremia (123.8 mmol/L) with asthenia and nausea persisted. Hormonal evaluation showed ACTH 43 pM/L with low cortisol 163.3 nM/L (confirmed), low plasma renin activity (0.3 µg/L/h), borderline-low aldosterone (47.2 pmol/L), and very low DHEA-S (<0.4 µmol/L). A 250 µg IV ACTH stimulation test showed no cortisol response. Abdominal CT showed bilateral adrenal enlargement with a hyperdense central area (~2 cm, HU 25–35) in the right adrenal gland; no suspicious lesion otherwise.

Anti-adrenal antibodies and anticardiolipin antibodies were negative. Testing was negative for tuberculosis and multiple infectious causes (candida/aspergillus antigens, CMV DNA, HIV, treponema, and serologies for cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, trypanosomiasis). She was not taking medications known to interfere with adrenal function.

Treatment with oral cortisone acetate led to rapid symptom improvement and normalization of sodium; she was discharged on glucocorticoid replacement. Follow-up showed persistently absent cortisol response to ACTH stimulation for months, with very low DHEA-S and generally normal PRA/aldosterone later. Repeat CT at 6 months showed normalization of adrenal size and resolution of the prior right-sided hyperdense lesion; later imaging showed normal left adrenal and a smaller, inhomogeneous right adrenal. Over 30 months, basal cortisol and ACTH progressively normalized while continuing a minimal dose of cortisone acetate, but cortisol remained nonresponsive to ACTH stimulation.

42-year-old woman evaluated at 16 weeks’ gestation for abnormal glucose; normal prepregnancy BMI (22.5 kg/m2) and negative family history of diabetes. Started insulin at 17 weeks in addition to diet; good glycemic control during pregnancy (mean HbA1c 5.4%). Delivered at 39 weeks (birth weight 3265 g). Postpartum OGTT: 2-hour plasma glucose >200 mg/dL with low insulin levels (5–23.6 mU/mL), C-peptide 1.1 ng/mL, and markedly positive anti-GAD antibodies (>2000 U/L); HbA1c 5.9%. Later required resumption of insulin with 4 daily injections; persistent poor metabolic control (HbA1c 9.5%).

A 4-year and 1-month-old girl evaluated after her younger brother was diagnosed with a metabolic disorder; she was generally in poor health, prone to colds, and had low height and weight. Newborn screening showed elevated acylcarnitines (C6, C8, C10, C10:1, C12, C14, C14:1, C14:2). On examination: weight 13 kg (−1 SD) and height 97.8 cm (−1 SD); neurologic exam was normal with symmetric knee and Achilles reflexes, intact sensation, and negative pathologic signs. Repeat testing showed increased C6, C8, C10, C10:1, C12, C14:1, C14:2 and elevated urinary organic acid 3-3-hydroxyphenyl-3-hydroxypropionic acid. Whole-exome sequencing was performed to confirm the suspected metabolic condition. Treated with riboflavin (vitamin B2) 50 mg twice daily and coenzyme Q10 50 mg twice daily. Six-month follow-up: weight 14 kg (−1 SD), height 100.2 cm (−1 SD); acylcarnitines remained elevated and urinary 3-3-hydroxyphenyl-3-hydroxypropionic acid remained elevated (23.44). One-year follow-up: weight 14.8 kg (−1 SD), height 105.1 cm (−1 SD); acylcarnitines remained elevated and urinary 3-3-hydroxyphenyl-3-hydroxypropionic acid normalized.

Two-day-old small for gestational age neonate transferred to PICU for severe hyperammonemia requiring emergency hemodialysis (ammonia up to 850 microg/dl). Initially breastfed; presented day 2 with recurrent hypothermia, poor sucking, and excessive weight loss. Partially compensated lactic acidosis (lactate 7.0 mmol/L, pH 7.14) and hyperammonemia with initially normal transaminases. Worsening coagulopathy/acute liver failure (INR ~2.1–2.45) not correctable with vitamin K; bilirubin elevated; aPTT prolonged; transaminases remained near reference range. Managed with protein cessation, high-glucose anabolization, nitrogen scavengers (phenylacetate/benzoate), carglumic acid, L-arginine, L-carnitine, vitamins; required intubation, vasopressors during dialysis. Suspected portal vein thrombosis after umbilical catheterization; partial recanalization with heparin. Metabolic workup: plasma amino acids not suggestive of urea cycle disorder; acylcarnitine profile unremarkable. Urine organic acids: massively increased lactate and pyruvate, significant ketonuria, and markedly elevated 3-methylglutaconic acid (3-MGA). Treated additionally with riboflavin, thiamine, coenzyme Q10. Dialysis stopped after 4 days; ammonia remained mildly elevated but did not spike with protein reintroduction. On day 13 sudden deterioration with focal seizures; brain MRI showed multiple supratentorial medullary lesions with diffusion restriction. Reintubation; recurrent hepatic synthetic and cardiovascular decompensation; death at 15 days. Postmortem trio whole-genome sequencing found homozygous pathogenic SERAC1 splice variant (NM_032861.4: c.1888_1828+10delinsACCAACAGG).

Laboratory tests showed ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism. Three 1.5T MRI studies showed no apparent pituitary lesion. Dynamic imaging evaluations were performed at ages 9, 10, and 12. Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling was indicated but results were unclear due to technical problems. At age 12, a 3T dynamic pituitary MRI with gadolinium demonstrated a 2.9 x 2.6 x 2.5 mm contrasting hypocaptive lesion in the adenohypophysis adjacent to the left cavernous sinus. The patient underwent transsphenoidal surgery at 12 years 11 months and received prednisone for two years postoperatively. After biochemical cure, she had persistent poor growth despite a responsive growth hormone test after glucagon stimulation, was treated with recombinant growth hormone, and was labeled as having idiopathic short stature. Final height was 1.41 m versus family target height 1.61 m.

A 48-year-old female with past history of hyperthyroidism not under treatment presented with 3 days of altered sensorium, abdominal pain, cough, fever, shortness of breath, loose stool and vomiting. On arrival: GCS 13/15, pulse 136/min, BP 80/50 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 90% on 10 L oxygen, temperature 102°F. Exam: thyroid swelling, bilateral pitting edema, jaundice; chest with bilateral crepitations; other systems unremarkable. BWPS 75. Labs: TLC 17,000/mm3, platelets 110,000/mm3, Hb 10 g/dl, urea 90 mg/dl, creatinine 1.8 mg/dl, Na/K normal; total bilirubin 6 mg/dl (direct 2.3), total protein 5.9 g/dl (albumin 2.9), ALT 356 U/L, AST 301 U/L. Thyroid tests: FT3 4.2 ng/dl, FT4 5 ng/dl, TSH ≤0.01 mIU/ml. Chest X-ray: bilateral pneumonia. Treated with IV fluids, vasopressors, broad-spectrum antibiotics, carbimazole and propranolol with gradual hemodynamic and mental status improvement; transferred out of ICU day 9; follow-up at 2 weeks with continued carbimazole.

A 57-year-old woman presented with an intra-abdominal mass. History of hypertension treated with an alpha-blocker (terazosin) and a calcium-channel blocker (amlodipine). Vitals at presentation: BP 126/57 mmHg, HR 98 bpm. Exam: non-tender spherical mass palpable in the right upper abdomen. Markedly elevated urinary catecholamines. Abdominal CT: large right adrenal mass (16 × 15 × 10 cm) with compression of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava; no clear invasion of surrounding tissues; adherent to but not involving the IVC wall. ECG: sinus rhythm. Echocardiography: normal ventricular function. Other labs and chest X-ray normal. Pre-op plan: multidisciplinary management; BP stabilized to ~120–130/65–85 mmHg with terazosin and amlodipine; no beta-blocker added; ASA class 2; surgery after 3 days of preparation. Intra-op: marked hemodynamic instability during tumor mobilization with hypertensive surges up to 255/158 mmHg and tachycardia up to 150 bpm; treated with phentolamine and sodium nitroprusside. Severe hypotension occurred during IVC clamping and after tumor removal/unclamping, requiring ~10 minutes of resuscitation with external cardiac massage, repeated boluses of epinephrine/norepinephrine, rapid volume expansion; massive blood loss (7300 mL); operative time 420 minutes. Post-op ICU stay 3 days; discharged day 9; hypertension resolved after tumor removal; follow-up showed normalization of urinary and blood catecholamines, aldosterone, and cortisol; R0 resection with clear margins on pathology.

A 62-year-old man with coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and depression with suicidal ideation was found poorly responsive. EMS glucose was 49 mg/dL with improved cognition after IV dextrose. Over the prior 24 hours he had loose stools, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and memory loss; family reported multiple pills missing from home medications (metformin, empagliflozin-metformin, glipizide).

On admission: BP 103/52 mmHg, HR 72, RR 18, temp 95.8 F; fatigue, weakness, confusion. WBC 13.6k/uL; infectious evaluation later negative (blood cultures, COVID-19 test, urinalysis), and empiric ceftriaxone was stopped. Creatinine 7.22 mg/dL and BUN 46 mg/dL indicated acute kidney injury. Lactate 7.1 mmol/L, pH 7.258 with anion gap 23 mmol/L indicated high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Acetaminophen level was 11.4 mcg/mL. Treated with N-acetylcysteine, bicarbonate, and octreotide. Metformin level returned elevated at 23 mcg/mL. CT abdomen/pelvis showed a nonobstructing calculus at the lower pole of the left kidney and mild perinephric stranding.

No improvement with volume; progressive worsening with new right-sided flank pain, abdominal distension, and left lower quadrant tenderness, declining urine output, vomiting, and diarrhea. Hemodialysis was initiated on hospital day 2 for persistent lactic acidosis and worsening renal function, with rapid improvement in acidosis and renal function after renal replacement therapy. Metformin was discontinued and he was discharged on insulin.

A 14-year-old female was the firstborn child of non-related, healthy parents, with no previous family genetic disorders and a healthy 9-year-old sibling. The mother was aged 20 years during conception, and the father was aged 26 years. Normal weight and height data were recorded throughout pregnancy. According to the parents, the patient appeared to be a healthy newborn, and the patient's development and growth was normal until her second year of age.

A 58-year-old woman was referred to clinical genetics. She had a mandibular swelling; biopsy showed an oncocytoma in the submandibular gland. She had multiple hemangiomas/cavernous malformations in the cerebrum and cerebellum, first diagnosed at age 48. Past history included pulmonary bullae diagnosed at age 35 after a spontaneous pneumothorax postpartum. At age 48 she developed a goitre and facial rash. Genetic testing identified heterozygous frameshift mutations in FLCN (c.158del, p.Gln53fs) and CCM2 (c.319C>T, p.Gln107*). Follow-up renal imaging showed multiple small kidney cysts and pulmonary bullae.

A 60-year-old woman with no past medical history and no prior surgeries presented with 4 days of abdominal pain and vomiting and 2 weeks of generalized weakness, minimal appetite, non-bloody non-bilious emesis, and periumbilical abdominal pain. On admission: HR 116, BP 96/59, RR 20, T 36.6 C. Exam: soft, non-distended but tender abdomen; erythema around the umbilicus with a yellow center draining serous fluid. Initial labs: Na 132, Cl 91, BUN 55, glucose 156, Cr 0.88, venous pH 7.46, pCO2 30, HCO3 21, lactate 3.3, anion gap 19, albumin 3.4. CT abdomen: umbilical hernia with incarcerated small bowel and free air consistent with perforated viscus. Treated with IV fluids and ertapenem and underwent exploratory laparotomy with washout of pus/feculent material and resection of 60 cm necrotic small bowel; required ICU care intubated on norepinephrine and propofol. Post-op day 1 ABG: pH 7.28, pCO2 33, HCO3 15.5, lactate 1.6, anion gap 18, albumin 2.8; persistent metabolic acidosis despite resuscitation. Repeat laparotomy showed no new perforation/necrosis. Additional labs: CK 29, serum osmolality 298, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L with normal blood sugars and no diabetes history. Metabolic acidosis resolved within 12 hours after starting 5% dextrose infusion. Subsequent surgery: ileocecectomy, end ileostomy, abdominal wall closure; later normalization of acid-base status.

An 80-year-old man presented with abdominal pain and nausea. Imaging (US/CT) showed a large right upper abdominal fluid collection and gallbladder stones. No history of abdominal surgery or trauma. Exam: slight right upper quadrant tenderness with palpable mass. Labs notable for low albumin (2.3 g/dL), elevated ESR (82 mm/h) and CRP (5.2 mg/dL), low calcium (7.7 mg/dL); viral hepatitis markers negative. Repeat CT showed a large right hepatic subcapsular collection (18.9 cm). MRI demonstrated multiple common bile duct stones with biliary tree dilatation and a large subcapsular fluid collection around the lower margin of the right hepatic lobe without direct communication with the biliary system. ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction was performed. US-guided percutaneous drainage aspirated 800 mL of bile-stained fluid; drain fluid bilirubin was markedly elevated (total 22.3 mg/dL, direct 18.9 mg/dL) and gram stain showed a Gram-negative bacillus. Persistent residual collection and continued drainage despite catheter placement prompted repeat ERCP, which showed contrast extravasation from a distal biliary radicle in the right hepatic lobe with communication to the collection. Placement of a common bile duct stent led to cessation of drainage; subsequent follow-up CT scans were normal.

Male twin neonate, birth weight 1970 g, born at 34 weeks + 2 days by caesarean section; admitted to NICU. Brief transient respiratory distress requiring a few hours of mechanical ventilation. Day 1: vital signs stable; abdomen soft without tenderness; abdominal radiograph showed slight pneumoperitoneum; no metabolic acidosis; C-reactive protein 0.05 mg/dL. Day 2: still vital signs stable but imaging showed increased free intraperitoneal gas; ultrasonography showed increasing ascites. Emergency diagnostic laparoscopy revealed turbid bilious ascites; no evidence of gastric, duodenal, or colonic perforation, suggesting a small-intestinal source. The small intestine was exteriorized; a perforated diverticular outpouching with intestinal fluid leaking from an everted tip was found and the involved segment was resected; remaining small intestine normal. Postoperative course uneventful. Pathology: no acute inflammation and no heterotopic mucosa.

Female patient with dyslipidemia (triglycerides up to 1,087 mg/dL) referred for dyspepsia attributed to an 8-mm esophageal granular cell benign tumor. Routine labs showed elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 69 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 154 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) 624 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 136 U/L. Family history of gastric cancer. Taking gastric protection medication 40 mg daily.

An 11-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a long history of abdominal pain, profound chronic constipation, and encopresis. Over 2 weeks he developed increasing abdominal pain with nausea and diminished appetite, unable to attend school or tolerate solid foods. On exam he was tachycardic, emaciated, with a hugely distended but nontender abdomen with palpable stool; he could not stand straight. Rectal exam showed the rectum filled with hard stool and blood at the anal verge. Abdominal X-ray confirmed severe stool burden. He was admitted after deterioration and received two 500 mL saline enemas; within 10 minutes of the second enema he acutely decompensated with a tense firm abdomen, sudden hypotension, escalating tachycardia, acute respiratory distress with tachypnea, accessory muscle use, oxygen saturation 79% on room air, and decreased mental status. Resuscitation included fluids, intubation/ventilation, and vasopressors with persistent instability. Chest X-ray showed severe elevation of both diaphragms with cardiac compression (false appearance of dextrocardia), decreased lung volumes, and compressed trachea. Abdominal imaging showed new air-fluid levels without free air. He underwent emergent manual fecal disimpaction; a large quantity of stool was evacuated under significant pressure with immediate improvement in hemodynamics and ventilation/oxygenation, allowing weaning off vasopressors and extubation 6 hours later; mottling/cool extremities and priapism resolved. Labs showed tissue hypoxia with metabolic and respiratory acidosis and early coagulopathy. Postoperative X-rays initially showed no free air. Approximately 36 hours later he developed free intraabdominal air; surgery found a pinhole perforation at the apex of an enormously dilated rectosigmoid and performed a Hartmann procedure with descending colostomy. Biopsies and investigations for congenital aganglionosis/other motility disorders were negative. He recovered and later had colostomy reversal; he remains well on daily PEG 3350.

Male in early 30s with a 2-year history of fistulizing inflammatory bowel disease unresponsive to mesalazine. Colonoscopy showed scattered ulcers, scars, and polypoid hyperplasia; colon histology showed crypt distortion and crypt abscesses. Started on adalimumab monotherapy (160 mg loading, then 80 mg every 2 weeks). Four months after starting therapy, developed multiple scaly erythematous eruptions and pustules on ankles, lower legs, knees, elbows, palms, and soles.
