Skin biopsy showed epidermal psoriasiform hyperplasia with Kogoj microabscesses, spongiotic intraepidermal vesicle with neutrophils, and dermal eosinophils. The biologic was stopped and switched to ustekinumab; treated with topical fluticasone. Lesions resolved within four months and bowel disease entered remission.

Systematic review of Australian case law (1981–2018) involving incidents in Australian hospitals where an item used during surgery was unintentionally left in a patient, including civil claims, criminal cases, medical disciplinary matters, and coronial cases. Cases where an item was intentionally left and later removed without incident and with no attributed harm were excluded. Searches used legal/health regulatory databases (e.g., LexisNexis, AustLII, Coroners’ Courts summaries, civil/administrative tribunal decisions, AHPRA board/panel tribunal hearing summaries) with terms relating to surgery/medical care, retention, adverse events, and counts. Cases were coded and narratively synthesised to identify antecedent risk patterns, estimate patient risk, explore prevention/mitigation strategies, and describe long-term patient impacts, using an accident causation framework (multiple system barriers/defences and failures).

19-year-old girl with 15-year history of gastrointestinal bleeding and persistent anemia (Hb down to 4 g/dL), positive fecal occult blood, and multiple cutaneous small vascular lesions on the feet. Multiple venous-appearing vascular malformations throughout the GI tract documented by colonoscopy, upper endoscopy, transanal double-balloon endoscopy, capsule endoscopy, and contrast-enhanced CT (stomach, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, colon), with additional lesions in right pleural space, hepatic hilum, liver, and spleen. Childhood history of repeated resections of hemangiolymphangiomas of the right thoracic wall. Prior laparotomy in childhood with multiple GI lesions; pathology showed cavernous hemangioma. Recurrent/worsening bleeding despite beta-blocker therapy and oral iron, requiring frequent transfusions. Imaging showed enlargement of known lesions. Underwent extensive surgical management with multiple enterotomies/gastrotomy/colotomy, wedge resections, ligation/resection, and argon plasma coagulation; >350 small-intestinal lesions treated; splenectomy with partial pancreatic resection due to invasion; ovarian cystectomy (mature teratoma). Postoperative endoscopy showed residual lesions in duodenum and colon; no bleeding or anemia for 5 years postoperatively.

Serum samples from a mother and her infant were obtained. First pregnancy in a 27-year-old woman of Eastern European origin with no significant medical history; pregnancy complicated by oligohydramnios, symmetrical intrauterine growth retardation, and reduced fetal movements. Term spontaneous vaginal delivery of a boy small for gestational age (2.270 kg; head circumference 33 cm); Apgar scores not recorded; placenta not examined; infant initially described as in good condition. Left hip dislocation noted.

At 2 days of age, evaluation for poor feeding and hypoglycaemia found jaundice with coagulopathy (INR 2.3; nv <1.2) resistant to parenteral vitamin K, and poor liver synthetic function (albumin 22 g/L; nr 35–50). Hepatic and renal indices worsened despite treatment for presumed sepsis; transferred to a paediatric liver centre at 7 days of age. Laboratory findings included markedly elevated ferritin (1481 ng/mL; nr 20–300), severe coagulopathy (INR 5.37), low albumin (26 g/L), AST 44 IU/L, ALT 30 IU/L, and total bilirubin 292 µmol/L (nr 3–20). Prior to transfusion: low total iron-binding capacity (28 µmol/L; nr 50–72) and high transferrin saturation (72%; nr 20–50%). Immunoglobulins: IgG 5.53 g/L, IgM 0.63 g/L, IgA 0.63 g/L. Autoantibody testing detected antimitochondrial antibodies in serum from the child and mother.

At 12 days of age, a lower lip mucosa biopsy showed haemosiderin granules within submucosal acinar gland cells. Treated with intravenous desferrioxamine, sodium selenite pentahydrate, and N-acetylcysteine, plus blood/blood-product transfusions; received intravenous immunoglobulin at 10 and 16 days and a single-volume exchange transfusion at 21 days. Due to poor clinical status, listed for liver transplantation at 12 days; received a split liver allograft at 30 days. Explanted liver showed postnecrotic cirrhosis with canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis.

Post-transplant course: slow recovery; isolated episode of lip smacking; MRI showed normal brain structures with turricephaly; discharged at 92 days. Hip dislocation treated at 10 months. Food allergy (milk, wheat, egg) diagnosed at 13 months. EBV infection with high viraemia and later febrile upper respiratory illness with lymphadenopathy; improved with immunosuppression adjustment; normal development at 22 months without evidence of hepatobiliary disease though EBV viraemia persisted.

Serial serum samples from child (presentation through 17 months, pre/post transplant) and mother (at infant presentation and 4 and 10 months postpartum) were tested for autoantibodies using indirect immunofluorescence on rat tissues and HEp-2 cells and immunoassays (ELISAs, line immunoassay, Western blot) including assays for mitochondrial antigens (PDC-E2, BCOADC-E2, OGDC-E2) and IgG subclass-specific reactivity.

A 43-year-old male presented with 1 day of fatigue and 2 days of fainting, cold sweats, and black stool. No known chronic disease or regular medication use. One week earlier he had received leech therapy to the lumbar and lower abdomen for infertility treatment, with five bite sites in the lumbar region and four in the suprapubic region. On arrival: BP 97/56 mmHg, HR 115/min, SpO2 96%, temperature 35.3°C; ECG showed sinus tachycardia. He was pale, cold, and diaphoretic; abdominal exam normal; melena on rectal exam. Labs: hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL (MCV 89 fL), platelets 179,000/µL, aPTT 25.6 s, PT/INR 1.1; hemoglobin dropped to 6.1 g/dL one hour later; liver and kidney function tests normal. Treated with IV saline (500 mL/h) and IV pantoprazole bolus then infusion; hypotension persisted despite fluids, requiring transfusion of erythrocytes and fresh-frozen plasma with hemodynamic stabilization during the second unit. Gastroduodenoscopy showed hyperemic, edematous gastric fundus/corpus/antrum mucosa and deformity of the pylorus and bulb. No re-bleeding occurred during hospitalization; discharged after 7 days without complications.

A 74-year-old man presented with sudden-onset behavioral abnormalities (indoor urination and poriomania). Brain MRI previously ruled out intracranial lesions. Psychiatric disorder was suspected and quetiapine was tried without improvement. EEG showed generalized continuous slow waves. Blood tests showed marked hyperammonemia (218 microg/dL), later fluctuating with mild-to-moderate elevations (e.g., 135 microg/dL) despite normal consciousness and no focal neurologic deficits or signs of chronic liver disease/cirrhosis (including no asterixis). Family intermittently witnessed abnormal behaviors. He had severe constipation and regularly used laxatives. Abdominal contrast CT demonstrated large portosystemic venous shunts: a right portal-to-middle hepatic vein shunt and a left portal-to-left hepatic vein shunt. Managed conservatively with advice to maintain laxative use and hydration to prevent constipation/dehydration; remained symptom-free on follow-up.

Male child, 6 years old, with sudden onset dyspnea for 8 hours prompting emergency visit. Perinatal/neonatal exams normal. Prior visit for “bronchitis” 1 year earlier; no abnormality on auscultation then. On presentation: nasal flaring, positive triple concave sign, tachycardia 140/min, tachypnea 53/min, oxygen saturation 87% on room air. Chest X-ray and CT showed stomach displaced into the thoracic cavity with marked gastric distension causing mediastinal shift; left lung compressed/atelectatic and positioned superior to the intrathoracic stomach. Initial nasogastric decompression attempt unsuccessful due to distress; later successful decompression after anesthesia with release of large amount of gas and ~400 mL gastric contents. Thoracoscopic surgery performed; intraoperatively colon, spleen, and stomach were herniated through a small diaphragmatic defect; organs reduced to abdomen and diaphragmatic defect repaired. Postoperative radiographs normal; uneventful recovery and 1-year follow-up without vomiting, abdominal pain, or respiratory distress.

In November 2024 at a hospital in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, a 27-year-old systemically healthy male was referred from an endodontic clinic after auto-transplantation of tooth #28 to replace a non-restorable tooth. Clinical examination showed a single isolated deep buccal recession (8 mm) with buccal probing depth 1 mm and buccal clinical attachment loss 9 mm, no bleeding on probing, no interproximal attachment loss, and absence of keratinized tissue apically. Minimal keratinized tissue at the site caused discomfort during brushing; adjacent area had a wide band of keratinized tissue (~4 mm) and a shallow vestibular depth. Pre-surgical oral hygiene instruction and supragingival prophylaxis were provided. Surgical management included partial-thickness flap with vertical incision, root surface preparation, harvesting a palatal graft (8 mm x 24 mm) with half left epithelized and half de-epithelized, placement with epithelized portion over tooth #25 and de-epithelized connective tissue portion over the recession site, flap repositioned laterally/coronally to cover the connective tissue, and suturing. Post-op care included chlorhexidine rinses, soft diet, ibuprofen, and suture removal at 14 days. At 6-week follow-up, keratinized tissue increased by ~3 mm, gingival thickness increased, and approximately 25% root coverage was achieved.

23-year-old female with discolored maxillary right central incisor. History of malaligned tooth and orthodontic treatment completed 2 years ago. Negative response to vitality tests. Mild pain on percussion and palpation. Digital periapical radiograph shows obliterated canal with diffuse periapical radiolucency. Yellowish-grey crown discoloration. Periodontal pocket depth normal. Endodontic access revealed calcification; canal located with explorer and patency achieved with size 08 K-file; working length determined radiographically; cleaning and shaping to size 30/.04 with rotary files; irrigated with 3% sodium hypochlorite and 15% EDTA alternating with saline; obturated with gutta-percha and calcium hydroxide–based sealer using cold lateral condensation. Coronal GP removed 2–3 mm below canal orifice and covered with glass ionomer barrier. Internal bleaching performed using 35% hydrogen peroxide gel in pulp chamber with sealed access; repeated three times at 5-day intervals until satisfactory shade achieved; final composite restoration placed 7–10 days later.

A 70-year-old woman with pancreatic cancer underwent pancreaticoduodenectomy and required postoperative nutritional support with enteral feeding. She developed a postoperative small-bowel obstruction identified on day 5 and required surgical intervention; she was managed in critical care with vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, and was receiving octreotide. Concomitant medications included laxatives. She was ultimately discharged home alive after a prolonged hospitalization (37 days).

A 78-year-old man presented with repeated vomiting for 4 days. CT showed a duodenal tumor with multiple liver masses. Barium contrast study demonstrated severe stenosis in the third portion of the duodenum. Curative resection was not indicated, so palliative laparoscopic gastric partitioning gastrojejunostomy was performed. Postoperatively, diet was resumed on day 4 and imaging on day 8 showed good patency through the anastomosis. A posterior lobe cerebral infarction occurred on postoperative day 12; no delayed gastric emptying occurred. Discharged on postoperative day 30.

A breast papillary carcinoma subtype characterized by slow biological activity and gradual progression, typically luminal type, Nottingham grade 2, and low TNM stage. Compared with invasive ductal carcinoma, it shows more favorable pathology with lower tumor T stage, lower axillary lymph node metastasis rates (~11.6%–17.25% vs ~32.6%–50%), lower Ki-67, higher hormone receptor positivity, and lower HER2 amplification; larger tumor size and lymphovascular invasion are less prevalent. Reported case: 59-year-old with ~10-year natural history; large primary tumor (~10.4 × 7.2 × 3.5 cm) grew <2 cm over a decade without treatment, no distant metastases; IHC stable with ER/PR positive, HER2 (C-erbB2) negative, Ki-67 ~10%. Genomic features in papillary carcinoma subtypes show similarities (loss of 16q; gain of 16p and 1q), fewer aberrations and minimal p53 expression; PIK3CA mutations in ~40% have been observed; transcriptomic differences relate to cell adhesion/migration genes. Organoid drug sensitivity testing in a papillary carcinoma case showed high efficacy of fulvestrant among tested endocrine therapies.
diagnosis: Invasive papillary carcinoma of the breast

case_information: A 66-year-old male status post heart transplant on chronic immunosuppression (prednisone, tacrolimus, mycophenolate) presented with a gradually enlarging right neck mass and swelling of right preauricular, submandibular, and cervical lymph nodes. Labs showed mild leukocytosis. Fine needle aspiration was nondiagnostic; excisional lymph node biopsy showed a high-grade B-cell lymphoid neoplasm with CD20 positivity and a Ki-67 proliferation index of ~90%. CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis demonstrated lymphadenopathy in the right parotid and submandibular areas extending toward the floor of mouth and in the right cervical region; PET showed corresponding hypermetabolic uptake in the neck. Bone marrow biopsy/aspiration was negative. HIV, EBV, CMV, and hepatitis testing were negative. Ann Arbor stage IA. Immunosuppression was reduced (prednisone decreased, tacrolimus decreased, mycophenolate stopped). Treated with rituximab-based multiagent chemotherapy with initial complete remission followed by early local relapse; received salvage chemotherapy with progression and ulcerated/necrotic local disease; treated with radiation with transient response then progression; subsequent rituximab-based chemotherapy produced partial remission; underwent high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplant and achieved complete clinical remission without recurrence.

A 27-year-old woman, 16 weeks pregnant, with beta-thalassemia major treated with monthly blood transfusions and previously on deferoxamine (stopped due to pregnancy), status post splenectomy (2009), presented with swelling of the gums since early pregnancy, gingival bleeding, and halitosis. She had never previously visited a dentist. She was hospitalized for severe knee pain with inability to move and had fever; overall condition was weak.

Intraoral exam: diffuse gingival overgrowth with erythema, soft consistency, dark red rounded gingival margins, tenderness, and easy bleeding on labial/buccal/palatal/lingual areas; poor oral hygiene (OHIS 5.7); true periodontal pockets in all regions. Peripheral blood smear showed moderate anemia consistent with thalassemia, increased erythropoiesis activity, and suspected infection. Management involved multidisciplinary care with oral hygiene instruction, 3% hydrogen peroxide irrigation, chlorine dioxide mouthwash, petroleum jelly to lips, antibiotics (amoxicillin and metronidazole), and later scaling/root planing after systemic condition improved, with progressive resolution over ~3 months and no remaining oral complaints at follow-up.

A 72-year-old man with over 1 year of persistent left upper abdominal pain and anemia, and new-onset hypertension for 6 months. Physical exam showed epigastric discomfort and pallor. Prior GI endoscopy with biopsy at another center suggested adenocarcinoma of the gastric antrum. CT showed enlarged lymph nodes along the lesser curvature. PET/CT demonstrated thickened gastric antrum wall with a concave configuration, increased FDG uptake, invasion to the plasma membrane surface, and a posterior-wall lesion extending from the antrum to the upper lesser-curvature side, about 10×8 cm, with ulcerated infiltrate, irregular surrounding mucosa, and involvement of the gastric serosa. Treated with neoadjuvant oxaliplatin plus tegafur for three cycles with reduction in primary tumor size and lymph node shrinkage, then underwent radical gastrectomy. Intraoperatively, blood pressure fluctuated persistently >140 mmHg, peaking at 240 mmHg. Resection margins were repeatedly positive requiring extended resection, ultimately leading to total gastrectomy with negative margins; D2 lymph node dissection performed. Pathology: 1/11 lesser-curvature lymph nodes positive; other sampled nodes negative; pTNM pT2N1Mx. Histology showed tumor cells with round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, clear cytoplasmic borders; Ki-67 ~40%+. Immunohistochemistry: CK (AE1/AE3)+, CgA+, INSM1+; Syn−, CD56−. Postoperative catecholamine/metabolite testing showed most values within reference range but methoxy norepinephrine mildly elevated initially, later normalized on follow-up. No evidence of metastases at 7 months post-op.

A 48-year-old African American female with no contributory medical history presented with a red, 6.0 x 3.0 cm ulcerated palatal mass causing bone destruction and exposed dental roots, extending to the vestibular area of the right maxilla. Teeth were completely movable. No other lesions and no palpable lymph nodes. Radiographs showed a radiolucent lesion with floating right maxillary molars. Incisional biopsy showed an atypical round cell infiltrate; flow cytometry demonstrated monoclonal kappa-restricted B cells positive for CD20 and CD45, with Ki-67 and Bcl-2 positivity.

ESMO reported KEYNOTE-826 showing improved median progression-free survival with addition of pembrolizumab in advanced disease with PD-L1 CPS >1. Tumor tissue underwent next-generation sequencing and PD-L1 testing (results 2021-12-07): tumor mutational burden 25.27 Mut/Mb, microsatellite status stable (MSS), PD-L1 immunohistochemistry CPS 94. Based on these results, an immune checkpoint inhibitor (atezolizumab) was added in combination with the TP chemotherapy regimen on 2021-12-19. The patient developed thrombocytopenia with a platelet nadir of 25×10^9/L on day 10 post-treatment, which rose to 81×10^9/L after thrombopoietin treatment. Post-cycle CT showed marked reduction in bilateral pleural effusion and decrease in size of the cervical lesion; overall assessed as stable disease with a trend toward reduction.

A 31-year-old male with asthma and obesity presented with a progressively enlarging, increasingly painful left breast mass first noticed ~3 years prior. Exam showed a large, soft, uniform palpable left breast mass with enlarged superficial veins and inferior deviation of the nipple without discharge; no skin discoloration, dimpling, or thickening. He denied abnormal sexual features/function, trauma, and family history of breast disorders/cancer. Tumor markers and other labs were within normal limits. Bilateral mammogram showed a large encapsulated fatty mass occupying most of the left breast with central parenchymal distortion/asymmetry; ~20 cm diameter; BI-RADS 4; right breast normal. Focused ultrasound showed a hypoechoic mass at the 12 o’clock position. Surgical management included intra-operative US-guided core needle biopsy and left total mastectomy; core biopsy showed scant fragments of blood. Final pathology: benign nipple and unremarkable skin with a benign fat-containing tumor and fat necrosis.

62-year-old man with 2-month history of dysphagia; gastroscopy biopsy showed thoracic esophageal malignancy treated with radical esophagectomy (pathologic stage T2N0M0 IB) followed by adjuvant docetaxel-based chemotherapy complicated by recurrent severe thrombocytopenia responsive to recombinant human thrombopoietin, leading to chemotherapy discontinuation. In Jan 2021 developed recurrent dysphagia and CT showed metastatic disease (liver, cervical lymph node, and gastroesophageal anastomosis); tumor tissue showed PD-L1 positivity (TPS 10%, CPS 20) and was treated with camrelizumab plus cisplatin/5-FU but again developed grade 4 thrombocytopenia responsive to thrombopoietin; chemotherapy stopped and camrelizumab monotherapy continued with normal platelets. Due to progressive dysphagia, received intensity-modulated radiotherapy (54 Gy/28 fractions) to cervical nodes and anastomosis starting Mar 11, 2021. After combined immune checkpoint inhibitor and radiotherapy, platelet count rapidly fell to <25×10^9/L; thrombopoietin was ineffective; bone marrow aspiration excluded central etiology; oral corticosteroids (1 mg/kg/day) plus thrombopoietin started at platelets 20×10^9/L without recovery. Surgical specimen showed abundant CD68+ macrophages; NGS identified TP53 mutation (p.L114A) and increased copy number of KRAS and JAK2; JAK2 expression confirmed in tumor cells by immunohistochemistry/immunofluorescence. Dysphagia improved with radiotherapy but imaging showed progressive metastatic disease with new lung lesions and worsening diffuse liver involvement; developed fatigue, polypnea, rapid progression, then multiple organ failure and death.

A 51-year-old woman with a rare malignant salivary gland tumor that clinically mimicked a benign lesion. Histopathology showed epithelial clusters within large pools of extracellular mucin comprising most of the lesion, with prominent mucinous differentiation. Considerations included excluding mucoepidermoid carcinoma and the mucin-rich variant of salivary duct carcinoma. Tumor classification context referenced 2017 WHO grouping of mucinous-type lesions under adenocarcinoma not otherwise specified (NOS).

An 86-year-old male presented with acute shortness of breath and several months of unexplained weight loss. He had recent high-impact falls with a right femoral subcapital fracture treated by right hip hemiarthroplasty. Exam showed peripheral edema and hypoxia without fever or night sweats. Labs: elevated alkaline phosphatase and D-dimer; chronically low hemoglobin without acute drop; normal white cell count, neutrophils, and C-reactive protein. Chest radiograph unremarkable. Contrast CT abdomen/pelvis revealed a large heterogeneous complex cystic hypoenhancing left retroperitoneal mass posterior to the left kidney (13 x 12 x 24 cm; mixed density 9–32 HU) displacing the kidney and encasing left renal vasculature/collecting system at the hilum causing mild hydronephrosis. MRI showed heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity with multicystic areas, multiple T1 hyperintense foci consistent with hemorrhagic content, signal loss on out-of-phase chemical shift imaging indicating microscopic lipid, diffusion restriction in peripheral solid components, and avid enhancement of solid components post-contrast. Ultrasound-guided biopsy pathology confirmed the diagnosis; due to advanced age and frailty, no further management pursued.

A 71-year-old man from Sur de Bolivar, Colombia, with no known medical history, presented with 1 day of psychomotor agitation and incoherent speech. Initial outside labs showed moderate normocytic anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, and a thick smear reportedly positive for Plasmodium vivax; he was referred for suspected complicated infection with neurologic involvement. On arrival he was disoriented and somnolent without meningeal signs or focal deficits; non-contrast brain imaging was unremarkable. Labs showed elevated BUN, severe anemia with non-immune hemolysis markers, schistocytes on peripheral smear, and severe thrombocytopenia; repeat thick smear was negative. He was treated in the ICU with IV artesunate and supportive transfusions, but continued to have persistent neurologic, renal, and hematologic abnormalities with high transfusion requirements. Ongoing labs demonstrated a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia pattern and a high PLASMIC score suggesting severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. He improved markedly after initiation of plasma exchange and high-dose steroids, with recovery of neurologic status, renal function, and hemolysis indices. ADAMTS13 activity returned <0.1%, and relapse-prevention immunosuppression with rituximab was added; after multiple plasma exchanges and rituximab doses, platelets normalized and anemia/hemolysis and renal injury resolved, and he was discharged without neurologic deficits.

30-year-old male with multiple sclerosis on subcutaneous interferon beta-1a (44 mcg three times weekly) for 3 months, presented with massive epistaxis and ecchymoses. No trauma or GI/urinary bleeding. Vitals stable; oriented. Labs showed anemia (RBC ~2.77 mil/cu mm, Hgb 8 g/dL, Hct 25%, MCV 75 fL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 48,000), and acute kidney injury (urea 91 mg/dL, creatinine 3.3 mg/dL) with normal PT/PTT/INR. Reticulocyte count 0.3%; LDH 1050 U/L. UA unremarkable; echocardiography normal; liver tests and bilirubin normal. Infectious serologies (HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV, EBV), ASO, cultures, PPD, Wright/2ME negative. Direct/indirect Coombs negative; malignancy workup negative. Thyroid tests normal. Repeat labs over several days showed persistent cytopenias and elevated urea/creatinine; 24-hour urine studies normal. Peripheral smear: markedly decreased platelets; severe hypochromic RBCs with mild anisocytosis; WBC normal. Bone marrow aspirate/biopsy: good cellularity (~50%), decreased M/E ratio, blasts <5%, no dysplasia, increased megakaryocytes, no malignancy. Imaging normal. Autoimmune tests (ANA, complements, CH50, c/p-ANCA, anti-dsDNA, serum protein electrophoresis) normal. Kidney biopsy non-significant. Treated with prednisone, folic acid, vitamin B12; received packed RBCs and IV fluids. After stopping interferon beta-1a, CBC and renal function improved markedly within 2 days and normalized within 7 days.

A 30-year-old woman was admitted in 1994 for hematuria. A papillomatous bladder tumor was removed by transurethral resection. Histology showed papillomatous transitional epithelium without cellular atypia and no infiltrative growth in the subepithelial connective tissue. Recurrent bladder tumors were resected at 12 months (1995), 48 months (1999), 72 months (2001), 108 months (2004), and again in 2006; each showed a similar histologic pattern without infiltrative growth or progression in atypia. In December 2007, a right ovarian tumor and a left ovarian nodule were found and surgically removed; at the same time, small papillomas of the urinary bladder were endoscopically removed. Grossly, the right ovary was a 30 cm unilocular cyst containing bright yellow serous fluid, smooth externally with partial internal papillomatous vegetations. Microscopy showed a cyst with endoluminal papillae covered by transitional-type epithelium similar to the bladder tumors, without stromal invasion; the left ovarian nodule had similar histology. The uterus was normal. Immunohistochemistry on both the ovarian tumor and the recurrent bladder tumor: diffuse cytokeratin 7 positivity and cytokeratin 20 negativity. Post-operatively, there was no bladder tumor recurrence at 7 months.
diagnosis: Low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder

case_information: Observation of 39 patients with a neurodevelopmental genetic syndrome involving 16q24.3 deletions and pathogenic variants in ANKRD11: macrodontia not consistently present; some patients may live autonomously in adulthood; autism reported less frequently than previously thought. Two additional reported clinical findings include precocious puberty and a case of malignancy. ANKRD11 reported as a novel p53-interacting protein enhancing p53 transcriptional activity; ANKRD11 expression downregulated in breast cancer cell lines. A 17-year-old with left-sided paratesticular extrarenal malignant rhabdoid tumor had genetic testing showing a constitutional de novo 16q24.3 microdeletion with loss of the entire ANKRD11 locus. Speculation that ANKRD11 haploinsufficiency may increase cancer risk; currently no specific cancer surveillance recommendations due to insufficient data.

Adult female admitted March 2023 with nosebleed and headache. Prior sinus MRI showed bilateral sphenoid sinus and left ethmoid sinus tumors. Underwent surgical resection with macroscopic residual disease (R2 resection). Postoperative histopathology and immunohistochemistry: CKP+, CK8+, BRG-1+, SOX2+; partial P63+, Syn+, CD99+; INI-1−, CD56−, CgA−, S100−, SOX10−, calretinin−, NF−, GFAP−, NKX2.2−, PAX5−, TTF-1−, Bcl2−, vimentin−. Ki-67 ~70%. Stage examination: pT4N0M0.

10-month-old infant with 2 days of fever, vomiting, and diarrhea referred for blood test abnormalities. No relevant family history and no prior chronic symptoms (no liver/behavioral/psychiatric issues, no growth or developmental delay). Marked leukocytosis with anemia and mild thrombocytopenia; elevated CRP; hepatosplenomegaly and pigmented papules on extremities. Peripheral blood with very high WBC, monocytosis, elevated fetal hemoglobin, mild transaminase/GGT elevation. Bone marrow: hypercellular marrow, absent megakaryocytes, ~5% blasts, decreased mature granulocytes, no monoclonal proliferation; colony assay with spontaneous colony growth and hypersensitivity to GM-CSF. Somatic NRAS mutation (c.35G>A; p.G12D) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells; normal karyotype; no germline NRAS mutation.

Underwent conditioning and allogeneic cord blood transplant; early course notable for CMV pneumonia, pulmonary hypertension, hypertension, tubulopathy and nephrotic syndrome. Later developed gradual cytopenias and evidence of relapse with NRAS mutation reappearing. Started mercaptopurine, followed immediately by nausea/vomiting, hyperventilation, decreased vitality and impaired consciousness. Severe hyperammonemia (ammonia 472 µmol/L) with respiratory alkalosis (pCO2 23.8 mmHg). Treated with sodium phenylacetate, sodium benzoate, and L-arginine with rapid normalization of ammonia and symptom resolution; mercaptopurine discontinued. Plasma amino acids: high glutamate with normal citrulline; urine organic acids: high orotic acid. Genetic testing identified an OTC gene mutation (c.119G>A; p.Arg40His). Subsequently maintained on nitrogen scavenger therapy and protein restriction without recurrent hyperammonemia; later received bridging therapy and a second allogeneic transplant with peri-transplant nitrogen scavenger coverage without another hyperammonemia episode; normal neurodevelopment and sustained remission.

A 74-year-old woman with diabetes presented to the Emergency Department with high fever and prostration. She had three recent admissions for acute urinary retention attributed to an infection despite negative urine cultures. On admission: C-reactive protein 16.7 mg/dL, creatinine 2.42 mg/dL, and marked pyuria (>70 cells/high-power field). Kidney ultrasound showed heterogeneous deposits in both upper renal calyces with absent Doppler color flow. Blood cultures were negative; urine culture grew fluconazole-resistant Candida glabrata. She was treated with intravenous caspofungin and was referred for bilateral nephrostomies with local amphotericin instillations due to concern for worsening renal function with systemic amphotericin B. She refused the procedural intervention and died.

A 40-year-old male with no medical history presented with persistent fever for five days. No cough, sore throat, hemoptysis, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, joint pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, rigors, night sweats, weight loss, recent travel, or sick contacts. Exam: temperature 38.2°C; few crackles on auscultation of the right upper lobe. Labs: microcytic anemia and elevated C-reactive protein. Chest radiograph: hazy opacities and inhomogeneous infiltrations in the right upper lung zone. Infectious workup: blood and sputum cultures obtained; two AFB smears negative. Blood culture (1/1) grew Streptococcus cristatus after one day; sputum gram stain showed polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Treated with IV ceftriaxone for seven days; echocardiography showed no valvular vegetation; repeat blood cultures after 72 hours showed no growth. Discharged on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate; asymptomatic at one-month follow-up.

A 32-year-old Japanese male undergoing intensive chemotherapy with dasatinib for acute leukemia achieved complete remission, then during consolidation therapy developed high fever (39.2°C) and severe rapidly worsening lower back pain radiating to the right axilla with profound neutropenia (WBC 430/mm3). Initial CT showed no clear abnormalities, but FDG-PET demonstrated increased uptake in the iliac bones and right sacrum, suggesting osteomyelitis. Needle aspiration biopsy of the iliac bone showed Gram-positive bacteria; blood cultures also showed Gram-positive organisms that were initially not identifiable. Direct 16S rRNA sequencing of blood culture identified Clostridium innocuum, confirmed by culture from iliac crest bone marrow. The organism was resistant to vancomycin (MIC 8 µg/mL) and susceptible to ampicillin, piperacillin/tazobactam, meropenem, clindamycin, and metronidazole. Treated with piperacillin/tazobactam, metronidazole, and clindamycin with gradual fever resolution; persistent lumbar pain led to CT detection of a small iliacus muscle abscess requiring CT-guided drainage (cultures negative). After prolonged antibiotics, pain resolved and chemotherapy was restarted.

9-year-old boy with recent close household exposure to confirmed COVID-19 (mother and younger sister PCR-positive ~3 weeks prior); he had a brief earlier episode of low-grade fever and mild URI symptoms around that time but was not tested.

Current illness: 8 days of fever progressing from intermittent to persistent despite antipyretics; 5 days of abdominal pain with watery yellow diarrhea progressing to vomiting and anorexia; fatigue and decreased urination; occasional dry cough. Developed bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection and red full lips; white coating on tongue; itchy pink blanching maculopapular rash on palms, soles, and left knee; bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (mobile, smooth, nontender, 1.5–3 cm). No chest pain, shortness of breath, neurologic deficits, mucocutaneous desquamation, petechiae, or eschar.

Initial evaluations elsewhere: treated with amoxicillin for presumed tonsillitis without improvement; later labeled gastroenteritis; later suspected sepsis/typhoid. Labs at private clinic: lymphopenia 0.6×10^9/L (5%), granulocytosis 11.8×10^9/L (91.8%), slightly elevated CRP; dengue and scrub typhus antigen tests negative; abdominal ultrasound normal.

On admission: T 39.4°C, RR 50, HR 150, SpO2 95% RA (later 93% requiring 1 L/min O2); BP later noted 90/60. Fatigued but initially alert; mild intercostal retractions; reduced heart sounds; generalized abdominal tenderness with RUQ guarding; no hepatosplenomegaly.

Hospital course/investigations: cultures (blood, throat, urine, stool) negative; repeated SARS-CoV-2 rapid test/GeneXpert/RT-PCR negative during admission; chest x-ray mild cardiomegaly with clear lungs; echocardiogram showed mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function (EF ~45–51%) with no coronary artery dilatation; ECG normal; urinalysis unremarkable. Later outpatient SARS-CoV-2 IgG positive.

Treatment and response: clinical worsening on day 9 led to IVIG 2 g/kg once + methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 3 days + low-dose aspirin; brief empiric antibiotics. Fever and systemic symptoms improved within 24–48 hours; tachycardia/tachypnea resolved, oxygen no longer required; lymphopenia and LV dysfunction resolved; discharged after 5 days on aspirin. Post-discharge: transient knee pain and transient bilateral foot swelling; follow-up CBC/CRP normalized and ESR improved; repeat echocardiograms normal.

A 48-year-old woman with 5 months of vaginal itching and white liquid vaginal discharge, refractory to multiple empiric treatments for presumed yeast infection (oral fluconazole, topical clotrimazole, tioconazole ointment, and intravaginal boric acid). Past history includes mild gastritis (on omeprazole) and irregular uterine bleeding controlled with transdermal estrogen/progesterone hormone therapy. Monogamous with husband; abstinent for several months due to symptom severity. Exam showed vaginal erythema and white liquid discharge. Vaginal discharge culture grew Paecilomyces lilacinus in pure culture (no baseline KOH). Treated with itraconazole 200 mg orally twice daily for 3 weeks with complete resolution of discharge and marked improvement of pruritus; 6 months later remained asymptomatic with negative vaginal fungal culture and negative KOH. Immune evaluation unremarkable: normal serum protein electrophoresis with IgG/IgA/IgM, normal C3/C4, ESR, CBC, CD4/CD8 counts; HIV antibody negative; anergy panel reactive. Isolate sent for species confirmation and antifungal susceptibility testing using standardized broth macrodilution methods and temperature-dependent growth studies on fungal media.
diagnosis: Fungal vaginitis due to Paecilomyces lilacinus

case_information: 52-year-old African American man with HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy (emtricitabine/tenofovir and ritonavir-boosted darunavir) with CD4 399 cells/µL (22%) and undetectable viral load. History of recurrent genital ulcerative disease with incomplete response to prolonged oral therapy and suppressive therapy; recurrent episodes despite courses of oral medication, chronic suppression, and subsequent intravenous cidofovir without significant improvement. Treated with a 21-day course of intravenous foscarnet plus topical imiquimod with partial response, then resumed oral therapy; after four months developed four tumorous/exophytic, nontender nodular lesions (1–2 cm) on the left scrotum and a 5 cm perineal mass. Routine CBC and metabolic profile normal. Restarted intravenous foscarnet (40 mg/kg twice daily) plus topical imiquimod; biopsy obtained due to concern for malignancy. Biopsy showed ulcerated epidermis with acute inflammation and prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate; epidermal cells at ulcer base with viral cytopathic changes and multinucleated giant cells; immunostains positive for HSV-1 and HSV-2. CMV immunostain, EBV (EBER) in situ hybridization, GMS and Fite stains negative; viral cultures negative. No significant lesion size change after two weeks of foscarnet. Leflunomide 20 mg orally twice daily added while continuing foscarnet and imiquimod, leading to ~80% reduction in perineal lesion size; continued leflunomide after discharge with ongoing improvement and near-complete resolution by nine months.
diagnosis: Acyclovir-resistant anogenital herpes simplex virus infection

case_information: A 38-year-old man with HIV infection diagnosed in 2016 on intermittent antiviral therapy, on boosted protease inhibitor (darunavir/ritonavir) monotherapy for 6 months, presented with 2 weeks of acute diarrhoea occurring 10–20 times/day, non-bloody and non-mucoid, associated with significant weight loss and cramping abdominal pain. No recent travel or raw/uncooked food intake. Exam: hypovolemia/dehydration with significant cachexia, hyperactive bowel sounds, no abdominal tenderness, normal digital rectal exam. Labs: mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia; CD4 <20, very high viral load; slightly elevated urea without creatinine elevation; blood cultures negative. Stool cultures grew a bacterial organism on two separate occasions; susceptibility showed intermediate sensitivity to ciprofloxacin and high sensitivity to erythromycin. Treated with oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days with complete symptom resolution and subsequent negative stool cultures. Later developed nosocomial pneumonia, colitis due to another pathogen, and disseminated opportunistic infection, and died from respiratory failure due to severe pneumonia 4 weeks after admission.

In October 2019, a 51-year-old woman from rural Santander, Colombia presented with 5 days of fever and shivers with epigastric pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and one episode of hematemesis. Past history included hypertension and dyslipidemia; medications: enalapril, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, and aspirin. Exam showed hemodynamic instability with tachycardia, hypotension requiring vasopressors, delayed capillary refill, dehydration, petechiae on extremities, bilateral basal rales, and painful hepatomegaly (4 cm). Labs: pancytopenia with severe thrombocytopenia (7,000/mm3), marked transaminase elevation (~50× normal), LDH >1000, normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; prolonged PTT with normal PT. Imaging: chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound with free fluid in abdomen and pleural effusion; hepatomegaly. Echocardiography reported bubbles in right-sided chambers without shunt. Doppler/CT portal venous phase showed acute complete non-cirrhotic thrombosis in proximal portal vein. Anti-DENV-1 IgM ELISA positive. Required ICU care with vasopressors for 11 days for distributive shock; treated with steroids for suspected immune thrombocytopenia and started on LMWH once platelets >70,000/mm3; received piperacillin-tazobactam for 7 days starting day 6. Extensive workup for other hemorrhagic fever syndromes/infections (blood/urine/stool cultures; malaria, Chagas; hepatitis A/B/C; CMV; HIV; leptospira) and for thrombotic microangiopathy/inherited/acquired thrombophilia (APS, protein C/S, factor V Leiden, homocysteine, antithrombin III, ADAMTS13) was negative; no hemolysis on smear; C3 low with normal C4; ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA negative. At 8-week follow-up Doppler and lab abnormalities normalized; steroids and anticoagulation stopped after 3 months.

Patient had resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid. No clinical or mycobacterial improvement after 2 weeks of first-line regimen (RHZE). Developed cervical lymph node involvement. Did not return for follow-up and died shortly after hospitalization.

43-year-old woman with 6 months of low-grade fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, migratory arthralgias of arms and legs, xerostomia and dry eyes, weight loss, and fatigue. CT and excisional biopsy of a left axillary lymph node performed for lymphadenopathy. Initial histology showed follicular-pattern lymphoid hyperplasia suspicious for follicular lymphoma; immunohistochemistry: preserved nodal architecture, high Ki-67 in germinal centers, predominantly CD20+ cells in germinal centers with Bcl-2 negativity in most germinal-center cells, paracortical CD3+ T-cell predominance, CD30 positive only in rare immunoblasts, HIV p24 negative; no cytologic atypia; interpreted as mixed (cortical and paracortical) hyperplasia without malignant lymphoproliferative disease. Exam: enlarged movable cervical (~1.5 cm), submandibular and right axillary (~2 cm) lymph nodes, painless to mildly tender. CBC and blood chemistry normal. Ophthalmology/dental evaluation: keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia; unstimulated whole saliva flow 0.06 mL/min; Schirmer test 2 mm/5 min. Autoantibodies: ANA positive; anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB (including SS-A 52/60 IgG and SS-B IgG) positive; dsDNA, anti-ribosomal P, anticentromere, Sm, Sm/RNP, RNP, Scl-70, Jo-1 negative. History of tick bite 1 year prior; no rash noted. Serology for Borrelia: enzyme immunoassay and Western blot positive for anti-Borrelia burgdorferi IgG and IgM; negative for Borrelia afzelii and Borrelia garinii antibodies. Re-review of lymph node histology noted pseudogranulomas with homogeneous contents surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltration and forming connective tissue pseudocapsule with numerous macrophages consistent with specific granulomatous lymphadenitis. Treated with doxycycline 200 mg/day for 30 days with normalization of temperature, improvement in sicca symptoms, and regression of lymphadenopathy.

38-year-old Guatemalan soldier evaluated after recurrent febrile illness and fatigue following return from a 9-month deployment in Africa (DRC: Dungu, Bangadi, Bunia; short travel to Uganda, Kenya). Used an untreated bed net and took weekly mefloquine prophylaxis with imperfect adherence. Post-deployment screening by malaria microscopy and PCR was negative. Two months after return, traveled to malaria-endemic regions in southern/eastern Guatemala, developed fever and fatigue, was clinically diagnosed and treated with chloroquine injections without lab confirmation with transient improvement. Three weeks later fever and fatigue recurred; local microscopy reported malaria but species identification was questioned. In Guatemala City, thin blood film showed malaria parasites with atypical morphology. CBC: thrombocytopenia (71,000/µL) and anemia (Hb 12 g/dL). Rapid dengue test indicated current/recent dengue infection; other labs normal. Due to travel history and microscopy doubts, molecular testing (nested PCR and SYBR qPCR) on blood confirmed a non-falciparum Plasmodium mono-infection; sequencing and external confirmation at a reference lab established the specific species and classic type. Treated with chloroquine over 3 days plus 14 days of primaquine; clinical and hematologic improvement and follow-up testing at day 1, 1 month, and 2 months confirmed parasite clearance. Household contacts tested negative; home sprayed with deltamethrin.

20-year-old woman at 18 weeks of gestation presented to the emergency department with generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Previously diagnosed with disseminated intravascular coagulation, intrauterine fetal death, multi-organ dysfunction syndrome and septicaemia. RT-PCR positive for coronavirus. Labs: hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, leukocytosis 22.8×10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 108.9×10^9/L, prolonged PT 24.4 s (control 11 s) and APTT 44.1 s (control 30 s), markedly elevated D-dimer 2880 ng/dL, fibrinogen 270 mg/dL, hyperbilirubinemia (total 4.6 mg/dL, direct 2.28 mg/dL), elevated AST 120 U/L, ALT 162 U/L, ALP 326.6 U/L, urea 47.2 mg/dL, creatinine 2.81 mg/dL; electrolytes near normal. Blood cultures negative after 48 hours. Condition deteriorated despite treatment and she died on hospital day 2. Autopsy histopathology: lungs with diffuse interstitial edema and acute/chronic inflammation; numerous septate fungal hyphae with acute-angle branching invading blood vessels on special stain. Other organs (kidney, liver, spleen, uterus) with fibrin thrombi and variable tissue necrosis without fungal invasion.

An 85-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Rai III/Binet C) previously treated with chlorambucil/rituximab (temporary improvement) and briefly exposed to ibrutinib (stopped after ~30 days due to gastrointestinal intolerance) was admitted in late July 2018 with fever, myalgias, anorexia, and worsening fatigue. CBC showed moderate lymphocytosis (~24,000/µL) with mild anemia and thrombocytopenia; C-reactive protein and procalcitonin were normal. Empiric antibiotics were started. Over subsequent days she rapidly developed neurologic deterioration with psychomotor agitation, stereotyped purposeless lower-limb movements, and altered mental status. Head CT was unremarkable; EEG showed diffuse background slowing without focal spikes. Lumbar puncture: normal opening pressure, clear CSF, 44 WBC/µL (predominantly mononuclear), elevated CSF glucose, and elevated CSF protein. Treated empirically with IV acyclovir for suspected viral encephalitis. Serum and CSF testing showed positive West Nile virus IgM; other microbiologic tests on serum/CSF were negative; serum West Nile virus PCR was positive. Despite supportive care, consciousness progressively declined to unresponsiveness, and she died 16 days after admission. CCR5 gene sequencing showed no alterations.

25-year-old G3P0020 at 36 3/7 weeks with singleton pregnancy presenting with acute-onset severe constant aching/sharp back pain and fever; recent recurrent left antecubital abscesses requiring drainage with culture showing MRSA treated with clindamycin. Initially afebrile; left antecubital fossa nodularity and lumbar tenderness; fetal testing reassuring. Labs: WBC 21 K/uL, CRP 27 mg/L, ESR 63 mm/hr. Developed hypotension and fever; started on vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam. Blood cultures grew gram-positive cocci, later MRSA. Lumbar MRI for persistent severe pain showed small dorsal spinal collection and left psoas muscle edema; neuro exams initially normal. Progressive worsening pain with new bilateral lower-extremity weakness; repeat MRI with gadolinium showed extensive epidural collection from T5-6 to T8-9 causing mild thecal cord compression and another collection from L4 to S1. Due to worsening neurologic symptoms and difficulty ambulating, cesarean delivery performed followed by thoracic laminectomy/decompression; intraoperative cultures grew MRSA. Postop course complicated by persistent MRSA bacteremia; repeat MRI showed residual thoracic collection with cord compression at T6-T7 and left psoas muscle collection; required re-exploration/laminectomy and prolonged IV antibiotics (vancomycin plus ceftaroline). History evolved to later endorsement of intravenous drug use. Discharged after blood cultures cleared; neurologic deficits improved but with ongoing residual weakness, pain, and incontinence.

A 35-year-old immunocompetent woman with 6 months of swelling of the right index finger and limited range of motion. Works handling aquatic products and had a finger injury while working with lobsters and oysters. Received local wound closure and empiric antibiotics/anti-inflammatory treatment for suppurative tenosynovitis without improvement. Persistent swelling; exam shows an unhealed incision without obvious exudation, limited finger motion, and fingertip numbness. Labs: mild monocytosis (0.63 x 10^9/L) and mild thrombocytosis (365.9 x 10^9/L); otherwise normal/negative WBC, biochemical, and immunological tests. Histopathology: fibrous connective tissue hyperplasia, marked inflammatory cell infiltration, and granuloma formation. Ziehl-Neelsen stain positive for acid-fast bacilli in pus. Culture on Columbia blood agar grew white colonies after 7 days; colonies turned yellow after light exposure (photochromogenic). Treated with surgical drainage plus rifampicin and clarithromycin for 3 months with symptom resolution and no relapse at 6-month follow-up.

A 34-year-old man received a kidney-pancreas transplantation. Perioperative prophylaxis included ampicillin and cefotaxime. Immunosuppression included steroids, antilymphocyte globulin, and cyclosporine; later treated with anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody for acute kidney rejection. He had refractory urinary infection (Enterococcus faecalis and Morganella morganii) treated with amoxicillin and ciprofloxacin, and a right basal lobe focal bronchopneumonia. On post-operative day 50 he developed intense soft-tissue inflammation at the first left metatarsophalangeal joint, progressing to an abscess with a cutaneous fistula and extensive involvement of most of the foot. Radiography showed a small osteolytic/osteo-lacunar lesion in the head of the proximal phalanx of the first toe. Purulent material culture identified Nocardia asteroides. Treated with amoxicillin-based therapy for three months with complete resolution.

A 17-year-old male presented with pain and swelling in the upper left anterior region for 10–12 days and a history of trauma 7 years earlier while playing cricket. Clinical exam showed a fractured tooth in relation to 22 with extraoral swelling extending from the lower border of the infraorbital margin to the upper lip. The tooth was tender on vertical percussion, had no mobility, and was nonresponsive to thermal sensibility testing. Intraoral periapical radiograph showed a large periapical radiolucency associated with 22, extending from the distal surface of 21 to the mesial surface of 23. Nonsurgical endodontic treatment was initiated, but a persistent “weeping canal” prevented achieving a dry canal despite calcium hydroxide and triple antibiotic paste used as intracanal medicaments over several weeks, leading to consideration of an apical surgical approach. CBCT revealed a single canal with normal root anatomy and an intact buccal cortical plate despite the large lesion. Guided apical surgery was planned and performed with a printed surgical template to remove and later reposition a buccal cortical bone block; pathological soft tissue was curetted and sent for histopathology. Root-end resection (~3 mm) was performed with orthograde MTA obturation done prior to surgery; PRP and bone graft were placed, the cortical plate was repositioned and stabilized with PMMA-based bone cement, and the flap was sutured. Follow-up at 3 and 12 months showed the patient asymptomatic with radiographic evidence of complete healing.

A 79-year-old man presented with progressive dysphagia over 8 months, worsening in the past few weeks, with difficulty swallowing solid foods and preference for pureed/liquid diet. He reported odynophagia without dyspnea or dysphonia. Modified barium swallow suggested an obstruction in the upper third of the esophagus, but upper GI endoscopy showed no intraluminal lesion. After endoscopy he developed persistent neck pain; CT cervical spine demonstrated significant anterior osteophytes from C2 to C6, with the largest measuring 21 mm (anteroposterior) causing extrinsic impingement on the esophagus. Managed conservatively with diet modification and NSAIDs.

15-year-old competitive male swimmer with prior bilateral arthroscopic subacromial decompression. One week after reaching maximal medical improvement, sustained a right shoulder dislocation while swimming (self-reduced) and presented 3 days later with mild pain (3/10) and <20% normal function. Exam: no deformity; tenderness at bicipital groove; ROM to 150° scaption, 45° external rotation, internal rotation to T10; positive Neer, Hawkins, O'Brien, valgus sheer, and anterior load tests; negative posterior load, belly press, and lift-off. MRI showed humeral head subluxation with posterior humeral head contusion and a reported Buford complex; treated with physical therapy. After 6 weeks: persistent moderate pain (4/10), function <50%, instability with an episode of subluxation; discomfort with apprehension and anterior load exams. MRI rereview suggested abnormal inferior anterior labral tissue consistent with labral injury. Underwent arthroscopy: complete disruption of labral tissue from 3 o’clock to 6 o’clock; associated anteroinferior articular glenoid cartilage lesion (6 mm x 8 mm); posterior and superior labrum intact; no rotator cuff or biceps tendon damage. Postoperative course: at 3 months no pain and 85% function with improved ROM; at 5 months traumatic fall onto outstretched hand with transient pain and apprehension; MRI showed intact repairs; conservative management led to resolution by 6 months with 95% function, full comfortable ROM, and negative provocative tests.

Young healthy 19-year-old male MMA athlete sustained a direct blow to the anterolateral left thigh from a strong kick during a fight. Presented with moderate pain and swelling of the thigh extending to the knee, restricted knee range of motion, and painful difficulty with weight-bearing causing a limp. Admitted for monitoring/observation and pain control; pain progressively worsened, was not relieved by potent analgesia, and disturbed sleep. Exam: gross swelling of the left thigh, markedly tense thigh compartment, tenderness, increased pain with passive stretch, palpable distal pulses and no neurovascular deficit. Left thigh circumference initially 2 cm larger than the contralateral side, progressing to 6 cm discrepancy during admission. X-ray of left femur showed no fracture. MRI of left thigh showed high-grade musculotendinous injury with intramuscular hematoma (~8.5 x 3 cm) in the vastus lateralis. Underwent emergency left thigh fasciotomy, followed by second-look washout/partial closure on day 2 and third-look complete closure on day 3; gradual improvement with physiotherapy and return to usual activities by 6 months.
diagnosis: Acute compartment syndrome of the thigh

case_information: No family history of genetic disorders, significant medical conditions, or similar fractures; no history of major diseases. Right upper limb exam: no significant tenderness or swelling; intact function; normal elbow range of motion; no abnormal findings. Radiographic imaging 9 months postoperatively showed no signs of healing at the fracture sites.

A 61-year-old competitive male cyclist with insidious onset left perineal pain during cycling, later noticing a tender perineal mass. No visible abnormality. Palpation revealed a firm, rubbery, mildly tender nodule (about 1 cm transverse and 4 cm longitudinal) adjacent to the left ischial tuberosity, not fixed to muscle or bone. High-resolution greyscale ultrasound showed a well-defined, heterogeneous, predominantly cystic mass inferior to the left scrotum measuring 5.0 x 2.4 x 4.0 cm, containing hypoechogenic material and with no increased vascularity. Patient preferred conservative management. Cycling biomechanics evaluation found underwear worn under cycling garment, worn/low-quality padding, excessive saddle height (static knee flexion angle 22°) and excessive saddle setback (10.5 cm), with initial saddle pressure mapping showing front:rear pressure balance 62:38. After adjustments (knee flexion angle 31°, setback 6.8 cm) and saddle changes, pressure distribution improved (front:rear 46:54; increased left ischial loaded area; reduced peak pressure). Returned to cycling without symptom recurrence at 2-year follow-up.

A 62-year-old male presented with left foot pain and limping. Exam showed swelling and tenderness over the medial cuneiform. He had foot trauma nine months earlier treated conservatively. AP and lateral foot radiographs and CT demonstrated sclerotic fracture ends with displaced fracture fragments in the medial cuneiform. Operative management included a longitudinal incision over the medial cuneiform, debridement of sclerotic bone ends and fibrous tissue, reduction, internal fixation with four screws, a mini plate, and a staple, plus iliac crest cancellous autograft placed into the defect. Postoperative AP and lateral radiographs were obtained.

6-year-old girl fell at school onto an outstretched hand. Had a prior mid-shaft both-bone forearm fracture treated 5 months earlier with flexible intramedullary titanium elastic nails. Presented to ED with obvious right upper-limb deformity but denied pain; isolated injury, clinically stable, distal neurovascular status intact. X-rays showed a new fracture through the previous fracture site. Managed with closed reduction under general anesthesia by correcting the angle of the intramedullary nails until acceptable reduction achieved. Discharged the next day; subsequent follow-up confirmed radiologic and clinical union. Intramedullary nails removed 6 months later and discharged from care.

14-year-old female Chinese semi-professional tennis athlete with recurrent right shoulder pain after a forehand stroke with left trunk rotation. Initial mild pain resolved after 2 days of rest; reinjury 5 days later with same mechanism caused 8/10 pain and immediate loss of upper extremity function. X-ray and MRI ruled out epiphyseal plate, ligamentous, or labral damage. Reports weakness with shoulder flexion, abduction, and external rotation, along with kinesiophobia, limiting ADLs and tennis. Remote assessment included active ROM measured via smartphone angle app and partner-assisted strength testing. Special test cluster performed (Painful Arc, Drop-arm, Infraspinatus test, Hawkins-Kennedy) showed positive signs.

38-year-old woman admitted to ICU after a fall during a suicide attempt 30 minutes earlier. Alert on arrival; extremities without neurovascular deficits. Unable to move right arm and leg. Approximately 3 cm open wound in the anterolateral thigh. Imaging: right femoral neck and shaft fractures, right acetabular fracture (AO type B3), and right humeral shaft fracture; CT also showed right pulmonary contusion and liver contusion; injury severity score 29. Initial surgery 5 hours post-injury: antegrade intramedullary nailing of right humerus and retrograde intramedullary nailing of right femoral shaft, followed by cannulated cancellous screw fixation of right femoral neck. Second surgery 7 days later for acetabular fracture: modified Stoppa approach for transverse fracture reduction and reconstruction plate fixation, then Kocher-Langenbeck approach for posterior wall fixation with reconstruction plate. Early postoperative course uneventful; partial weight-bearing allowed at 8 weeks after second operation. After starting partial weight-bearing, developed increasing right hip and thigh pain with inability to continue gait training. Radiographs showed hypotrophic nonunion of the right femoral shaft and loosening of femoral neck screws. Femoral reconstruction performed 15 weeks after injury: removal of implants, insertion of bipolar head prosthesis with long stem and proximal/distal interlocking screws; femoral shaft dynamization performed. Post-reconstruction: pain resolved; non-weight-bearing 4 weeks then gradual progression to full weight-bearing by 8 weeks. At 1 year: no activity restriction; radiographs with good callus formation in pelvis and femur and no prosthesis loosening.
diagnosis: Nonunion of fracture of shaft of femur

case_information: 18-year-old female with high-voltage electrical injury after accidentally touching a live current line with bare hand and falling prone. Sustained burns involving left upper extremity and left lower extremity with involvement of the foot. Local exam prior to surgery: exposed subcutaneous tissue in left axillary region; blackening of skin of left hand and axilla; tendons and bone exposed in left forearm; edema of left arm; black eschar on left forearm; maggots and dead necrotic tissue over left hand extending to mid-forearm. Left leg: superficial burn in calf region; second-degree burn on anterior leg with absent pulsation; sensory and motor exam without impairment. Estimated total body surface area burned 18% (rule of nines). CBC showed low hemoglobin with low sodium and potassium. Blood culture grew Pseudomonas species. Underwent operative debridement of wounds over left axilla and foot/feet with removal of slough/necrotic tissue; post-op course included ICU observation. Post-operatively had severe pain (VAS 7.9/10), edema, reduced joint range of motion, and decreased muscle strength; referred for physiotherapy and rehabilitation; follow-up at 15 days assessed ROM, pain, and ADLs (Barthel index).

Ten adult rehabilitation patients (6 male, 4 female; mean age ~47 years) were undergoing forearm physiotherapy after elbow or wrist joint fractures, assessed 7–10 days after splint removal. No fracture fragment instability, no severe pain, no upper-limb kinaesthetic/tactile sensory disorders, and no cognitive impairment. Clinical assessment showed limited functional elbow flexion–extension range of motion (flexion below functional range and limited extension), limited pronation–supination range of motion, low affected-hand grip strength on Jamar testing, mild pain on VAS, and substantial self-reported upper-limb disability on the Italian DASH questionnaire. Patients then participated in controlled, moderate-load training tasks involving elbow flexion–extension and/or forearm pronation–supination with adjustable velocities and assistive/resistive/zero-force haptic feedback, with parameters constrained to safe tolerances based on calibrated patient capacity; patients were instructed to report pain/discomfort during exercise.
diagnosis: Sequelae of fracture at wrist and hand level

case_information: A 45-year-old woman with prior childhood lower-extremity surgeries for congenital deformity, including distal femur stapling epiphysiodesis complicated by asymmetric physeal closure and later valgus femoral osteotomies, now presents with progressive knee pain and functional limitation. Exam shows moderate valgus laxity in flexion with otherwise intact collateral ligaments, reduced knee range of motion (about 5–85 degrees), ability to extend/flex against resistance, and intact peripheral pulses. Imaging (radiographs/CT/3D-CT and long-leg alignment films) shows combined extra-articular deformities: approximately 17 degrees varus at the supracondylar femur and 14 degrees valgus at the proximal tibial diaphysis, with the mechanical axis passing just medial to the tibial plateau; also noted patella baja. BMI 32 kg/m2; no other comorbidities; nonsmoker. Underwent complex knee reconstruction with joint replacement using stemmed components combined with closing-wedge corrective osteotomies of both tibia and femur and tibial tubercle osteotomy exposure; postoperative course included anticoagulation and physiotherapy with delayed weight-bearing. At 5-year follow-up she ambulated without pain or support, had improved knee scores and range of motion, healed osteotomy sites, and corrected limb alignment.

A 6-and-a-half-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with neck pain after falling from a bouncy castle. A cervical X-ray initially described C3–C4 retrolisthesis. He was discharged with a foam collar, ibuprofen, and follow-up with orthopaedics and a CT. CT three days later showed a 2 mm C4–C5 anterolisthesis with increased interspinous process space and no fractures, not confirming the initial X-ray finding. MRI the next day showed C5–C6 interspinous ligament oedema suggestive of a sprain and superficial posterior paraspinal muscle oedema around C2. Managed with physiotherapy; at one-month follow-up there were no lasting symptoms or damage.

11-year-old boy (30 kg) with entanglement injury in rotavator blades 8 hours prior. No loss of consciousness or vomiting. Primary survey: airway/breathing/circulation stable; GCS 15/15; hemodynamically stable. Secondary survey: severe facial avulsion/degloving with complete avulsion of nasal bones and septum from glabella extending as inferiorly based flap to upper lip and cheeks; cartilaginous septum separated from perpendicular plate of ethmoid; left medial canthal ligament torn and displaced; missing central incisors; airway assessment not possible due to facial injury. Lower limb injuries: bilateral tibial shaft fractures with extensive degloving injuries to both lower limbs; right closed mid-shaft tibia fracture (AO 42-A3); left open comminuted tibial shaft fracture with butterfly fragment (AO 42-B3), Gustilo-Anderson grade IIIB; distal neurovascular status intact bilaterally. Additional contaminated lacerated wounds over right lower quadrant (8×2 cm), right inguinal region (15×4 cm), and right lower leg (5×4 cm); extensive degloving over left groin, thigh, leg, foot. Other system exams normal; CT brain/thorax/abdomen/spine normal; chest radiograph normal. Labs: hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, WBC 15,000/cumm, platelets 280,000/cumm; creatinine/electrolytes/glucose normal. Received IV antibiotics (metronidazole, amikacin, cefuroxime) and tetanus toxoid. Multidisciplinary operative management: tracheostomy under local anesthesia for anticipated difficult airway; facial debridement and repair with nasal septal suturing and internal nasal splints; subsequent repeated wound debridements and VAC dressings with split-thickness skin grafting for left leg; left tibia debridement and fixation with interfragmentary screws plus ankle-spanning external fixator; right tibia treated with closed elastic intramedullary nailing; eventual fracture union and wound healing over months with removal of external fixator and return to full activities by 6 months.

A 56-year-old obese male with 7 days of low back pain radiating down both lower extremities and mild 4/5 right foot drop. Lumbar MRI showed a large central L2-3 disc lesion with spinal canal narrowing causing marked thecal sac/nerve root compression. Intraoperatively, when positioned prone on a Jackson table, preoperative SEP/MEP baselines were completely lost and immediately returned when repositioned supine; signals were again lost when repositioned prone. Surgeons proceeded with emergent L2-L3 decompressive surgery, after which SEP/MEP signals returned to baseline bilaterally. Postoperatively, the patient fully recovered.

76-year-old female with hypertension (previously resolved with mild sodium restriction) developed distal interphalangeal joint stiffness and spontaneous pain in Dec 2011; treated with bucillamine 300 mg/day starting Jan 2012 with symptom resolution and initially normal renal function and negative urinalysis. In mid-March 2012 developed edema and weight gain; afebrile, no recent infection; BP 130/77 with periorbital and lower-extremity edema. Labs: total protein 4.8 g/dl, albumin 1.9 g/dl, creatinine 0.63 mg/dl (eGFR 68.6), CRP 0.04; ASO 28; complements normal; circulating immune complex negative. Urinalysis: hematuria 30–49/HPF with many RBC casts; proteinuria 4.67 g/day. Serologies: ANA 40x; RF 29; anti-CCP >300; MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA, anti-GBM negative; ANCA IF negative; hepatitis B/C negative; chest CT without pulmonary hemorrhage/interstitial disease/pleurisy. Bucillamine stopped; proteinuria improved and albumin recovered within 2 weeks but renal dysfunction progressed and hematuria worsened. Kidney biopsy: 23 glomeruli, 5 globally sclerosed; slight endocapillary proliferation with inflammatory infiltration; crescents in 7 glomeruli; no arteritis or peritubular capillaritis. Immunofluorescence: fine granular IgG (3+), C3c (3+), C1q (1+) along capillary walls; IgG subclasses positive (IgG1 3+, IgG2 1–2+, IgG3 1–2+, IgG4 3+). Electron microscopy: segmental subepithelial deposits along GBM with extensive foot process effacement and podocyte injury. Persistent severe hematuria with rapid eGFR decline to ~50; treated with two 3-day courses of methylprednisolone 0.5 g/day followed by oral prednisolone 25 mg/day, which halted eGFR decline and resolved hematuria; steroids stopped due to psychiatric symptoms and given IV cyclophosphamide 0.5 g; no recurrence of hematuria/proteinuria over 2 years but chronic reduced eGFR persisted.

A 72-year-old man on chronic maintenance dialysis with hypertension and diabetes was transferred in April 2020 for worsening pneumonia after 10 days of outpatient antibiotics for fever and cough. Respiratory failure progressed; CT showed severe bilateral pneumonia. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive and he required ICU care. He was intubated on hospital day 3 and started on favipiravir on hospital day 4. From hospital day 9, D-dimer rose rapidly; on day 10 the PaO2/FiO2 ratio fell and repeat CT showed worsening bilateral ground-glass opacities; lung-protective ventilation was initiated for acute respiratory failure. Anticoagulation prophylaxis was started on day 12 with continuous unfractionated heparin titrated to keep APTT 1.5–2× baseline; antithrombin III levels dropped and required frequent replacement. Despite this, ultrasound on day 19 showed a right femoral vein thrombus. On day 27 he developed shock and contrast CT demonstrated an acute pulmonary arterial occlusion. He developed multiple organ failure and died on hospital day 39. During ICU renal replacement therapy starting day 3, the extracorporeal circuit repeatedly clotted despite escalating unfractionated heparin (circuit life 110–240 minutes); after switching anticoagulant to nafamostat mesylate on days 31 and 34, circuit clotting did not occur.

A 69-year-old male with hypertension, diabetes (diet controlled), history of morbid obesity status post gastric bypass, and metastatic prostate cancer presented with progressive chronic kidney disease and subnephrotic-range proteinuria. Glomerular filtration rate declined by >5 ml/min/1.73 m2 per year. Medications: atorvastatin, amlodipine, aspirin, calcium carbonate, leuprolide. No known drug allergies. Family history notable for a brother with renal failure of unclear etiology in his forties. Review of systems notable for peripheral neuropathy with unstable balance; denied hypohidrosis, extremity pain, gastrointestinal complaints, rashes, or cardiac symptoms; denied skin issues. Exam: BP 160/78, pulse 72, BMI 24.5; no abnormal lung, heart, abdominal, extremity, or skin findings. Labs: creatinine 4.3 mg/dL, BUN 47 mg/dL, CO2 19 mg/dL; electrolytes otherwise normal. CBC: hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL with normal platelets and WBC. Urinalysis with mild proteinuria; urine protein/creatinine ratio 2.2. SPEP, UPEP, and serum free light chains without abnormalities. Kidney ultrasound showed slightly atrophic kidneys with echogenic parenchyma. Kidney biopsy: light microscopy with normocellular glomeruli, uniform capillary walls, prominent podocytes with foamy cytoplasm; ultrastructural exam with osmophilic lamellated inclusions in podocytes with concentric/striped appearance (myelin-like lamellated inclusions). Alpha-galactosidase enzyme activity low (21 nm/hr/mg protein; reference 50–150). GLA gene testing showed missense variant c.682A>C (p.Ala228Cys); daughter and grandson tested positive for same variant. In vitro mutation testing suggested suitability for migalastat therapy.

A 27-year-old Hispanic male presented with one week of rash followed by generalized headache and fever (103 F). He had recently had his lamotrigine dose increased from 50 to 100 mg daily and was also taking fluoxetine. Exam showed a fine erythematous maculopapular rash on hands, legs, and back. Initial labs: normal CBC and CSF; rising creatinine from 1.16 to 1.9 mg/dl over 2 days, progressing despite hydration to a peak creatinine of 7.5 mg/dl by hospital day 4. Urinalysis: 3+ protein, 2–5 RBC/hpf, 10–20 WBC/hpf, and 1–5 eosinophils/hpf; urine protein/creatinine ratio 3.3 mg/mg. Head CT unremarkable. Autoimmune serologies (complement levels, ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM) negative; EBV/CMV/HIV serologies negative. Suspected medication-related systemic reaction; lamotrigine and fluoxetine stopped. Kidney biopsy showed tubulointerstitial inflammation consistent with acute interstitial nephritis; skin biopsy showed perifolliculitis and superficial perivascular dermatitis. Treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone with improvement in rash and renal function (creatinine to 2 mg/dl in 3 days) and resolution of proteinuria; later returned to baseline. Fluoxetine was restarted without complications; discharged on a prednisone taper.

A 60-year-old male presented to the emergency department two hours after an intentional ingestion of ~500 milliliters of a commercial herbicide containing diquat dibromide 2.30%. Initial exam showed no hypoxemia, circulatory, or renal failure but did show depressed mental status, followed within 30 minutes by rapid mental status decline requiring intubation for airway protection. Direct laryngoscopy revealed mucous membrane erosion in the posterior pharynx. An orogastric tube suctioned 400 mL of green gastric contents. Activated charcoal was not given due to delayed arrival. A blood toxin level within 4 hours was 9.9 microg/mL (reported as typically associated with lethal outcome). In the ICU he received N-acetylcysteine, ascorbic acid, vitamin E, and dexamethasone. Within 24 hours he developed nephrotic-range proteinuria with proximal tubular dysfunction (glycosuria, phosphaturia, increased bicarbonaturia), then acute kidney injury (GFR 17 mL/min/1.73 m2) with worsening anion gap metabolic acidosis requiring continuous renal replacement therapy. He also developed rapid transaminase elevation and signs of hepatic failure (INR 1.4). Respiratory status deteriorated about 36 hours after ingestion with refractory hypoxemia and chest imaging compatible with ARDS. Although echocardiogram and circulatory status were initially normal, he later developed irreversible shock with hyperlactatemia requiring vasopressors around 36 hours. Despite maximal supportive care, progressive multiorgan failure was fatal.

An 83-year-old Japanese man with hypertension and chronic heart failure due to bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome, on long-term warfarin after pacemaker implantation, presented with persistent worsening macroscopic hematuria with clots and acute kidney injury. Prior intermittent macroscopic hematuria over years; underwent prior transurethral resections for a papillary bladder tumor (initially no malignancy) and later noninvasive papillary urothelial carcinoma (pTa, N0, M0). Ten days before admission, cystoscopy showed a jet of bloody urine from the right ureteral orifice without apparent bladder tumor recurrence. On admission: right costovertebral angle tenderness, mild bilateral leg edema; urinalysis with numerous RBCs and no casts; urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.17; serum creatinine 2.41 mg/dL (0.96 mg/dL three weeks earlier); hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL; CRP 0.9 mg/dL; INR 1.44. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a high-density area from the right kidney to ureter and deformity of the inferior pole of the right kidney unchanged for 2 years; no hydronephrosis. Hematuria persisted despite stopping anticoagulation. Ureteroscopy showed thick blood clots in the upper to mid ureter; IVP demonstrated a right renal papillary tumor; biopsy and washing cytology from the right renal pelvis showed urothelial carcinoma, leading to right laparoscopic nephroureterectomy 41 days after AKI onset. Pathology showed a 2-cm poorly demarcated papillary tumor in the right renal pelvis with invasion into renal parenchyma beyond the muscular layer (pT3, N0, M0). Renal histology showed tubules filled with RBCs and debris with tubular dilation, flattened epithelium, acute tubular injury/regeneration, mild interstitial fibrosis with mononuclear infiltration, focal glomerular ischemic changes and global sclerosis, and moderate arteriosclerosis; immunofluorescence negative for IgG/IgA/IgM/C3/C4/kappa/lambda and electron microscopy without electron-dense deposits. Creatinine peaked at 2.96 mg/dL and improved to 1.66 mg/dL by 3 months. Macroscopic hematuria resolved 2 days after surgery with no recurrence at 8 months; warfarin was not resumed.
diagnosis: Invasive urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis

case_information: Pediatric patient with recurrent nephritic and nephrotic syndrome and persistently very low complement activity (C3 <10 mg/dL, CH50 <12). After 3 years of normalized urinalysis and recovered renal function on immunosuppression/antithrombotic therapy, relapse at age 13 with worsening renal function (creatinine up to ~1.02 mg/dL; eGFR ~57 mL/min/1.73 m2), heavy proteinuria (~12 g/g creatinine), hematuria, leukocyturia, and dyspnea requiring oxygen due to pleural effusion. Kidney biopsy showed severe diffuse endocapillary and mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis with one cellular crescent. Treatment with steroid pulses, ACE inhibitor/ARB, prednisolone, dipyridamole, warfarin, and mycophenolate was ineffective; FFP had no benefit. Soluble C5b-9 was markedly elevated during the acute phase (~4964 ng/mL). After meningococcal vaccination, anti-complement C5 therapy was started (900 mg weekly x4, then every 2 weeks), with rapid disappearance of leukocyturia (next day), improvement in creatinine within 3 days, normalization of kidney function within 7 weeks, resolution of pleural effusion and oxygen requirement, and reduction of sC5b-9 to normal range. Proteinuria improved (about 12.9 to 2.5 g/g creatinine within 1 month) and remained stable on continued therapy; biopsy later showed decreased isolated C3 deposits and reduced IgG staining.
