When infusion intervals were extended and then stopped, proteinuria and leukocyturia rose and nephritic/nephrotic syndrome recurred, improving again promptly after restarting anti-C5 therapy.

43-year-old Hispanic male with hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3. Kidney biopsy approximately 10 years earlier showed Oxford classification M1E0S1T0 with immunofluorescence demonstrating mesangial staining for IgA (4+), IgM (1–2+), C3 (trace–1+), and kappa/lambda (3+ each). Treated with benazepril (eventually increased to 40 mg daily); hydrochlorothiazide discontinued 5 years prior. Dapagliflozin prescribed October 2022 and started January 2023. Despite supportive therapy, progressive decline in kidney function (eGFR 41 mL/min/1.73 m2 in 2015 to 28 mL/min/1.73 m2 in October 2022) and rising proteinuria (551 mg/g in 2015 increasing to ~1100 mg/g by October 2022; 1339 mg/g in December 2022). Started delayed-release budesonide 16 mg daily in November 2022 after risk/benefit discussion given degree of kidney impairment. After 12 months, eGFR remained stable and proteinuria decreased to 452 mg/g by November 2023; no notable medication side effects reported through January 2024.

65-year-old male undergoing first-stage revision total knee arthroplasty after multiple prior failed two-stage revisions for an infected left knee. Comorbidities: diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, congestive heart failure, gastroesophageal reflux disease. No known allergies or prior anesthesia complications. Pre-op meds: furosemide, gabapentin, carvedilol, lansoprazole, docusate, enalapril.

Intra-op: received cephalexin; cloudy joint fluid noted and sent for culture; debridement/irrigation performed; new cement spacer created using 5 bags Simplex P mixed with 26.4 g tobramycin and 9 g vancomycin. Brief hypotension on induction requiring pressors; intermittent vasopressor support during case (phenylephrine, epinephrine, norepinephrine). Extubated and initially stable.

Post-op: celecoxib 200 mg BID, aspirin 325 mg BID, continued lansoprazole. Started on IV vancomycin 2 g q12h and piperacillin-tazobactam; cultures grew Corynebacterium striatum and piperacillin-tazobactam was stopped.

POD2: nonoliguric rise in creatinine from 0.9 to 1.5 mg/dL, worsening over subsequent days; nephrology considered multifactorial causes including intraoperative hypotension and nephrotoxic medications (celecoxib, lansoprazole, IV vancomycin). POD3: vancomycin level 53.8 mcg/mL; IV vancomycin and celecoxib discontinued; started doxycycline.

POD6: creatinine peaked at 8.62 mg/dL with hyperkalemia 6.3 mmol/L and ECG changes; treated with calcium gluconate and kayexalate; emergent hemodialysis and ICU transfer. Serum tobramycin level 13.7 mcg/mL. Hemodialysis repeated POD7 and POD8 with downtrending tobramycin; after stopping dialysis, urine output adequate but tobramycin levels began rising again.

POD13: decision made to remove the antibiotic cement spacer; spacer explanted and replaced with a spacer containing 4 g cefazolin. Afterwards creatinine improved to 3.72 mg/dL and tobramycin level to 0.6 mcg/mL at discharge. Two-month follow-up creatinine stabilized around 2.28 mg/dL without hyperkalemia or oliguria.
diagnosis: Acute kidney failure with tubular necrosis

case_information: Four retrospectively selected patients aged 70–81 years with chronic kidney disease stage 3 or 4 and multiple comorbidities, notably diabetes and hypertension. One patient had severe stage 4 disease with baseline eGFR <20 mL/min/1.73 m². Managed with a multifactorial treatment approach and followed for 6–7 years, with outcomes tracked by CKD progression markers including eGFR, serum creatinine, and other renal chemistry parameters.

A 19-year-old deceased kidney donor died from craniocerebral trauma with terminal serum creatinine 54 µmol/L. Donor and recipient were at the same hospital. The left kidney was procured after ligation of the left renal artery and vein and immediately cold-flushed via the left renal artery and preserved in ice-cold University of Wisconsin solution. The right kidney underwent an ischemia-free procurement and preservation approach using in vivo and ex vivo normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) with a Liver Assist device: abdominal aorta and right renal artery and the inferior vena cava and right renal vein were dissected; ureter was divided with a tube placed for urine drainage; a 34Fr caval cannula was placed in the infrarenal IVC for venous outflow to the organ reservoir; a 20Fr cannula was inserted into the infrarenal abdominal aorta for arterial inflow; suprarenal abdominal aorta and suprarenal IVC were clamped to establish in vivo NMP. The right kidney was then harvested and moved to the organ reservoir for ex vivo NMP; suprarenal IVC diameter was reduced to 1.5 cm with 6-0 Prolene. Continuous NMP was performed for 110 minutes at 37°C with oxygenation; perfusion pressure 52–70 mmHg and flow 130–184 mL/min remained stable; perfusate creatinine and urea stayed low; the graft produced urine throughout and urine pH and specific gravity were comparable before procurement, during NMP, and after reperfusion. The graft was transplanted into the recipient right iliac fossa with re-establishment of an in vivo NMP circuit; donor suprarenal aorta and IVC were anastomosed end-to-side to the recipient right external iliac artery and vein using 6-0 Prolene; NMP was stopped after establishing recipient blood supply; approximately 50 mL perfusate was flushed; cannulas were removed and donor infrarenal aorta and IVC were closed; ureteroneocystostomy was performed. Recipient operation time was 135 minutes.

Infant followed by nephrology and urology teams. Urine output and kidney function remained normal. Renal dynamic imaging 1 month after discharge showed fair perfusion of both kidneys and clear excretion. Follow-up at 8 months: parents report satisfactory voiding; urinary tract ultrasound normal.

40-year-old male with 7 months of facial puffiness and bilateral lower-extremity pitting edema. No bony pain, oral ulcers, arthralgia, skin rashes, or features of connective tissue disease. BP 110/70; systemic exam normal. Urinalysis: 4+ protein, no active sediment; 24-hour urine protein 6.9 g/day. BUN 25, serum creatinine 2.06 mg/dL. Serum total protein 5.5 g/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL. Hyperlipidemia: total cholesterol 352, triglycerides 328 mg/dL. Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibodies, HIV I/II negative. ANA, rheumatoid factor, cryoglobulins, ANCA negative; complements normal (C3 110 mg/dL, C4 20 mg/dL). Kidney ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys. Kidney biopsy: diffuse thickening of glomerular capillary walls with podocyte lifting; silver stain shows spikes; no mesangial/endocapillary proliferation or tubulointerstitial/vascular lesions. Immunofluorescence: granular IgG with kappa light chain and IgG3 plus C3 along glomerular capillary loops (3+); IgA, IgM, lambda, and C1q negative; no tubular basement membrane deposits. Serum/urine immunoelectrophoresis negative for monoclonal proteins, but serum free light chains elevated with kappa 1088 mg/dL, lambda 208 mg/dL (ratio 5.2). Skeletal survey normal. Bone marrow: 3% plasma cells. Treated with bortezomib-thalidomide-dexamethasone for 6 monthly cycles with proteinuria reduced to 3.1 g/day, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, albumin 3.1 g/dL; follow-up free light chains kappa 29 mg/dL, lambda 14 mg/dL (ratio 2.01).
diagnosis: Membranous glomerulonephritis with monoclonal IgG3 kappa deposition

case_information: A 24-year-old man presented with macrohematuria, general malaise, fever, and progressive renal dysfunction. Vitals included fever up to 39.4 C, tachycardia, and tachypnea. Physical exam revealed a pansystolic murmur at the 4th left sternal border. Urinalysis showed marked hematuria and proteinuria with numerous RBCs and granular casts. Labs showed rising BUN/creatinine with reduced creatinine clearance, anemia, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR), hypocomplementemia (low C3/CH50), circulating immune complexes/cryoglobulinemia, and elevated D-dimer; autoimmune serologies including anti-DNA and ANCA were negative. Echocardiography demonstrated congenital ventricular septal defect and tricuspid valve vegetation with regurgitation. Multiple blood cultures grew Propionibacterium acnes. Renal biopsy showed crescentic glomerulonephritis with interstitial inflammatory cell infiltration and immune deposits (C3 and IgM) in capillary walls and mesangium. Renal function worsened despite initial antibiotics but improved after change in antibiotics plus a short course of low-dose corticosteroids, with normalization of complements/inflammatory markers and clearance of bacteremia; subsequently underwent tricuspid valve repair and VSD closure with recovery of renal function.

A 12-year-old L. fulica kept in an aquarium with two other adults; adopted at 6 years old from an experimental station with irregular food and water supply. Current diet included vegetables, fruits (including bananas), and animal protein (gammarus). Husbandry issues included difficulty maintaining appropriate humidity despite spraying water; temperature about 23°C. Clinical signs included beginning esophageal protrusion; later mantle collapse and marked edema of the foot and head; body weight 453 g. Radiographs (laterolateral, dorsoventral, craniocaudal) showed severe renal enlargement with a moderately bumpy renal surface. CT later demonstrated renal enlargement with heterogeneous parenchyma and several elongated hyperdense intraparenchymal areas; other organs appeared hypodense and were poorly differentiable due to severe edema. Euthanasia performed; pathology showed severe renal tissue degeneration with abundant crystalline deposits and larger accumulations of excretory material/cellular debris; foot connective/muscular tissue contained multiple slit-like empty spaces consistent with extracellular edema.

31-year-old primigravida referred at 20 weeks’ gestation with newly detected heavy proteinuria, normal blood pressure, and anasarca. Proteinuria first noted at 16 weeks; no symptoms suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus or vasculitis. Past history of recurrent falls in childhood and corrective surgery for fixed flexion deformities of the elbows; no known prior renal disease. No developmental delay, no consanguinity, and no family history of renal disease.

Exam: bilateral pedal edema and ascites; fixed flexion deformities at both elbows; swan-neck deformities of interphalangeal joints; nail pitting (more marked on radial side); patellae not palpable bilaterally.

Imaging: X-rays with hypoplastic patellae, radial head subluxation at elbow, and symmetrical bilateral iliac horns.

Labs: nephrotic-range proteinuria (11 g/day) with hypoalbuminemia and hypercholesterolemia. ANA, C3/C4, rheumatoid factor, and anticardiolipin antibody negative. Ultrasound: normal unobstructed kidneys; intrauterine fetal demise at 22 weeks followed by spontaneous expulsion. Post-abortion developed left renal vein and inferior vena cava thrombosis; anticoagulated. Serum creatinine remained normal; albumin improved and proteinuria progressively decreased on follow-up with resolution of thrombosis on Doppler.

Fifty-six-year-old male, initially diagnosed in 1996 with an anterior skull base tumor after presenting with headaches. Underwent prior surgery at another center. In 2016 presented with recurrence with intranasal and right orbital invasion; complete excision performed via combined transcranial and endoscopic transnasal approaches. Anterior skull base defect required microsurgical reconstruction with an anterolateral thigh free flap anastomosed to temporal vessels using a saphenous vein graft. Received hypofractionated radiosurgery in January 2017 (total 25 Gy in 5 fractions) due to proximity to optic pathways/critical structures. One year later developed further recurrence with nasal skin infiltration, pial and brain parenchyma infiltration, and right level II cervical lymphadenopathy; neck node biopsy confirmed metastatic spread from the tumor with Ki-67 labeling index 20%. Chest/abdomen CT performed to exclude other metastases; brain CT showed bone erosion. Underwent total resection including superior orbital rim, nasal dorsum, medial orbital wall, nasal bones, upper medial maxillary sinus wall, ethmoidal cells, and vomer; frozen-section margins negative. CSF leak occurred after resection of tumor adherent to prior flap and was primarily closed. Reconstruction performed with a DIEP flap (8×4 cm skin paddle) converted from planned rectus flap due to lack of suitable local pedicles, with a chimeric segment of rectus muscle to extend pedicle to 10 cm; anastomosed to facial artery and thyrolinguofacial trunk. Selective right level II neck dissection performed. Postoperative course uncomplicated; good healing and cosmetic outcome; no early imaging evidence of recurrence. Adjuvant radiotherapy was indicated but refused. Died one year later from pneumonia.

14 year 8-month-old male with dysmorphic features and history of developmental delay, learning difficulties, disruptive behaviors, and reported regression of learning. Born at 35 weeks gestation; fetal ultrasounds normal; birth weight 2637 g; mild neonatal jaundice; 5-day hospitalization for breathing difficulties. Motor/language milestones: sat at 1 year, walked at 13–14 months, first words at 3.5 years. Diagnosed with Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder at age 8. At genetics evaluation: weight 47.2 kg (20th %ile), height 162 cm (22nd %ile), head circumference 53.2 cm (30th %ile). Physical findings include dolichocephaly with prominent occiput; long narrow face; heavy eyebrows with medial flare; sparse fine scalp hair; telecanthus (OCD 9.6 cm, ICD 3.9 cm); very soft ear cartilage with bilateral Darwinian tubercles; esotropia; narrow/short philtrum; bifid uvula; high palate; broad nasal bridge and tip; receding anterior hairline with widow’s peak. Pubertal development barely beginning Tanner II. Additional findings: hyperconvexed nails; collapsed foot arches; slight scoliosis; large-appearing elbows with prominent carrying angles; dry skin with eczema on dorsum; numerous nevi (notably under left eye). In 8th grade, in special education, functioning around a 2nd grade level.

12-year-old boy admitted with 3-week history following hepatitis B vaccination of limb weakness and altered consciousness, with persistent high fever (38–38.5°C). No headache, dizziness, nausea/vomiting, sphincter dysfunction, or visual symptoms; optic nerve exam normal. Past history of essential thrombocythemia with relapse 2 years prior; no toxin exposure, allergy, surgery, trauma, transfusion, or family history.

Exam: somnolent and uncooperative; pupils equal/reactive; bilateral light reflexes intact; limb strength about grade II with hypotonia; abdominal and cremasteric reflexes absent; bilateral Babinski and Gordon signs positive; ankle clonus present; neck stiffness.

Labs: WBC 15.8×10^9/L with neutrophils 85.2%; procalcitonin 0.05 ng/mL; CRP 1.14 mg/dL; ESR 50 mm/h; IgG elevated (1750 mg/mL); IgA/IgM/C3/C4 normal; sputum cultures negative. Serum total protein and albumin decreased.

CSF: pleocytosis 52/µL (leukocytes 40/µL), 90% mononuclear; Pandy negative; CSF protein normal; glucose mildly increased; chloride mildly decreased; oligoclonal bands present. Aquaporin-4 antibody negative. CSF/blood cultures and PCR/serologies for bacteria, TB, common viruses (HSV, CMV, EBV) and fungi negative.

MRI (day 3): brain FLAIR showed widespread abnormal signals; spinal cord MRI showed multifocal, longitudinal strip-like T1/T2 signal abnormalities in cervical cord and lumbosacral enlargement region. Evoked potentials (brainstem auditory and somatosensory) abnormal; visual evoked potentials normal.

Treatment with high-dose methylprednisolone and IVIG (with empiric antibiotics/antivirals) led to marked clinical and CSF improvement; complete recovery by ~4 months; no relapse over 3 years follow-up.

10-year-old previously healthy boy with normal psychomotor development and good school performance.

Acute illness: 3 days of high fever (39.5°C) of unclear infectious cause, self-resolved. One day after defervescence developed poor communication, fatigue, lethargy, drowsiness.

Seizures: episodes beginning with eye deviation/rotation with head motion (either direction) progressing to generalized convulsions with cyanosis/purple coloration and loss of consciousness; 1–2 minutes; urinary incontinence; post-episode lethargy. Multiple localized seizure types later with confusion, disorientation, amnesia, insomnia, hyperactivity/irritability, abnormal movements (twisted mouth); no autonomic dysfunction; speech dysfunction noted.

Initial workup: CSF 0 cells/mm3 with normal protein/glucose; microbiology negative (HSV, Japanese encephalitis virus, bacterial cultures); CSF anti-NMDAR antibody negative; blood ANA negative; brain MRI normal. EEG showed focal-onset paroxysmal activity in the left hemisphere with inhibited background activity.

Initial treatments/course: empiric acyclovir started then stopped after 3 days; high-dose methylprednisolone 20 mg/kg/day for 5 days starting in week 2; IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days; prednisone 1 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks; antiepileptics (oxcarbazepine, topiramate; later levetiracetam) and haloperidol at night. Weekly maintenance IVIG for 5 weeks. Seizures stopped after ~14 days, then relapsed to ~3–4/week; cognitive-behavior and memory improved but remained hyperactive/agitated. Cancer screening (CT chest, abdominal ultrasound) normal.

Follow-up at 3 months: continued 1–2 seizures/month; returned to school; high performance on Raven’s matrices (IQ 125); Vanderbilt scales showed residual hyperactivity/attention issues with reduced behavioral disturbance; repeat MRI normal.

Relapse at 5 months: recurrence of multiple seizures; CSF 8 WBC/mm3 with normal protein/glucose; indirect immunofluorescence panel in CSF/blood for AE-associated antibodies (NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, GABABR, AMPAR) showed AMPAR antibody positivity. MRI normal. EEG showed generalized paroxysmal epileptic activity maximal in the left temporal lobe with abnormal slow-wave background. Repeat cancer screening (CT chest, abdominal ultrasound) normal.

Treatment after relapse: methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day for 5 days; antiepileptic regimen adjusted (oxcarbazepine increased to 1800 mg/day; levetiracetam adjusted to 3000 mg/day; topiramate maintained at 300 mg/day). Marked reduction in seizure frequency to occasional brief seconds-long events without cyanosis; behavioral disturbances improved; Raven IQ remained high (110).

58-year-old right-dominant male with diabetes presenting with bilateral recurrent symptoms after multiple prior decompression procedures (four on the left, two on the right). Prior left-side surgery complicated by wound infection/hand phlegmon requiring re-exploration and secondary intention healing, followed by worsening complaints. Ultrasound and EMG confirmed persistent entrapment. Planned repeat decompression with microscopic neurolysis and consideration of protective nerve wrapping due to scarring risk. Intraoperatively the median nerve was markedly scarred and could not be covered with a local fat flap; the nerve was wrapped with meshed acellular dermal matrix after neurolysis. On the right side, an additional median artery was found and resected. Postoperative course uneventful with complete symptom resolution and VAS 0 at follow-up.

42-year-old female with recently diagnosed hypertension not on medication presented with 4 hours of inability to use the right upper and lower limbs, with giddiness, projectile vomiting, and numbness of the right half of the body. On exam: conscious and oriented; pulse 90 bpm; BP 170/110 mmHg; pupils equal and reactive. Eye movement findings: complete horizontal gaze palsy involving the left eye, nystagmus of the right eye on abduction; right upward gaze palsy; only ocular movement possible was abduction of the right eye. Motor exam: right upper limb power 3/5 with distal handgrip ~70%; right lower limb power 2/5; left-sided power preserved; plantar responses mute bilaterally; sensory exam normal. Non-contrast CT brain showed hemorrhage in the left midbrain and upper pons. Treated with antihypertensives; improved ocular movements on long-term follow-up and able to do routine activities.

Over 12 months of investigations, no cause identified. Progressive, fluctuating bilateral visual loss beginning at age 10 years 11 months: VA 6/60 both eyes, improved to 6/36 after 1 month; 6 months later left eye 6/60 with right 6/6; 4 months later VA 6/60 both eyes; last ophthalmology follow-up at age 12 years 4 months VA 6/60 right and 3/60 left. Could detect colors on Ishihara but could not read letters. Visual fields without specific defect. Pupillary reactions normal with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy repeatedly normal with healthy optic discs and maculae. Neurological and other examinations initially unremarkable. VEP delayed bilaterally with normal ERG at age 12 years. Cranial/orbit MRI and EEG normal. Testing for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy normal. Skin and muscle biopsy without inclusion bodies; blood film no lymphocyte vacuolation. Electron microscopy of buffy coat showed rare membrane-bound electron-dense granular material associated with a lipid droplet in lymphocyte cytoplasm. Leukocyte enzyme analysis: very low palmitoyl protein thioesterase 1 activity (2.2 nmol/hr/mg protein; normal 17–139) with normal tripeptidyl peptidase 1 activity (214 nmol/hr/mg protein; normal 42–339). Molecular testing (CLN1 exons 1–9): heterozygous p.Cys96Tyr and p.Arg151X variants. By neurology follow-up at age 12 years 10 months: persistent poor vision with emerging behavioral and cognitive problems (increasing immaturity, loss of skills, significant memory change); no seizures or motor dysfunction to date.
diagnosis: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis due to palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1 deficiency

case_information: 66-year-old man with heavy tobacco use (30 cigarettes/day for 45 years) developed sudden right-sided hemiplegia and dysarthria at 7:30 a.m. Exam: right facial palsy, dysarthria, right arm paralysis, right arm/leg paresthesia; NIHSS 6. MRI DWI: small acute ischemic lesions in the left putamen, corona radiata, and part of the left MCA territory; MRA: left MCA occlusion; T2WI: no obvious thrombus. Perfusion–diffusion mismatch suggested salvageable tissue. Treated with IV alteplase after BP management; proceeded to endovascular therapy. Angiography showed distal left MCA occlusion with collateral flow from ACA via pial anastomoses. Stent retriever achieved flow restoration but showed poor stent expansion with residual focal stenosis; only minimal thrombus retrieved and significant stenosis persisted with rapid restenosis after standard balloon angioplasty. Required prolonged angioplasty using a perfusion balloon while maintaining distal perfusion; adjunct antiplatelet loading (aspirin/clopidogrel) and IV ozagrel; intra-procedure heparinization (ACT ≥200). No evidence of cardiogenic embolic source on postop ECG/echo. Neurologic deficits resolved (NIHSS 0 next day). Follow-up imaging showed no infarct expansion, satisfactory distal perfusion with mild residual stenosis, and improvement in stenosis at 3 months; discharged day 7 without deficits; continued antithrombotic and statin therapy.

13-year-old boy, born at term by elective caesarean after uneventful pregnancy; birth weight 4060 g; no perinatal diseases. Reported psychomotor delay (sat unsupported at 8 months, walked at 18 months). Admitted at age 13 for mild intellectual disability and dysmorphic features. Neurologic exam: mild clumsiness, no focal signs. Growth: weight 42.8 kg (50–75th percentile), height 161 cm (75–90th percentile), head circumference 52 cm (3rd–10th percentile). Facial features: hypertelorism, wide flat nose. Pectus excavatum and chest asymmetry. Ultrasound: absence of right pectoralis major and minor muscles. Standing full-length spine X-ray: thoracolumbar scoliosis without vertebral abnormalities. No kidney/urinary tract/cardiac anomalies on ultrasound. Ophthalmology: intermittent exotropia, bilateral myopia, normal fundus. Brain MRI: cerebellar vermis hypoplasia. EEG and BAEP normal. Psychometric testing: cognitive impairment (<5th centile on Raven's Progressive Matrices).

57-year-old male presenting with diplopia and left-sided hemidysesthesia; no fever, headache, vomiting, vertigo, hypertension, or trauma; no prior CNS history. Exam: right abducens (sixth cranial nerve) palsy, other cranial nerves normal; no other neurological signs. Blood and CSF hematological/biochemical tests normal; serologies including parasite antibodies negative. Non-contrast CT: multiple high-intensity patchy calcifications or hemorrhagic-appearing foci around cortical and subcortical regions of cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, and brainstem. Susceptibility-weighted MRI: numerous additional thick lesions distributed throughout brain (cerebrum, cerebellum, thalamus, brainstem) not seen on T1/T2 GRE; lesion sizes 0.5 mm–3 cm (average ~0.9 cm). Family: asymptomatic 63-year-old brother with similar multifocal lesions on SWI (including sellar region and parietal lobe); 53-year-old sister with no lesions on SWI; parents deceased, no MRI available. Genetic testing performed on CCM1/CCM2/CCM3 coding exons by PCR and Sanger sequencing; variants assessed with in silico tools and compared against mutation databases; variants further checked in 200 ethnically matched controls.

Multiple patients undergoing lumbar spine surgery under general anesthesia (e.g., L5–S1 decompression, L4/5 discectomy/microscopic discectomy, TLIF, lumbar instrumentation) developed recurrent abrupt intraoperative hemodynamic events temporally associated with electrocautery and/or dural handling/manipulation near the lumbar levels. Events included episodes of marked bradycardia (down to 10 bpm), severe bradycardia with hypotension (e.g., 60/40 mm Hg), progression to asystole requiring CPR (including in prone position), and fluctuating severe hypotensive/hypertensive episodes. Episodes improved with cessation of the surgical stimulus and/or treatment with IV anticholinergics (e.g., atropine) and vasopressors (e.g., ephedrine); symptoms resolved by the end of surgery in the fluctuating case.

44-year-old female with history of epilepsy since childhood and asthma, previously seizure-free for several years on long-term topiramate and valproic acid (valproic acid ~30 years; topiramate ~27 years). Takes duloxetine 30 mg BID for anxiety and ibuprofen as needed.

Presented with breakthrough generalized convulsive episode (5–10 minutes) with hand twisting and frothing at the mouth, followed by ~15 minutes unresponsiveness; treated by EMS with 10 mg midazolam.

In ED: post-ictal; recurrent hypoglycemia (BG 61 mg/dL then 51 mg/dL) temporally associated with recurrent tonic-clonic seizures despite dextrose 50% boluses and continuous dextrose infusion. Levetiracetam and later lacosamide added; antiepileptic drug levels within normal limits.

Persistent hypoglycemia with seizures despite D5 infusion; hypoglycemic panel unremarkable; adrenal challenge test, growth hormone deficiency work-up, and continuous video EEG unremarkable. Non-contrast CT showed no acute findings.

Carnitine testing revealed low free and total carnitine. After stopping valproic acid and starting L-carnitine supplementation, glucose normalized, dextrose infusion discontinued, and patient remained seizure-free at discharge.

A 37-year-old woman was referred to rehabilitation after a recent acute neurological event. Past history includes a neurocutaneous disorder diagnosed at age 19 after removal of a plexiform neurofibroma in the right foot, with optic nerve glioma and multiple café-au-lait macules; no genetic confirmation was performed. At age 29 she developed balance impairment, gait ataxia, and mild left lower-limb paresis; brain/spinal MRI showed multiple demyelinating lesions (left thalamus, right pallidus, cervical cord at C2, C4, C5), visual evoked potentials had markedly increased latency, and CSF showed oligoclonal bands; immunomodulatory therapy with teriflunomide was started. Over time she developed hypertension and dyslipidemia. No family history of stroke, smoking, atrial fibrillation, or atrial heart disease. At age 37 she had sudden-onset right upper-limb weakness with speech and swallowing impairment and gait ataxia; initial CT excluded hemorrhage and she received systemic thrombolysis with partial benefit. Subsequent MRI demonstrated recent lesions involving the left thalamus/internal capsule and the right lenticular nucleus. Ten days later she was transferred for post-acute rehab with left-sided hemiparesis, balance impairment, and speech/swallowing disorders; functional follow-up continued for 3 years with greatest gains in the first 5 months and stability at 1–2 years.

12-year-old girl with 6 months of generalized tonic-clonic seizures and 2 months of headache with episodic vomiting. Neurologic exam without focal deficits; bilateral papilledema on fundoscopy. Routine blood/biochemical tests normal. Brain MRI: large, well-defined predominantly cystic right parietal lesion extending from cortex to periventricular region, no perilesional edema; mass effect with effacement of cortical sulci, ipsilateral sylvian fissure and lateral ventricle, and significant leftward midline shift. Lesion hyperintense on T2/FLAIR and T1; peripheral foci with blooming on GRE suggesting calcifications. Post-gadolinium: peripheral enhancement with a strongly enhancing mural nodule. Underwent right parietal craniotomy with gross total excision; tumor largely cystic with a small soft vascular suckable solid component; well-demarcated, no hemorrhage or necrosis. Histopathology: perivascular arrangement of tumor cells with short stout cytoplasmic processes forming pseudorosettes; no necrosis, mitoses, or vascular proliferation. Tumor cells spindle-shaped with moderately eosinophilic cytoplasm and eccentrically placed nuclei; immunopositive for GFAP, vimentin, and S-100. Referred for adjuvant radiotherapy.

47-year-old female with progressive limb weakness beginning in the left upper limb (Oct 2016) with rapid deterioration over months, developing dysarthria, choking with liquids, difficulty with fine motor tasks (lifting/fastening buttons), and limited walking endurance (<100 m). No initial weight loss; no remarkable past medical history. Neuro exam: no obvious muscle atrophy; fasciculations in bilateral biceps/triceps; weakness (MRC 3/5 upper extremities, 4/5 lower extremities); diffuse hyperreflexia (4+), hyperpharyngeal reflex and palmomental reflex; bilateral Hoffman signs positive; no sensory or cerebellar deficits. MRI brain and cervical spine normal. EMG: active and chronic denervation in all limbs plus sternocleidomastoid and paraspinal muscles. NCS: decreased CMAP amplitudes in right median and ulnar nerves. Labs: CBC/biochem/thyroid/tumor markers normal; hepatitis negative; ANA 1:3,200 and AMA >1:40; immunoglobulins and complement near normal. Sjogren workup (SFR, CFS, BUT, SIT, SSA, SSB) negative. Chest CT: multiple subpleural inflammatory nodules without cough/fever. Upper abdominal CT: splenomegaly and cirrhosis with abnormal liver morphology/rough surface; enlarged porta hepatis lymph nodes; no intra/extrahepatic bile duct dilatation/stenosis. Treated with UDCA and riluzole. Follow-up: became bed-bound with dysphagia and ~40 kg weight loss by 1 year after symptom onset.

General exam: barrel-chested appearance; short neck with low posterior hairline; abnormal scapulae; toe webbing. At age 12: weight 36.6 kg (75%ile), height 126.4 cm (<5%ile), BMI 34 (>95%ile), head circumference 50.5 cm. Palate and cardiac exams normal. Neurologic: normal language and gregarious social interaction; occasional tics and stereotypy; cranial nerves normal; diminished distal strength in both hands and thumb abductors; reflexes 2+ symmetric; clumsy/slow fine hand movements; decreased light-touch sensation in hands. Ratings: YGTSS total tic score 6; CY-BOCS 16; DuPaul ADHD Rating Scale 17. Imaging/CT: fusion of cervical and thoracic vertebrae; scoliosis; hypoplastic thumbs; multiple digit anomalies of feet and hands. Genetic testing (CGH SNP array): ~3 Mb hemizygous microduplication at chromosome 22q11.2 involving ~20 genes expressed in brain/bone; parental testing negative, consistent with de novo event.

A 45-year-old obese woman presented for evaluation of symptomatic large breasts. After consultation, she elected to undergo bilateral breast reduction using a Wise pattern with an inferior pedicle. Questions raised include: indications for breast reduction and commonly used techniques; advantages/disadvantages of the Wise pattern inferior pedicle approach; advantages/disadvantages of liposuction-based breast reduction; and common complications of breast reduction.

33-year-old woman with normal intelligence and illiteracy; height 160 cm, weight 53 kg. Reproductive history 2-0-1-2 with moderate menstrual flow. Noted premature ovarian failure. Physical findings include a long face and hyperextended finger joints.

65-year-old postmenopausal woman (menopause at 50), asymptomatic. Screening chest X-ray showed multiple pulmonary nodules. Thoracic–pelvic CT demonstrated uterine enlargement with multiple lung tumors; no other distant metastases. Pelvic exam: cervix largely replaced by tumor; uterus adult-head-sized with poor mobility suggesting possible parametrial invasion. Pelvic contrast MRI: mass involving cervix through uterine corpus (~15 × 8.5 × 10 cm) with heterogeneous low T1/T2 signal and focal hemorrhage; suspected anterior serosal infiltration. Tumor markers (SCC, CA125, CA19-9, CEA) within normal ranges. Cervical biopsy: superficial squamous epithelium without atypia; deep layer showed nests/clusters of small bare-nucleus–like atypical cells with high N/C ratio and coarse chromatin; p16 negative; partial synaptophysin positivity. Endometrial cytology showed similar high N/C bare-nucleus–like cells. Treated with multiple cycles of paclitaxel/carboplatin with marked shrinkage of uterine mass and radiographic disappearance of lung lesions, followed by modified radical hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and sampling of a mildly enlarged left obturator node (no nodal metastasis). Surgical specimen: tumor contiguous from cervix to corpus; histology showed mixed duct-like/cord-like/solid-alveolar carcinoma patterns with a component of atypical spindle cells; immunostaining variably positive for GATA3, CD10, calretinin, TTF-1, and PAX8; ER negative. Gross/histologic distribution favored a corpus-centered origin rather than squamous epithelial cervical origin. Later developed acute neurologic symptoms 17 weeks post-op; brain MRI showed multiple cystic white-matter masses consistent with metastases; brain lesion biopsy showed similar morphology to uterine tumor; treated with gamma-knife.
diagnosis: Mesonephric-like adenocarcinoma of the uterine corpus

case_information: On hospital day 2, the patient had progressively increasing vaginal bleeding with passage of clots. She was started on 40 mg oxytocin intravenously to encourage uterine contractions, with minimal improvement later that evening. Over 24 hours, 12 peripads were soaked with blood and clots. By the end of day 2, hemoglobin was 9.1 g/dL and hematocrit 28.1%. Oxytocin was continued for 24 hours with plans to reassess bleeding the following day. Echocardiogram showed mildly reduced right ventricular systolic function without other abnormalities.

A 36-year-old woman with two prior cesarean sections presents with 18 months of amenorrhea and periodic lower abdominal distension. Physical exam unremarkable. 3D gynecologic ultrasound shows intrauterine adhesions and left hydrosalpinx. Preoperative hysteroscopy finds a large defect at the 12 o’clock position in the cervical canal; the scope passes easily into the urinary bladder and the uterine cavity cannot be accessed. Cystoscopy shows a ~10 mm contracted scar with decayed tissue on the posterior bladder wall; bilateral ureteral orifices normal. Laparoscopy shows dense adherence of the lower anterior uterine wall to the posterior bladder wall and bilateral hematosalpinx. Surgical exploration identifies a tract between the posterior bladder wall and the anterior cervix; adhesions are released, the tract/scar excised, and the bladder repaired in two layers with uterine reconstruction. Postoperatively she voids normally after catheter removal and menstruation returns to normal; follow-up hysteroscopy shows restored uterine continuity and no cervical canal obstruction or new intrauterine adhesions.

49-year-old woman (P2L2) with 3 months of per vaginum discharge and spotting; previously regular cycles. No history of radiation, tamoxifen, or estrogen use. Known hypertension; pallor present; BP 150/90 mmHg; Hb 7.9 g/dL. Per speculum: friable cauliflower-like mass ~6×8 cm completely filling the vagina, bleeding on touch. Per vaginal: mass ~10-week size; fornices free. Ultrasound: heterogeneous mass 5.9×3.4×6.3 cm in vaginal canal with inferiorly displaced uterine fundus/body; impression of large prolapsed submucosal fibroid with uterine inversion or large cervical growth. CECT abdomen: uterine inversion with structure occupying vaginal canal; surrounding hypodense lesion ~3.5 cm thick. Tissue fragments sent for histopathology; immunohistochemistry showed weak CD10 positivity and desmin negativity. Underwent vaginal debulking, Haultain’s operation with uterine repositioning followed by hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Final pathology: >10 mitoses/10 HPF, extensive hemorrhage and necrosis, >50% myometrial invasion, estrogen and progesterone receptor positive. Planned for postoperative radiotherapy.

Mean patient age 33.00±14.89. Mean BMI 27.05±2.55. Mean gravida 3.24±4.23, parity 3.19±4.18, live births 3.14±4.21, abortions 0.05±0.22. Mean lesion size 5.62±1.77. Mean age at female genital cutting 7.33±1.77 years; mean age at onset of cyst growth 18.05±8.18 years. Most patients had female genital cutting type II (85.7%). Most common complaint was a discomforting mass in the vagina. Pathology most commonly showed an epidermal cyst. Among type II patients, 66.7% were married.

A 28-year-old married woman with primary amenorrhea was evaluated for a shapeless pelvic mass and to assess for functional ovaries and a uterus. Secondary sexual characteristics were present (pubic/axillary hair Tanner III; breasts Tanner IV). Vaginal exam showed a blind-ending vagina; uterus not palpable. Thelarche and pubarche began around age 13; no family history of amenorrhea. Labs: FSH 2.5 mIU/ml, LH 3.5 mIU/ml, prolactin 9.45 ng/ml, creatinine 0.6 mg/dl (all within normal range); AMH 1.5 ng/ml (below normal). Buccal smear for Barr bodies was normal. Ultrasound showed complete absence of the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, with normal-sized ovaries containing follicles 10–14 mm; renal findings included an ectopic 95×72 mm pancake-shaped kidney in the left pelvic cavity with absent kidneys in the usual locations. Pelvic MRI confirmed the absent uterus/cervix/upper vagina with normal ovaries and confirmed the ectopic pancake kidney without hydronephrosis; MR angiography showed the middle sacral artery as the principal arterial supply to the pelvic kidney.

A 6-hour-old term female neonate (2330 g) with a pink 4×4 cm mass protruding through the introitus since birth; cervical os seen at the tip of the mass. External genitalia normal. No bleeding or discharge. Mass is digitally reducible and increases in size when the baby cries. Passed meconium, active, sucking well, normal vital signs and intact neonatal reflexes initially. Coexisting 4×4 cm lumbosacral defect mostly skin-covered with a small open lower edge and no discharge; bilateral clubfoot with minimal leg/foot movement. Transfontanelle ultrasound: mild dilation of lateral and third ventricles consistent with mild hydrocephalus. Abdominal ultrasound normal; CBC normal; creatinine 0.4 mg/dL. Managed by catheterization, manual reduction of the vaginal mass, and strapping/bandage from lower abdomen/buttocks/legs to mid-thigh with anal opening; after 72 hours the mass was completely reduced with no recurrence.

50-year-old morbidly obese woman (BMI 39), para 2, with prior hysterectomy and prior bladder suspension procedure. Over 2 months noticed a vaginal bulge mainly with wiping; discomfort with intercourse and increased urine leakage during intercourse. Reports stress urinary leakage and urgency-related leakage, daily pad use, and nocturia; denies recurrent UTIs or vaginal bleeding. Pelvic exam: bladder neck well supported, no leakage with Valsalva; grade 2–3 anterior vaginal wall prolapse, grade 2 apical descent, and grade 3–4 posterior vaginal wall prolapse; bimanual exam negative. Counseled on pelvic floor exercises, weight loss, pessary vs robotic abdominal prolapse repair; returned after 5 months with ~35 lb weight loss and worsening symptoms with activity, elected surgical management; planned urodynamics and started vaginal estrogen. Underwent robotic pelvic adhesiolysis, abdominal mesh suspension of the vaginal apex with anterior and posterior vaginal attachments to the sacral promontory with peritoneal closure, plus retropubic mid-urethral sling placement; intraoperative cystoscopies confirmed no bladder injury and bilateral ureteral efflux; minimal blood loss and uncomplicated recovery.

Admitted to gynecology on January 12, 2022 for abnormal vaginal bleeding for 2 months. Gynecologic exam: vaginal patency; superfluous mass on the upper third of the right vaginal wall (~3 cm diameter, ~0.8 cm at the tip); cervix smooth; uterus anterior, normal size, non-tender; no obvious bilateral adnexal abnormality. Pathology from vaginal wall mass tissue: hypodifferentiated adenocarcinoma with mostly degenerated necrotic cells. Immunohistochemistry: CK5/6 small focal+, CK8/18+, p16 partial+, p40-, Ki-67 scattered+, vimentin-, GATA3 focal+, CK7+, ER <1%+, PR <1%+, HER2 0. Pelvic MRI with contrast: occupying lesion on right upper-middle vaginal wall (polyp considered; biopsy recommended to exclude malignant change) and pelvic effusion.

34-year-old Gravida 11 Para 3073 at 16 weeks 1 day gestation with 2 days of progressively worsening nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea worsened by eating, followed by severe diffuse abdominal tenderness and intractable abdominal pain worse with movement and breathing despite IV analgesia. Pregnancy previously unremarkable. Past history: endometriosis, infertility. Surgical history: two prior cesarean sections and left salpingo-oophorectomy for ectopic pregnancy. Initial labs (CBC, CMP, amylase, lipase) normal. MRI/MRCP obtained to evaluate for appendicitis/gallbladder disease showed a large amount of intraperitoneal fluid of unclear etiology and an intrauterine fetus. After ~12 hours, transferred with hemodynamic deterioration: tachycardia, dyspnea, chest pain, worsening abdominal pain, and hemoglobin drop from 11.7 g/dL to 7.9 g/dL. Transabdominal ultrasound showed a single intrauterine pregnancy low in the uterus with marked thinning of the anterior myometrium at the implantation site and significant hemoperitoneum; fetal heart tones in the 140s. Emergent laparotomy performed; operative findings included a 2 x 1 cm defect in the right lower uterine segment with massive intra-abdominal bleeding and placental invasion into the posterior bladder requiring modified radical hysterectomy, right ureterolysis, and cystotomy with bladder repair; estimated blood loss 3,150 mL with transfusion support. Postoperative ICU admission and additional PRBC transfusions; discharged postoperative day 4 with Foley catheter and planned cystogram prior to removal.

In Germany, the first transplantation of ovarian tissue was performed in 2007 and the first live birth was achieved in 2011 in a 25-year-old cancer survivor. The special aspect was that the ovarian tissue was transported overnight prior to freezing. In the FertiPROTEKT network up to 2015, 95 orthotopic transplantations in 74 patients were performed, with pregnancy and delivery rates of 33% and 25%, respectively. In a subgroup of 30 women with overnight-transported tissue before freezing, pregnancy and delivery rates were 46.7% and 43.3%. Several centers in Germany reported successful procedures, with the greatest experience at University Hospital Erlangen, which had 1 live birth and 2 ongoing pregnancies at the time of the report.

27-year-old para 3 underwent laparoscopic hysteropexy for uterine prolapse (pre-op point C +1 cm corrected post-op to -6 cm). Conceived 1 month after surgery. Booked late for antenatal care (first visit at 18 weeks). Booking notes mentioned prior prolapse surgery but she was not referred to consultant-led care and had midwife-led low-risk antenatal pathway with no additional scans. Presented at 39+4 in labour with ruptured membranes and thick meconium. On-call obstetrician identified prior hysteropexy and proceeded to emergency caesarean section. Caesarean was uncomplicated with well-formed lower uterine segment and no mesh avulsion. Male infant delivered, 2795 g (10th centile); prior three infants also 10th centile. Did not attend postnatal review.

A 14-year-old girl presented with sudden onset severe right-sided lower abdominal pain and vomiting for 2 days. No fever, chills, bowel or urinary symptoms, or abnormal vaginal discharge. No prior similar episodes. Regular menses (35-day cycle) since menarche 6 months ago with normal bleeding. No sexual intercourse and no prior gynecologic or abdominal surgeries.

Vitals normal. Tanner stage 3–4. Right iliac fossa tenderness without palpable mass, peritoneal signs, or organomegaly; normal bowel sounds. Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL with mild leukocytosis (11,300/mm3). Urinalysis normal; pregnancy test negative.

Transabdominal ultrasound: normal uterus and normal bilateral ovaries; right adnexal large tubular dilated cystic lesion (8.0 × 3.7 cm) with absent Doppler flow within the lesion, separate from the right ovary which had Doppler flow; no free fluid in pouch of Douglas. MRI: dilated tubular convoluted right adnexal lesion separate from the right ovary, predominantly fluid content, no internal septations.

Hospitalized; treated with IV antibiotics, paracetamol, and ondansetron. Diagnostic laparoscopy showed an enlarged right fallopian tube twisted three times on its own axis with gangrenous appearance; right ovary appeared normal without ischemia. Detorsion attempted but unsuccessful; complete right salpingectomy performed due to necrosis. Histopathology: excised fallopian tube with hemorrhagic necrosis, no malignancy. Postoperative course uneventful.

20-year-old thin-built woman of Middle Eastern descent, previously healthy and never sexually active, presented with recurrent episodes of sudden, profuse vaginal bleeding with large clots. Similar episode occurred two months earlier requiring multiple blood transfusions; tranexamic acid previously given caused anaphylaxis. No personal history of bleeding disorders; family history positive for breast cancer.

On presentation: estimated ~1 L blood loss, hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL, vitally stable; transfused 2 units PRBCs (Hb to 10.1 g/dL). Pelvic imaging reports described a posterior uterine wall vascular mass with intense enhancement, dilated vascular tufts, arterial-phase early filling of venous collaterals, and bilateral tortuous pelvic venous channels (left predominant). Pelvic MRI and transabdominal ultrasound showed a uterine vascular lesion with abnormal vessels/flow.

Hospital course: developed another sudden episode of heavy bleeding (~2 L) requiring ICU care and additional transfusions and blood products (FFP, factor VIIa, cryoprecipitate). Bleeding stopped spontaneously; patient refused vaginal approaches/tamponade and desired fertility-sparing management.

Underwent selective bilateral uterine artery embolization after multidisciplinary consultation. Angiography demonstrated direct arterial shunting into pelvic veins with an anastomotic branch between left ovarian and left uterine arteries; coil protection used, followed by embolization of uterine arterial feeders. Post-procedure course was stable with no further heavy bleeding. Follow-up MRI at 2 months showed decreased/thrombosed vascular lesion in some regions with persistent serpentine enhancing parametrial vascular channels. Subsequent follow-ups noted regular menses with minimal heavy flow limited to one day and no recurrent severe bleeding; ovarian reserve labs (AMH, FSH) within normal premenopausal range.

A 37-year-old Bangladeshi male with 1 month of central blurring of vision in the left eye. BCVA 20/20 right eye and 20/400 left eye. Anterior segment unremarkable; intraocular pressure 18 mmHg both eyes. Dilated fundus exam of the left eye showed neurosensory detachment of the macula with scattered subretinal deposits within the detachment; a pit-like defect was seen on the inferotemporal aspect of the optic disc, continuous with the area of retinal detachment. Right eye fundus normal. SD-OCT showed outer nuclear layer macular schisis with neurosensory detachment and a small area of outer retinal dehiscence in the foveal region; the schisis cavity communicated with the optic disc pit. Autofluorescence showed isoautofluorescence in the macula with multiple hyperautofluorescent spots corresponding to lipofuscin deposits. Fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrated temporal parapapillary hyperfluorescence due to leakage from the optic disc pit. Surgery was discussed but declined due to cost; focal argon laser photocoagulation was performed to the temporal optic disc margin; lost to follow-up.

A 45-year-old female with diabetes mellitus and a known history of chronic thrombocytopenia (initially presenting with menorrhagia) presented with sudden bilateral reduced vision for 3 weeks, associated with floaters. No history of trauma, intense exercise, heavy lifting, straining, vomiting, coughing, or vigorous sexual activity. Visual acuity was 6/36 (right) and 6/60 (left). Anterior segment exam was unremarkable. Fundus exam showed bilateral peripapillary, subhyaloid, and vitreous hemorrhage, worse in the left eye; no diabetic retinopathy changes were seen. No petechiae, bruising, or mucosal bleeding on systemic exam. Platelet count 120×10^9/L; hemoglobin 93 g/L; PT and aPTT normal. Treated with oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 1 week then tapered over a month; at 6 weeks hemorrhages were partially resolving with vision improving to 6/24 in both eyes. Vitrectomy was recommended for the left eye due to subhyaloid hemorrhage adjacent to the macula, but the patient had not consented.

A 69-year-old male with a medical history of stroke and type 2 diabetes for fifteen years presented with sudden and complete vision loss in the right eye. Visual acuity was counting fingers at 0.3 meters in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye.

24-year-old man with history of bilateral vernal keratoconjunctivitis since childhood with intermittent past topical steroid use. Best corrected visual acuity 6/9 right eye and 6/6 left eye. Right eye: gelatinous limbal lesion extending from 7 to 2 o’clock with vascular fronds on the surface, ~3 mm corneal encroachment with feeder vessels and pseudogerontoxon; Rose Bengal stain positive over the lesion; no papilla or foreign body on upper lid eversion. Left eye: pseudogerontoxon with no papillary or limbal activity. Rest of ophthalmic exam unremarkable bilaterally. Impression cytology from the right limbal lesion showed multiple pigment-bearing pleomorphic plump epithelial cells. Treated with two cycles of topical mitomycin C 0.04% with decrease in lesion size. Ultrasound biomicroscopy showed no scleral involvement. HIV 1/2 antibody negative. Lesion excised in toto with 4 mm wide margin using alcohol-assisted corneal epithelial removal/no-touch technique, cryotherapy to margins, and amniotic membrane transplantation. Histopathology: multilayered thickening of conjunctival epithelium with loss of polarity and nuclear atypia without basement membrane breach; stromal fibrovascular proliferation; graded as mild to moderate dysplasia. At 6-month follow-up, visual acuity 6/6 both eyes with no recurrence.

10-year-old male child with SWS presented with raised intraocular pressure in the left eye. Prior left-eye trabeculectomy with mitomycin C. Best corrected visual acuity: 6/6 right, 6/9 left. Intraocular pressure: 15 mmHg right, 37 mmHg left. Left eye slit-lamp: flat, avascular superior bleb with patent superior peripheral iridectomy; clear cornea; peripheral anterior chamber depth equal to corneal thickness. Fundoscopy: left cup–disc ratio 0.7. B-scan ultrasonography of left eye: diffuse choroidal haemangioma without retinal detachment. Treated with maximal antiglaucoma medications (dorzolamide/timolol, travoprost, oral acetazolamide) but with progressive optic nerve damage and persistently elevated IOP (23 mmHg) in left eye, leading to Ahmed glaucoma valve implantation. Postoperative day 1: visual acuity 3/60; shallow anterior chamber with choroidal detachment and exudative retinal detachment; treated with added oral prednisolone tapered over one month. Postoperative day 5: visual acuity 6/60, peripheral anterior chamber depth 1/2 central corneal thickness, IOP 9 mmHg. One month post-op: best corrected visual acuity 6/9, well-formed anterior chamber, IOP 12 mmHg, resolution of choroidal and exudative retinal detachment.

80-year-old female with hypertension and diabetes presented with sequential onset bilateral painless severe vision loss: sudden complete vision loss in the right eye, followed over the next month by the left eye. No systemic symptoms (no weight loss, fever, anorexia, fatigue, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, or myalgia). No transient vision loss, trauma, new headache, or sleep apnea. Past history includes endovascular coiling for a right distal internal carotid artery aneurysm (2015).

Exam: visual acuity light perception OD and finger counting OS; pupils 3 mm bilaterally with right relative afferent pupillary defect; extraocular movements normal; no temporal tenderness; other cranial nerves and motor/sensory exam normal. Fundus: no optic disc edema or hemorrhage; mild optic atrophy OD.

Fluorescein angiography: no leakage or filling defects; mild hypofluorescence OD. OCT: normal average RNFL thickness OU initially; decreased ganglion cell complex thickness OD; no significant inner retinal layer thickness change.

Labs: CBC essentially normal; CSF nonspecific; autoimmune/infectious/thyroid and demyelinating workup negative including AQP4 and MOG; ESR and CRP repeatedly normal.

Cardiovascular studies: ECG and 24-h Holter showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (up to 173 bpm). Echocardiography: severely enlarged left atrium, normal ventricular systolic function. Blood pressures during hospitalization 129/69–157/93 mmHg on antihypertensives.

Imaging: brain DWI showed multiple scattered acute diffusion-restricted lesions in bilateral periventricular white matter consistent with acute embolic infarcts; DWI also showed diffusion restriction in the posterior portions of both optic nerves with corresponding ADC hypointensity; contrast-enhanced T1 MRI showed enhancement of both optic nerves. Carotid Doppler: heterogeneous echogenic plaques in left internal carotid artery with mild stenosis; brain MRA showed arteriosclerotic changes.

Left temporal artery biopsy showed intimal thickening without evidence of arteritis. Treated with 5 days of IV methylprednisolone 500 mg and anticoagulation (apixaban) plus antiplatelet therapy (cilostazol) without visual improvement. At 2-month follow-up: no light perception in both eyes; fundus with pale mildly atrophic optic discs; OCT showed RNFL thinning OD and decreased ganglion cell complex thickness in both eyes.

Post-refractive surgery patient presenting months after flap-based corneal refractive surgery with unilateral inferior corneal steepening on topography and decreased visual acuity. Findings consistent with early postoperative corneal ectatic change, with minimal refractive changes and preserved uncorrected and corrected distance visual acuity initially. Intervention described: under-flap corneal collagen cross-linking technique where the flap is fully retracted, riboflavin applied only to the stromal bed, flap repositioned, and ultraviolet irradiation delivered to the corneal surface to stiffen the stromal bed. Follow-up data reported showing maintained visual acuity, refractive/topographic stability (including Kmax, topographic cylinder, corneal irregularity indices) at 6 months, with no evidence of progressive ectatic change; one eye followed longer with continued stability. Discussion notes many such patients lack routine postoperative topography surveillance and may present later with worsening vision and irregular astigmatism; early intervention aims to preserve vision and prevent progression.

A 43-year-old man with a history of a deep wound on the left side of the nose from a car accident 4 years earlier; initial emergency suturing was performed without imaging and no retained object was identified. Five months ago, an ulcer developed at the nasal root and gradually progressed into a sinus tract. CT of the paranasal sinuses showed a transverse linear hyperdense structure through the nasal bone (about 25 mm x 5 mm). An attempted intranasal removal at another hospital extracted only a small fragment (2 mm x 2 mm); postoperative CT showed the material had fractured into two pieces, with a larger fragment extending into the left orbit near the eye and the remainder still in the nasal cavity. On referral, exam showed longitudinal wounds on both sides of the nose; best-corrected visual acuity 20/20 with normal globe position and motility. MRI demonstrated two retained objects in the soft tissue behind the nasal bone and within the left orbit. Surgical exploration via infraciliary lower-lid approach removed the intraorbital object; subsequent exploration behind the nasal bone removed the second hard object. Postoperative CT confirmed complete removal of both retained objects.
The patient shows severe optic atrophy causing blindness.

35-year-old woman with 1-day history of right central scotoma and metamorphopsia, preceded by viral exanthem with macular rash on the hand and in the mouth; dermatologic findings consistent with a viral hand/foot/mouth-type illness and recent contact exposure from her daughter. Visual acuity initially 20/20 OU with right central scotoma, then declined next day to 20/80 OD. Fundus OD: macular intraretinal haemorrhage, intraretinal thickening, and retinal pigmentary changes temporal to the fovea; no peripheral vasculitis or chorioretinitis; OS normal. Infrared imaging: figure-of-eight/dumb-bell-shaped macular lesion; SD-OCT: IS-OS junction abnormalities with hyperreflective debris along the RPE. FFA: significant macular leakage without extra-macular abnormalities and no vasculitis. ICGA: blocked fluorescence in corresponding area. Treated with oral prednisolone 60 mg/day with gradual taper over ~2 months; scotoma became well-defined and constricted over days; visual acuity improved over weeks back to 20/20; skin lesions resolved within 2 weeks. Follow-up angiography showed no active leakage; ICGA later with irregular moth-eaten choroidal vasculature without abnormal hypercyanescence. Residual right macular scar with intraretinal pigmentary change and subretinal fibrotic scar on SD-OCT; autofluorescence initially hypofluorescent lesion that evolved into dumb-bell shape then constricted over follow-up.

36-year-old male with painless, non-progressive localized swelling of the left upper eyelid for 1 year, confined to the tarsal region with slight yellowish skin tinge. Previously treated as chalazion without resolution. Visual acuity normal with correction; intraocular pressure and extraocular movements normal. No erythema or tenderness; no pus, eyelash loss, lid margin changes, or prominent vessels; palpebral conjunctiva normal. Excision biopsy performed. Histopathology showed polymorphs and plasma cells, foamy macrophages with PAS-positive inclusions, and occasional Touton-type giant cells. Systemic parameters normal; no recurrence at 12-month follow-up.

41-year-old man with 2-month history of broken dental root of the right upper premolar; 4 days after being treated with antibiotics for a periodontal abscess developed rapidly progressive right facial/mandibular/cheek swelling, severe right periorbital edema, proptosis, ocular pain, decreased vision, diplopia, nasal stuffiness and nasal bleeding. Exam: right eye BCVA 20/100, IOP 54 mmHg, severe limitation of extraocular movements in all directions, marked eyelid tightness/tenderness, conjunctival injection/chemosis with conjunctival prolapse due to incomplete lid closure, corneal epithelial erosion with mild stromal edema; anterior chamber shallower than contralateral; initial pupils/fundus/color vision normal. Labs: elevated WBC, ESR, CRP. CT: severe right maxillary sinusitis; inflammation of right temporalis/masticatory muscles; marked orbital soft tissue and extraocular muscle inflammation. Treated with IV ceftriaxone and clindamycin plus IOP-lowering meds; swelling worsened leading to emergent maxillary sinus drainage. Next day sudden severe right vision loss to light perception with IOP 42 mmHg and afferent pupillary defect; fundus showed pale optic disc, cherry-red spot, retinal edema; fluorescein angiography showed delayed retinal circulation; CT showed severe proptosis and posterior globe deformation with optic nerve stretching. Interventions included ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis, lateral canthotomy; high-dose systemic steroids given. Culture from sinus drainage grew Staphylococcus epidermidis. Facial/periorbital edema and IOP improved; proptosis, motility limitation, and afferent pupillary defect resolved but vision did not recover.

A 31-year-old Turkish Caucasian male presented with slow, progressive vision loss in the left eye. No history of intraocular surgery, atopy, or eye rubbing. CDVA 20/20 right eye and 20/200 left eye. Slit-lamp exam: posterior embryotoxon, iris hypoplasia, and iridocorneal adhesions in both eyes; corectopia in the right eye; peripheral inferior corneal thinning and ectasia in the left eye. IOP 13 mmHg (right) and 16 mmHg (left). Gonioscopy: multiple broad iris processes and prominent Schwalbe’s line. Dilated fundus exam: normal maculas; no retinal anomalies; no glaucomatous optic disc or RNFL changes. Corneal tomography: slightly asymmetric bowtie pattern in the right eye; crab-claw pattern in the left eye; bell sign on 12-mm corneal thickness map in the left eye; Scheimpflug imaging confirmed peripheral thinning of the left cornea, right cornea unremarkable. No systemic abnormalities reported. Serial tomography over 6 months showed 1.6 D increase in maximum keratometry and 22-micron decrease in thinnest pachymetry in the left eye. Underwent epithelium-off corneal collagen cross-linking (8-mm, slightly inferiorly decentered; iso-osmolar 0.1% riboflavin for 30 min; UVA 3 mW/cm2 for 30 min). Followed 28 months: topography showed 1.1 D flattening of maximum keratometry and 88-micron decrease in thinnest pachymetry compared with preoperative findings; corrected distance visual acuity improved to 20/20 with a scleral lens; no complications.

75-year-old female with hypertension and ischemic heart disease presented with 6-hour history of left eye pain, blurring of vision, photophobia, and redness occurring the day after receiving first dose of intravenous zoledronic acid (4 mg in 100 mL normal saline over 15 minutes) for osteoporosis. No trauma, fever, or headache. Exam: left conjunctival hyperemia; best corrected visual acuity 6/9 (left) and 6/6 (right); intraocular pressure 10 mmHg (left) and 14 mmHg (right). Slit-lamp: conjunctival hyperemia, fine keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cells and flare; posterior segment normal; right eye normal. No proptosis, periorbital edema, ptosis, or ophthalmoplegia. CRP 84.4 mg/L and ESR 65 mm/hr; other basic investigations unremarkable. Workup for other causes (CBC, ACE, chest X-ray, RF, HLA-B27, p-ANCA/c-ANCA, and infectious serologies including EBV, CMV, HIV, VDRL, VZV PCR) negative. Treated with topical prednisolone with complete symptom and sign resolution by 2 weeks and no recurrence over 6 months.

A 13-year-old boy with a moderate autistic spectrum disorder presented with a 6-week history of bilateral decreased visual acuity, eye redness, light sensitivity, and inability to keep his eyes open; parents noted deteriorating alertness at home. He was started on topical steroids and lubricants for presumed severe viral conjunctivitis. Examination under anesthesia showed corneal and conjunctival xerosis. Conjunctival biopsy revealed diffuse abnormality with squamous metaplasia of the conjunctival epithelium, submucosal inflammation, and marked keratinization. Laboratory testing showed insufficient vitamin D (<15 ng/mL) and an undetectable level of vitamin A. Malabsorptive causes were excluded and diet was found to be severely restricted. Oral vitamin supplementation led to rapid improvement with complete symptom resolution within 1 week.

A 41-year-old male with hypertension has recurrent unilateral left-eye episodes about once yearly for seven years, presenting with redness, blurred vision, ocular pain, and marked intraocular pressure spikes (30–60 mmHg) requiring maximal topical and systemic pressure-lowering therapy. On presentation: left-eye visual acuity 6/18, RAPD negative, IOP 56 mmHg while using topical steroid and multiple IOP-lowering agents plus oral acetazolamide and glycerol. Anterior chamber shows 2+ cells with fine central keratic precipitates; conjunctiva white and cornea clear. Fundus shows cup-to-disc ratio 0.9 with advanced glaucomatous changes on visual field and OCT RNFL. Anterior chamber paracentesis performed; aqueous humor sent for RT-PCR. Treated with ganciclovir ophthalmic gel and underwent glaucoma drainage implant with a Paul tube due to advanced glaucoma and frequent relapses; later required stent removal for IOP rise, after which IOP stabilized without medications and no further inflammatory reactivation or glaucoma progression noted.

Mother died of cancer 4 years earlier; patient was present at death. Persistent guilt and self-blame about the death with feelings of being lost and sad. Ongoing yearning/longing to be with her and frequent crying spells triggered by intrusive recollections/flashbacks (~6 times/week). Recurrent nightmares in which his mother calls him but he cannot answer, with awakening drenched in sweat. Sleep disturbance (about 3 hours/night). Loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities (music instruments, sports). Low energy and poor appetite for ~5 months. Began using marijuana; family subsequently withdrew support. Symptoms became overwhelming and interfered with professional training, leading to medical leave; collateral reported mental health interfering with work. Denied current suicidal or homicidal ideation. Depression severity scores: BDI 19; HAM-D 21. Partial medication adherence. Treated inpatient with mirtazapine, sertraline, and prazosin; psychotherapy initiated and continued after discharge.

Youngest brother from a middle socioeconomic family; eutocic birth and normal developmental milestones. Childhood history includes asthma, enuresis, and night terrors. Sociable; no substance use disorder reported. Completed high school and began business management studies. Father has bipolar disorder type I.

Two weeks before travel to Brazil, experienced 10 days of increased energy and goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep/sleep disturbance, pressured speech, increased self-esteem, and racing thoughts; reports several similar past episodes. No prior history of full manic or major depressive episodes.

Following ayahuasca consumption, developed a manic episode with psychotic features; afterward, current mental state exam shows slowed/diminished speech, depressed affect, thoughts of hopelessness/ruin, no hallucinations or delusions, marked anhedonia, apathy, and clinophilia with normal sleep and appetite. Depressive episode began immediately after remission of the preceding psychotic episode.

Contextual considerations described: symptoms not consistent with typical transient ayahuasca-induced psychosis/intoxication; ayahuasca contains harmine with antidepressant properties (serotonin effects and reversible MAO-A inhibition); concern for antidepressant-associated switch to mania in a person with prior hypomanic episodes and family history.

Adolescent female patients (approximately 14–18 years; often late teens/early 20s) presenting with already significant weight loss and reluctance to eat, with no discernible organic pathology. Amenorrhoea reported; one case had infrequent binge episodes. Restlessness and high activity levels despite severe weight loss. Low pulse rate/other physical findings attributed to nutritional compromise and progression toward starvation. Tuberculosis considered due to weight loss but no supporting evidence. No clear medical cause identified; symptoms viewed as stemming from a morbid mental state. Background stressors/family factors noted in some cases (e.g., death of a sibling, nervous symptoms, epilepsy in family members), with occasional temperamental problems.

49-year-old Caucasian woman, 5 years status post right breast surgery and radiotherapy for localized breast cancer; completed anti-estrogen therapy (tamoxifen) 6 months prior. No evidence of tumor, metastases, or recurrence on exam before study start. Psychological assessment: longstanding depressive symptoms that worsened markedly after the cancer diagnosis; severe cancer-related fatigue since diagnosis. Prior psychotherapy for 6 months, ending 5 months before study start. At study start: very high depressive symptom score on CES-D (50/60) and maximal general fatigue on MFI-20 (20/20). Married, three children, physiotherapist; upper middle class; moderate alcohol use, non-smoker. Only medication: intermittent aspirin 500 mg. Study assessments included repeated self-report ratings of mood/irritation/mental activity (28-adjective questionnaire with 4-point Likert ratings) and daily physical strain via a 10-cm visual analog scale. Serial urinary IL-6 measured by ELISA and normalized to creatinine (HPLC creatinine), with time-series cross-correlation analyses (including ARIMA modeling and detrending) to relate IL-6 to symptoms/activity.

A 51-year-old female with self-reported bipolar disorder was brought to the emergency room by police for bizarre behavior at a bus stop with incessant yelling at bystanders. She had disorganized thoughts, poor sleep, rapid speech, labile mood, distractibility, auditory hallucinations, and grandiose delusions, and was placed on an involuntary psychiatric hold. She remained in the ED due to inability to place her on droplet precautions elsewhere and inability to reliably wear an infection-prevention mask. She had flu-like symptoms with a positive influenza swab and was started on oseltamivir. Over several days she had persistent agitation/aggression requiring multiple doses of antipsychotics/benzodiazepines (including haloperidol/lorazepam/diphenhydramine IM, olanzapine, chlorpromazine, clonazepam) and was started on valproic acid; she became increasingly somnolent with slurred speech, and on medical admission her valproic acid level was 166 mcg/ml. On the day she was medically cleared for psychiatric hospitalization, she developed difficulty breathing with hypoxia and tachycardia and bilateral expiratory wheezes; she was treated with bronchodilators. Chest X-ray suggested left-sided pneumonia and she received IV ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and fluids; CT angiography was obtained to evaluate for pulmonary embolism. She was admitted to medicine and then developed worsening agitation with respiratory distress and altered mental status, could not tolerate BiPAP, and was intubated for airway protection with hypoxic respiratory failure. CT angiography showed a sub-segmental pulmonary embolus; she was transferred to the MICU with combined hypercarbic and hypoxic respiratory failure attributed to COPD exacerbation with influenza, possible hospital-acquired pneumonia, and possible pulmonary embolism in the setting of prolonged ED stay/immobility, tachycardia, and high Well's score. She was started on heparin and improved, with resolution of respiratory distress and extubation the next day.
diagnosis: Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

case_information: Baseline and end-of-treatment assessments used the PANSS to measure psychotic symptom improvement and the RBANS (Form A at baseline, Form B at end-point) to assess cognitive effects. Response was defined as ≥30% reduction in PANSS total score. Some participants could not complete RBANS subtests involving drawing and writing due to physical restraints. Because memory impairment is a common adverse effect of electroconvulsive therapy, only RBANS immediate and delayed memory scores were reported. For participants under 20 years old, RBANS scoring used 20–39-year-old norms. Acceptability was assessed via adverse events and participants’ subjective complaints elicited at the end of 10 sessions with open-ended questions about experiences during and after MST, conducted by a trained psychiatrist. A Thymatron IV device with left and right frontal leads recorded EEG during induced seizures.

73-year-old man with bipolar I disorder and remote manic episodes presented with weeks of increasing confusion, tremor/rigidity, wandering/disrobing, disorganized behavior, fluctuating attention and orientation, irregular sleep, intermittent racing thoughts and subtle expansiveness/labile mood. Initially suspected medication toxicity; serum lithium level subtoxic (0.75 mmol/L) and broad medical/neurologic workup unrevealing (CBC, glucose/electrolytes, B12/folate, EEG, cultures, CXR, VDRL; no focal neurologic signs; substance withdrawal unlikely). Brain imaging showed incidental pituitary lesion with normal pituitary hormones and chronic ischemic changes; no malignancy. Baseline functioning reportedly high with only minor short-term memory issues. Psychotropics and other potential contributors were reduced/withdrawn without resolution; confusion persisted ~4 weeks with periods of agitation alternating with drowsiness/decreased level of consciousness. Given persistence of delirium-like state with intermittent manic features and bipolar history, ECT was initiated with marked improvement in orientation, agitation, thought organization, sleep, and cognition (MoCA improved from 15/30 to 24/30) and full recovery of orientation and functioning on follow-up.

A 24-year-old unmarried male, first-year M.Pharma student from a rural background, presented with stuttering during interactions with superiors, strangers, and in groups. Onset during childhood. Raised in an orthodox/traditional environment; played solitary games most of the time; emotional expression in male child not encouraged. Physically punished by father for untidy handwriting, leading to avoidance of conversing due to expectation of negative consequences. Quarrelled with friends when ridiculed. Focused on academics to avoid confrontation. Completed B-Pharma but could not get a job due to communication difficulties; perceived teaching/marketing roles as threatening and felt incapable of handling them. Avoided interacting due to fear of rejection and negative evaluation. Experienced anxiety symptoms during speaking difficulties. Interpersonal relationship with family not cordial. Family history in elder brother and nephew. As a child, extremely shy and reserved.

A 40-year-old man with hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg for 8 years was admitted for acute-onset fearfulness for 1 day. He had a 20-year history of progressively increasing alcohol use with episodes of loss of control, strong desire/compulsion to drink, and neglect of alternative interests. His last alcohol intake was a few days before admission and he had not previously quit. Family reported sudden behavioral change with suspiciousness toward his wife and others, believing policemen and armed people were following him and conspiring to kill him; he was unable to trust anyone and was convinced he would be harmed. He had decreased sleep and appetite, was apprehensive and guarded, with fearful mood, restlessness and vigilance. He reported visual phenomena: seeing his exact double (mirror-reversed) briefly (2–3 seconds) at dawn/dusk a couple of times, and initially seeing other people in small sizes. He had minimal hand tremor on extension; vitals stable and systemic exam unremarkable. Baseline labs were largely normal; liver function slightly deranged and ultrasound showed hepatomegaly with fatty changes. EEG was planned but not done. Treated with lorazepam, thiamine/multivitamins, and low-dose risperidone with gradual resolution of symptoms over several days; followed by abstinence-focused motivation/relapse prevention and tapering medications, remaining well on follow-up.

A 62-year-old Chinese female admitted for recurrent episodes of uncontrollable screaming and shaking of all four limbs for 4 days, occurring 2–3 times daily. Episodes were abrupt in onset, lasting minutes to an hour. Prodrome of uncomfortable coldness in the chest spreading to both arms and legs, becoming tingling followed by involuntary tremors. She reported feeling out of control, alternating laughing and crying, shouting incomprehensibly, and flailing her limbs. Associated fatigue and diaphoresis. No loss of consciousness and no amnesia. Persistent worry about future episodes and marked distress.

In the emergency department, an observed episode resolved within minutes after intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg; a subsequent episode 10 minutes later resolved within minutes after intravenous midazolam 1 mg.

Similar episodes occurred 3 years prior post-operatively after left open radical nephrectomy (received morphine intra-operatively and tramadol post-operatively). At that time, EEG and MRI brain were normal; episodes ceased after tramadol was stopped and clobazam was started.

Past psychiatric history included a prior diagnosis of major depressive disorder with low mood and fleeting suicidal thoughts in the post-operative period; treated with escitalopram up to 10 mg nightly for 2 years, later stopped.

No significant personal or family history of neurological or psychiatric illness. Medical history: essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus. No substance use.

On admission: normal vital signs, no focal neurological deficits. Mental state: neatly dressed, good eye contact, pleasant; euthymic with reactive affect; coherent relevant speech; no thought disorder, hallucinations, or delusions on exam. Investigations unremarkable including CT brain, EEG, and blood tests (thyroid function, electrolytes, renal and liver panels, full blood count, folate, vitamin B12).

During inpatient stay, she expressed new passive suicidal ideation due to distress from the episodes; denied preceding depressive/anxious symptoms and collateral history did not identify major psychosocial stressors.
