With further exploration, she disclosed spiritual concerns about “evil spirits,” including a belief that a past surgery had been delayed because they were “after” her, and prior experiences of hearing chanting for a week after surgery and seeing a “rotting corpse” on her bed. She believed supernatural forces caused the episodes and that they resolved with medication and religious blessings. She later reported similar episodes first occurred 30 years ago after an abortion and lasted a week, associated with guilt and shame despite spousal support.

40-year-old male brought to hospital by police with a court reception order after complaints from sister and neighbors. For ~4 years he held fixed beliefs that people in his locality were enemies who would kill him and his family; he prevented wife and children from leaving the house, stopped children from attending school, and spent the day guarding the gate. Unemployed and staying at home for 4 years. Further evaluation noted antisocial personality disorder and alcohol abuse. Over the last 1 year, his wife and children developed the same belief that local people wanted to kill them, stopped communication with neighbors/relatives, and became socially isolated; they had no prior psychiatric history but showed dependent personality traits. Family members were closely associated and none were employed. Onset of similar symptoms in other family members occurred about 3 years after onset in the primary patient. Family history: mother with unspecified psychiatric illness. No medical illness. Treated with risperidone (titrated to 6 mg/day) and ECT during ~2-month admission; wife/children refused treatment but their beliefs weakened over 2 months with limited contact. After discharge, family refused separation; patient was nonadherent and lost to follow-up after four outpatient visits.

A 33-year-old woman developed a severe depressive episode 4 weeks after her first delivery, with sleep disturbance and guilt. No personal or family history of psychiatric disorders. Routine physical examination and laboratory tests were normal. She wished to continue breastfeeding while receiving antidepressant treatment. She was treated at home with agomelatine 25 mg nightly for 12 weeks, with instructions to feed the infant before dosing and avoid breastfeeding overnight until pumping milk the next morning; daytime breastfeeding continued. Follow-up assessments every 2–4 weeks using the Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology–Self Report (16 items). Marked symptom improvement by week 4 (notably sleep), remission by week 8. Biochemical tests for mother and infant remained normal; infant development normal; no adverse events reported during treatment or after discontinuation.
diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset

case_information: Retail/online bank workers report intensified work pace and loss of the consultant/service role due to centrally issued monthly "production lists" requiring contact with specific customers to obtain appointments and sell mandated products regardless of customer needs. Workers feel constrained to meet preset sales targets and describe the experience as being like "caged chickens." Performance is perceived as rigorously monitored, quantified, and measured via new technologies by branch and area managers, with unclear/opaque evaluation criteria; despite formal claims that evaluation is unrelated to sales results, workers believe commercial campaign outcomes significantly affect appraisal.

54-year-old single, unemployed man with chronic, treatment-resistant psychotic illness and multiple psychiatric hospitalizations; past ECT twice; type 2 diabetes mellitus. One year of worsening persecutory/reference beliefs and auditory hallucinations with functional decline and a suicide attempt; recurrent readmissions; poor response to multiple antipsychotics and combinations; brief prior trial of clozapine discontinued for non-hematologic reasons. After transfer to chronic ward, refused medications and had aggravated hallucinatory behavior with commanding voices leading to self-harm. Clozapine restarted (100 mg/day titrated upward) with concurrent long-acting antipsychotic, benzodiazepines, laxatives, and oral hypoglycemic. Marked symptom improvement after 2 weeks but developed significant eosinophilia (up to 4.0 × 10^9/L, 34% of WBC). Medical evaluation (cardiac enzymes, ECG, liver function, renal indices, amylase/lipase, ESR, CRP) showed no evidence of myocarditis, hepatitis, nephritis, pancreatitis, or other inflammatory/end-organ involvement. Hematology recommended continuing the medication with close CBC monitoring; eosinophilia peaked during titration then resolved to normal within weeks as the dose was increased; partial remission of psychotic symptoms and no end-organ inflammation at discharge.

20-year-old unmarried male with onset of psychotic symptoms at 17 years (auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, disorganized thinking, violent/aggressive behavior). Initially modest academic functioning with mild hallucinations/paranoid ideation on paliperidone 3 mg/day; relapse after stopping medication. Multiple antipsychotic trials/augmentations (paliperidone, aripiprazole with biperiden, fluoxetine added for compulsive hand washing, risperidone oral solution, flupentixol decanoate) with poor symptom control and escalating aggression. Notable sensitivity to medication adverse effects including restlessness and parkinsonism; exam showed subtle left-sided weakness and mild rigidity with otherwise stable gait/ADLs. Brain CT/MRI demonstrated extensive bilateral intracranial calcifications involving globus pallidus, caudate nuclei, thalami, and subcortical areas without vascular abnormalities. Blood tests including ceruloplasmin, vitamin D, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, thyroid/parathyroid hormones, and alkaline phosphatase were normal. Genetic testing identified an SLC20A2 gene variant. After regimen adjustment, stabilized on risperidone 1.5 mg/day, valproic acid 1500 mg/day, and quetiapine 37.5 mg/day with residual mild psychotic symptoms but no disruptive behavior. CASI 75/100 with deficits in attention and abstract thinking/judgment; continued persecutory beliefs and passivity phenomena; agreed to long-term inpatient rehabilitation.

14.4-year-old girl with history of social and generalized anxiety disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and autistic traits. Over 1–2 years developed progressively restrictive eating: previously picky but would eat preferred foods; now refuses even preferred foods. Meals described by parents as a struggle; increased rigidity/controlling behavior, severe temper tantrums, sleep problems, and poor concentration. Appeared younger than age and showed marked hyperactivity/restlessness during consultation despite previously being a good student and no prior ADHD/school/behavior history. Weight at assessment ~3rd percentile; ~90% of expected based on growth curve with longstanding low appetite/underweight and selective eating. Grade 9 with 2-year history of social isolation and increased school anxiety; past bullying in elementary school; no recent acute stressor/trauma. Medical work-up negative. Family-based renourishment plus low-dose olanzapine; weight improved, eating variety increased, hyperactivity/restlessness diminished, increased engagement in therapy. Returned to partial school attendance with supervised snack/lunch. After reaching target weight, olanzapine stopped; fluvoxamine started for anxiety—higher dose caused agitation/pacing that resolved when dose reduced. By end of treatment: able to sit through sessions, less irritable, more cheerful/affectionate, more mature/articulate. Weight increased from 37.4 kg (93% TGW) to 46.5 kg (>100% of recalculated TGW).

33-year-old female with history of asthma and depression presented with 3 days of shortness of breath at rest worse with exertion, productive cough with yellow sputum, reported fever to 105°F at home, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia; denied recent infections, travel, or sick contacts. On arrival: T 98.8°F, HR 117 bpm, BP 86/43 mmHg, RR 20/min, O2 sat 97% on 2 L nasal cannula. Exam: tachypneic with crackles in right posterior lung field, no wheezing; tachycardic without murmurs; no rashes/skin lesions; neurologically intact. Labs: WBC 28,900/µL with neutrophilia and bands; lactate 3.1 mmol/L; CMP unremarkable; ABG pH 7.4, PaCO2 38, PaO2 98, HCO3 24; influenza A/B and COVID-19 negative. Imaging: chest X-ray with dense right upper lobe consolidation; CT angiography with severe dense consolidation of entire right upper lobe with air bronchograms and patchy consolidations in right middle/lower lobes. Treated with sepsis protocol (fluids, norepinephrine) and empiric vancomycin, cefepime, azithromycin; admitted to ICU. Over 4 days developed worsening respiratory failure and persistent leukocytosis; blood/sputum cultures and urine Legionella antigen negative; urine streptococcal antigen positive. Day 5 X-ray showed worsening dense right-sided pneumonia with new contralateral left lower field consolidation; intubated, lung-protective ventilation with prone positioning for persistent hypoxia; bronchoscopy initially showed inflamed mucosa without purulence/lesions/bleeding; BAL bacterial culture, fungal stain, and AFB stain negative; HIV negative; echo EF 55–60%. Day 8: bilateral lung whiteout and severe ARDS with PaO2/FiO2 98; required venovenous ECMO. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, systemic steroids, and vasopressors, no recovery; repeat bronchoscopy showed targetoid ulcerative lesions and airway erythema/edema with left mainstem narrowing; serum HSV PCR positive; BAL differential with mixed inflammatory cells; tissue studies negative for Gram stain, AFB, fungal stains, EBV, and CMV; no oral/genital/perianal/cutaneous vesicles noted. Treated with antivirals (ganciclovir then acyclovir) but progressed to multiorgan failure and died.

An 87-year-old female with a past medical history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, breast cancer (on letrozole), and diverticulosis was brought to the hospital with altered mental status and shortness of breath. In the emergency room, patient was hypoxic with labored breathing and was intubated. Her laboratory tests revealed white blood cell count of 9.9 x 103/mcL, D-dimer of 2.23 mg/L, and procalcitonin of 6.84 ng/mL. Computed tomography of the chest showed diffuse bilateral patchy ground glass infiltrates. Sputum cultures came back positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Patient was treated with remdesivir and dexamethasone. Patient was treated with ceftriaxone. Patient was extubated 2 weeks later but went into respiratory failure requiring reintubation. Patient got a tracheostomy and feeding tube placement. She had a prolonged stay in the hospital for a month. She was weaned to tracheostomy collar and transferred to a rehabilitation facility.

A 6-year-old boy with 2 months of recurrent breathlessness and cough after accidentally aspirating the base cap of a pen. Initial emergency rigid bronchoscopy at a private facility did not find any object; he improved slightly with medications. He re-presented to two tertiary hospitals where repeat bronchoscopies 4 weeks apart again failed to demonstrate any object; he was labeled with asthma and improved symptomatically on bronchodilators. Symptoms recurred; chest x-ray appeared normal. Repeat rigid bronchoscopy showed a pedunculated subglottic mass that was excised; histology showed fibrocartilaginous tissue devoid of epithelium; symptoms improved transiently. About 2 weeks later he returned with severe respiratory distress. Neck and chest CT demonstrated a thin mass just above and straddling the carina. Repeat combined flexible and rigid bronchoscopy identified an airway object covered with granulation tissue, which was extracted with complete symptom resolution.

50-year-old man admitted with progressive dyspnea, cough, cold sweats; year-long night sweats and 15 kg weight loss. Known HIV infection since 2003 with prior opportunistic pneumonia; had stopped antiretroviral therapy 1 year earlier. Lives in a homeless shelter. On admission: tachypneic, SpO2 88% on room air, HR 132/min, T 38.2°C; lungs mostly normal on auscultation except left lower side. Labs: CRP 64 mg/L, Hb 7.2 mmol/L, WBC 6.6×10^9/L, platelets 214×10^9/L; no renal/hepatic insufficiency. Immunology: CD4 0.039×10^9/L, CD8 1.2×10^9/L, CD4/CD8 ratio 0.033. Chest X-ray: bilateral diffuse ‘cloudy’ infiltrates. Treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics then cotrimoxazole and prednisolone for suspected opportunistic pneumonia; bronchoscopy with BAL performed. Immediately post-procedure developed acute dyspnea, hypoxemia (SpO2 82%) and subcutaneous emphysema; progressed to respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. CT chest after intubation: subcutaneous and mediastinal emphysema without pneumothorax; bilateral infiltrates/air bronchograms. On ICU: worsening extensive subcutaneous and mediastinal emphysema with swelling of face, arms, torso to scrotum; multiple bronchoscopies and CT scans showed no tracheal injury. Despite lung-protective ventilation, emphysema progressed; managed with infraclavicular skin incisions and negative-pressure wound therapy (VAC) at -125 mm Hg with subsequent marked improvement. Extubated after 17 days; ICU-acquired weakness and dysphonia noted; discharged to ward then rehabilitation; antiretroviral therapy restarted; viral load noted at 700,000 copies/mL during ICU course.

A 13-year-old boy with 3 months of cough and sputum after an episode where a wheat spike was inhaled during a deep breath, followed by coughing and choking/asphyxia. Evaluation for suspected airway foreign material included fiberoptic bronchoscopy showing a plant-like material in the right lower lobe bronchus with severely inflamed mucosa; removal attempt failed due to profuse bleeding. Chest X-ray and CT were obtained. Rigid bronchoscopy again found the material in the right lower lobe with extensive surrounding granulation tissue; removal attempts caused heavy bleeding and the object was fixed and could not be extracted. Thoracotomy revealed an inflammatory peripheral lung mass; opening the area entered a 2×2 cm pus-filled cavity containing the stalk, which was removed. The cavity was irrigated and a bronchial opening repaired; chest tube placed; postoperative broad-spectrum antibiotics given; chest tube removed after one week and discharged. Follow-up: mild hemoptysis with blood-streaked sputum during the first postoperative year; CT showed limited bronchiectasis localized to the affected area, which resolved with conservative management.

11-year-old boy with 2-day history of intermittent mild hemoptysis after a brief febrile episode (max 38.0°C) 6 days earlier and minor abdominal trauma (elbow injury) 3 days before admission. Progressed to recurrent coughing of bright/dark red blood 2–4 times/day (~30–40 mL/24 h), then on night of admission >10 episodes of 20–30 mL each with chest tightness and chest pain. No palpitations, epistaxis, skin bleeding, altered consciousness, hematuria, bloody stool, weight loss. On admission: afebrile, RR 30, HR 92, BP 107/80, SpO2 99% RA; decreased breath sounds right lung. Labs: WBC ~10×10^9/L, hemoglobin 141 then 134 g/L, platelets normal; CRP <0.2 mg/L; normal coagulation; normal liver/biochem/myocardial enzymes/urinalysis/ESR; negative infectious testing (bacteria, mycoplasma, TB, fungi); normal echocardiogram. Chest radiograph initially read as right lower pneumonia; later concern for right lung hemorrhage. Chest CTA: intra-alveolar hemorrhage, partial right bronchial stenosis, right middle-lobe atelectasis, partial right lower-lobe consolidation; pulmonary CTA without significant abnormalities. CTA/angiography: bronchial arteries with abnormal origin/course and dilated lumen; aortic angiography showed an ectopic bronchial artery arising from the right renal artery supplying the right lower lung with tortuous/disordered peripheral vessels and early visualization of pulmonary artery branch suggesting a bronchial–pulmonary artery fistula. Interventional embolization performed (microspheres/coil) with cessation of hemoptysis. Post-procedure right lung atelectasis due to airway clot burden; bronchoscopy removed large clots from right main/upper/middle bronchi with resolution of symptoms and atelectasis. No recurrent hemoptysis during 1.5-year follow-up; chest radiographs normal.

According to Canadian Airway Focus Group guidelines, the patient was assessed as having multiple risk factors for difficulty with mask ventilation, supraglottic airway ventilation, tracheal intubation by direct or video laryngoscopy, and extubation. A plan was agreed upon for flexible nasal intubation under topical anesthesia and sedation, aiming to minimize anxiety and stress, maintain spontaneous breathing, and allow rapid recovery if the procedure needed to be aborted. Remimazolam was selected as the primary anxiolytic, with special attention to optimal topicalization of the airway.

A 46-year-old man presented in early 2012 with a 16-year history of recurrent respiratory tract infections. He first presented in 1996 and in 2004 developed an empyema requiring thoracotomy and drainage. After drainage he remained relatively well but needed infrequent oral antibiotics for exacerbations of bronchiectasis, with repeated episodes of right basal pneumonia. Sputum culture grew Haemophilus influenzae. High-resolution CT in 2004 showed bronchiectasis, confirmed on repeat imaging eight years later. Past history included right lower lobe childhood bronchiectasis diagnosed after an episode of haemoptysis. A further HRCT demonstrated an intraluminal, solid area of high attenuation in the right lower lobe bronchus intermedius, with appearances consistent with an endobronchial foreign body or calcified secretion.

21-year-old male with history of mild childhood asthma presented to the emergency department with sudden onset chest and neck pain. Salbutamol provided no relief. Denied trauma or infective symptoms; no cardiovascular risk factors. Usual weightlifting two days prior without unusually strenuous activity. Reported inhaling a small amount of cocaine and ingesting two MDMA tablets about 20 hours before symptom onset while dancing. Exam: no airway compromise; subcutaneous emphysema in bilateral subclavian regions; tachycardia, hyperthermia, hyperreflexia. Nasendoscopy normal. Labs: mildly elevated CK 231, leukocytosis 14. Chest X-ray: significant mediastinal air and subcutaneous emphysema; CT: retropharyngeal emphysema extending from the aortic arch to the base of skull; no pneumothorax or pneumorrhachis. Gastrografin swallow: no contrast extravasation. Managed conservatively with monitoring; imaging on hospital day 3 showed resolution and patient discharged.

21-year-old male with 75% TBSA deep dermal to full-thickness burns and inhalation injury developed acute kidney failure requiring renal replacement therapy on day 2. Developed severe ARDS requiring initiation of veno-venous ECMO on day 6 after prone positioning and inhaled nitric oxide failed to improve respiratory function. After ECMO weaning and removal on day 19, later developed severe fungal bloodstream infection with respiratory insufficiency, PaO2/FiO2 59 mmHg and pH 6.99, requiring emergency recannulation for veno-venous ECMO on day 40. Despite maximal ECMO blood and oxygen flow, persistent systemic hypoxia attributed to hyperdynamic septic circulation with insufficient ECMO blood flow relative to cardiac output; an additional arterial outflow cannula placed in the brachiocephalic trunk to oxygenate the brain (V-V-A ECMO), followed by rapid lactate decline and improved systemic oxygenation. Successfully weaned from ECMO by day 62 and discharged to rehabilitation after prolonged hospitalization.

35-year-old Caucasian male evaluated in an adult program in 2002 with a history since age 16 of persistent cough and recurrent bronchitis. Sweat chloride testing repeatedly elevated at 79 mmol/L and 86 mmol/L. Produces ~1 tablespoon sputum daily; sputum cultures often grow Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenza, occasionally Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Genetic testing initially showed one F508del CFTR allele with the second allele unidentified; later full CFTR sequencing identified A457P (exon 10) in combination with F508del. No childhood issues aside from tonsillectomy. No problems maintaining weight and no steatorrhea; BMI 21.6 kg/m2 (104% ideal). Normal vitals; room-air oxygen saturation 96%. No nasal polyps or sinus tenderness. Trace digital clubbing. Spirometry: moderate obstructive defect (FVC 5.29 L, 91% predicted; FEV1 2.71 L, 62% predicted). Chest X-ray: significant hyperinflation and increased linear markings in right lower lung zones and perihilar regions. Normal liver function tests, fat-soluble vitamin levels, renal function, glucose, and CBC. Infertility evaluation showed atretic vasa deferentia confirmed by transrectal ultrasound with semen analysis demonstrating azoospermia. Lung function remained above national median from ages 17–20 while engaged with specialty care, then after being lost to follow-up from age 20 to 35 had accelerated decline in pulmonary function.

Male born full term underwent oesophageal atresia repair on day 1 of life. From 4 months of age had recurrent brief resolved unexplained events, frequent lung infections requiring hospital admissions, oesophageal dilations, and episodes of food lodging in the oesophagus causing respiratory difficulties. At 14 years continued eating difficulties with food frequently lodging and causing airway collapse symptoms; also reported poor physical activity performance. Bronchoscopy showed moderate collapse of the lower tracheal segment. Underwent surgical intervention at age 14. Postoperative course complicated by pneumothorax and atelectasis; discharged after 9 days. Three months later had another food impaction without respiratory difficulties. Eight months later bronchoscopy showed reduced posterior wall intrusion; spirometry flow-volume curve improved with normalised expiratory slope. At 18-month follow-up reported improved physical activity and complete relief from respiratory difficulties triggered by lodged food.

A 71-year-old man with COPD and chronic hypoxemic respiratory failure on 2 L/min supplemental oxygen, heavy smoking history, and multiple comorbidities presented with 10 days of worsening shortness of breath. SARS-CoV-2 and group A strep tests were negative. He had been treated empirically with oral levofloxacin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia, but his oxygen requirement increased to 4 L/min and his productive cough worsened with blood-streaked sputum (no fresh blood or clots). He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable with oxygen saturation 98% on 4 L/min nasal cannula. Labs showed peripheral eosinophilia (9.2%, absolute 770/µL), markedly elevated ESR (104 mm/hr), elevated CRP (18.1 mg/dL), and elevated IgE (848 IU/mL). Chest x-ray showed migratory peripheral right upper and middle lung opacities. CT chest showed peripheral right upper lobe opacities including a focal 5 × 3.2 cm area, right hilar lymphadenopathy, emphysematous changes, and a few scattered pulmonary nodules. Additional work-up was negative (viral respiratory panel; ANA/ANCA; bacterial and fungal blood cultures; beta-(1,3)-D-glucan; Strongyloides IgG; urine Legionella antigen). Bronchoscopy was deferred due to comorbidities. He was treated with oral prednisone 40 mg daily with gradual symptom improvement; at 1-month follow-up, symptoms improved, eosinophilia resolved, and CT showed resolution of the right upper lobe opacities.

A 42-year-old woman with a tracheal lesion, previously macroscopically resected with rigid bronchoscopy, was scheduled for tracheal resection and reconstruction. She had no comorbidities. Intraoperative management included standard monitoring (ECG, pulse oximetry, EtCO2, blood pressure, depth of anesthesia monitoring), induction with lidocaine, fentanyl, propofol, and rocuronium, placement of an iGel laryngeal mask airway, arterial line placement, and bronchoscopic airway topicalization with 2% lidocaine. A thoracic epidural catheter (T6–T7) was placed and dosed with ropivacaine and fentanyl; anesthesia was maintained with propofol, dexmedetomidine, and sufentanil infusions. A vagus nerve block with ropivacaine was performed. Spontaneous ventilation was restored after reversal with sugammadex and supported with minimal pressure support and low PEEP, maintaining oxygen saturation >95%. Robotic thoracic approach via a single right 4th intercostal incision was used; pleura anterior to trachea was dissected, the vagus nerve was tacked posteriorly, the lesion was localized under bronchoscopic guidance, the trachea was transected above and below the lesion, and two tracheal rings were removed, followed by tracheal reconstruction with continuous suture and a negative leak test. FiO2 was transiently reduced below 30% during monopolar cutting, then increased to maintain oxygenation during reconstruction. Emergency backup ventilation strategies were prepared but not needed. ABG during reconstruction showed pH 7.30, pCO2 43 mmHg, pO2 100 mmHg; hemodynamics and oxygenation remained stable. Emergence was uneventful; postoperative course included epidural and multimodal analgesia with mild pain and no nausea/vomiting; discharged home on postoperative day 9.

63-year-old male with asthma, nasal polyposis, and chronic rhinosinusitis referred in 2018 for difficult-to-control asthma and suspected reactions to several analgesic/anti-inflammatory drugs. History of intermittent abdominal pain since 2000 with recurrent peripheral eosinophilia. In 2006 admitted for refractory abdominal pain and postprandial symptoms; celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and infection excluded; upper endoscopy showed duodenal eosinophilic inflammation and symptoms improved with systemic corticosteroids. In 2017 readmitted for uncontrolled abdominal pain with moderate eosinophilia; upper endoscopy and ileocolonoscopy showed eosinophilic inflammation involving multiple GI segments with dense eosinophilic infiltrates (>50 cells/HPF in ileum and colon) and endoscopic erosions/hyperemia. Work-up excluded eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (negative ANCA; normal ECG/echocardiogram; normal thoracic CT; skin biopsy without vasculitis). Respiratory history includes progressive cough, dyspnea, and wheeze despite inhaled therapy; spirometry with obstructive pattern and bronchodilator response. Reported dyspnea with multiple NSAIDs (nimesulide, aspirin, diclofenac, metamizole), consistent with NSAID-exacerbated respiratory reactions; provocation testing not performed due to systemic steroids. From 2019 required frequent systemic corticosteroids for worsening GI symptoms; treated with benralizumab with marked improvement in asthma control and GI symptoms, normalization of blood eosinophils, steroid dose reduction, and subsequent endoscopic remission of GI eosinophilic inflammation.

A 68-year-old man with cardiac amyloidosis developed a postoperative condition following heart transplantation. Lymphangiography via inguinal lymph node access showed no leaks and no distinct cisterna chyli. The thoracic duct was accessed via direct cervical percutaneous cannulation at its confluence with the left subclavian vein under ultrasound guidance with fluoroscopic confirmation. Retrograde cannulation allowed fluoroscopic visualization of a leak, treated with embolization using microcoils and a liquid embolic agent (ethylene vinyl alcohol). Chylous output decreased to ~200 mL/day after embolization, but pleural fluid re-accumulated and thoracic duct ligation was performed 15 days later, with no recurrence during 1.39-year follow-up.

15-month-old boy with recurrent viral and RSV infections presented RSV-positive on viral RT-PCR and was admitted to the PICU for respiratory failure requiring intubation with prolonged respiratory support. Treated with high-dose IV steroids, HFOV, nitric oxide, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. During hospitalization had persistent viral positivity with continued RSV plus rhinovirus and enterovirus. Immune evaluation showed absent pneumococcal titers despite age-appropriate pneumococcal vaccinations; formal evaluation limited by inability to receive Pneumovax due to age. Developed progressive T-cell lymphopenia (partly attributed to steroids). Genetic testing showed a heterozygous pathogenic CARD9 variant (p.Val13Ile) with increased susceptibility to opportunistic fungal infections; started on Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis due to low T-cell count. Did not follow expected RSV course (no improvement after 5–7 days), with prolonged intubation and persistent viral positivity raising concern for immune dysregulation. Clinical status improved marginally after IVIG 500 mg/kg on day 18, then improved after ASCENIV 500 mg/kg; by day 28 RSV cleared on sequential rapid test and RT-PCR. Planned to continue immunoglobulin replacement until reevaluation; T-cell counts later improved and PJP prophylaxis was discontinued.

A 14-year-old previously healthy boy presented with left periorbital swelling and redness for 1 year and progressive muscle weakness and joint pain for 4 months. Exam showed violaceous discoloration and swelling around the left eye, papules over the metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, and proximal muscle weakness (3/5) with distal weakness (4/5). Labs: CBC normal, ESR 33 mm/hr, CRP 0.383 mg/L; AST 281 U/L, ALT 95 U/L, ALP 149 U/L, GGT 24 U/L; creatine kinase 4585 U/L. ANA negative and ENA panel negative; renal and thyroid function normal. MRI of muscles demonstrated diffuse muscle edema involving pelvis, thighs, legs, upper extremities, and back consistent with inflammatory myopathy. CT orbit showed anteromedial/superior left orbital soft tissue swelling with minimal postcontrast enhancement, appearing as left preseptal periorbital cellulitis without abscess. Lower lid biopsy showed no malignant cells or acid-fast bacilli; tuberculosis culture negative after 8 weeks. Muscle biopsy: perivascular chronic inflammatory infiltrates in perimysial areas with scattered mononuclear cells between fibers, mild-moderate fiber size variation, myofiber necrosis/regeneration, focal perifascicular atrophy; ultrastructural myofibrillar disarray with scattered rod-like structures and cytoplasmic bodies. Skin biopsy from left lower lid: mild hyperkeratosis with heavy chronic lymphoplasmacytic inflammation around hair follicles, mild dermal fibrosis, focal solar elastosis, and pigment incontinence. Treated with prednisolone and methotrexate with marked improvement over 6 months (normalized strength, fading rash, reduced muscle enzymes).

24-year-old woman with 3 years of recurrent episodic right-sided headaches and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, often preceded by vertigo. New episode with more severe right hemicranial headache of different character with retro-orbital pain for 15 days, followed 10 days later by diplopia and progressive right eyelid drooping. Exam: feeble left radial and brachial pulses; marked inter-arm blood pressure difference (right 170/110 mm Hg, left 90/60 mm Hg); bilateral renal bruits (left > right). Neurologic exam: right third and fourth cranial nerve palsies; otherwise normal. Labs: ESR 88 mm/hr; routine urine/CBC/biochemistry normal. Extensive autoimmune/vasculitis serologies negative (RF, ANA, anti-dsDNA, antiphospholipid Ab, PR3-ANCA, MPO-ANCA). Infectious testing negative (VDRL, HIV, hepatitis B/C); chest X-ray, calcium, ACE normal; TB screening (TST/Quantiferon) negative. CSF: 2 lymphocytes/mm3, protein 75 mg/dl, glucose 78 mg/dl (serum 112); cytology negative; CSF gram/AFB stains, fungal studies, VDRL, cultures, and TB PCR negative. Brain MRI: thickened enhancing pachymeninges in bilateral frontal and right temporal regions extending to cavernous sinus; T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in right temporal lobe. DSA: stenosis of left subclavian artery distal to vertebral origin, ostial stenosis of left renal artery, and narrowing of abdominal aorta at renal artery level with normal terminal aorta and common iliacs. Echo: mild aortic regurgitation with normal LV function. EEG: intermittent epileptiform discharges over right temporal region. Meningeal biopsy declined. Treated with high-dose prednisolone with resolution of cranial nerve palsies and normalization of ESR; blood pressure controlled on atenolol and seizures on phenytoin; persistent inter-arm BP difference; follow-up CT at 6 months showed resolution of meningeal enhancement; remained asymptomatic at 1 year with normal ESR and renal function.

27-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes (mild retinopathy and neuropathy) and inflammatory arthritis treated over years with NSAIDs, methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and then monthly golimumab with sustained remission. Later developed new-onset hypertension with preserved renal function. In 2015, routine 24-hour urine showed albuminuria (420.53 mg/dU) and proteinuria (0.47 g/dU), with oscillatory hypertension and occasional ankle oedema. Labs: mild anemia, normal electrolytes, normal BUN/creatinine and preserved eGFR, low-normal serum albumin, normal CRP with ESR 20 mm/h; normal serum protein electrophoresis and immunoglobulins. Immunologic workup negative/unremarkable (C3/C4, ANCA, ANA/ENA, anti-GBM). Hepatitis B/C and HIV negative. Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys with hyperechogenic parenchyma. Kidney biopsy: diffuse mesangial hypercellularity; small perihilar segmental sclerosis in 1/17 glomeruli; tubular degenerative changes; arterial intimal deposits; no interstitial inflammation/fibrosis. Immunofluorescence: diffuse mesangial IgA with moderate C3 and lambda light chains; low IgM and kappa; no IgG/C1q/fibrin; moderate C3 in arteries. Electron microscopy: mesangial inflammatory infiltrates and several subendothelial/subepithelial deposits; some podocyte loss; no features of diabetic nephropathy. After ACE inhibitor, proteinuria progressed to 3.0 g/dU with stable eGFR, prompting discontinuation of golimumab and treatment with cyclophosphamide plus prednisone, then azathioprine with tapering steroids, leading to improving proteinuria and stable eGFR. Later switched to rituximab for arthritis control; azathioprine stopped; subsequent complete resolution of proteinuria (0.09 g/dU) with normal kidney function and controlled blood pressure.

Thirty minutes after administration of PBV, a 63-year-old woman developed profound hypotension with systolic blood pressure falling to 65 mmHg. No cutaneous manifestations were noted, and there was no laryngeal oedema or bronchospasm. She improved after treatment with three 3 mg boluses of ephedrine, 200 mg hydrocortisone, 10 mg chlorpheniramine, 1 litre crystalloid and 500 mL colloid over 30 minutes. Six weeks later, skin prick testing showed a 6 mm positive response to PBV, with negative responses to all other drugs tested. Past history included mild asthma and wheeze within 2 hours of ibuprofen ingestion on two occasions without other associated features.

A 59-year-old Japanese man presented with a 1-year history of nasal obstruction and a 2-month history of slight headache. Nasal examination showed swelling and crust formation of the bilateral inferior turbinate. CT showed mucosal swelling in the bilateral ethmoid sinuses and soft-tissue filling in the right sphenoid sinus. Endoscopic sinus surgery revealed easy bleeding and granulomatous mucosa in the bilateral ethmoid sinuses; histopathology showed necrotizing vasculitis with multinucleated giant cells. Systemic evaluation showed no abnormalities on brain MRI or chest CT; urinalysis without hematuria or proteinuria; normal tympanic membranes; no hearing or visual loss. Serum PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA were negative. Eighteen months later, he developed diplopia and sudden severe right-sided headache. Endoscopy showed slight edematous mucosa; the right sphenoid sinus opening was closed by granulation. CT demonstrated a right sphenoid sinus lesion eroding the clivus with dural thickening; gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI showed dural thickening around the right cavernous sinus and clivus. MRA/cerebral angiography showed narrowing at the C5 portion of the internal carotid artery; no ischemic attack. PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA remained negative. Treated with IV methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral prednisolone and cyclophosphamide, later tapered and transitioned to azathioprine; headache resolved immediately, imaging showed reduced dural thickening and improved ICA flow; persistent right abducens nerve palsy and mild saddle nose deformity.

A 45-year-old male with no significant medical history was urgently admitted (February 2018) for polyarthritis and splenomegaly. On admission: leukopenia (1.31 x 10^3/µl), mild normocytic anaemia, neutropenia (0.51 x 10^3/µl), lymphopenia (0.54 x 10^3/µl), elevated CRP (16.57 mg/l), low-titre rheumatoid factor (23 IU/ml), and ANA 1:320. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly to 192 mm. Hydrocortisone stimulation test showed no adequate rise in neutrophils (no increase ≥ 2 x 10^3/µl). Bone marrow aspiration biopsy excluded a proliferative process. Rheumatology evaluation showed active, symmetrical peripheral inflammatory arthritis with DAS28 6.5; joint ultrasound confirmed synovitis. Anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) > 200 U/ml; ENA and anti-dsDNA negative. Neutrophil count remained < 1.5 x 10^3/µl with splenomegaly and persistent cytopenias.

Treatment course: initially glucocorticosteroids plus hydroxychloroquine 200 mg/day (Feb 2018–May 2019) without ability to taper prednisone below 20 mg/day; persistent high disease activity (DAS28 > 5.1), elevated inflammatory markers, and ongoing neutropenia requiring intermittent granulocyte growth factors and antibiotic prophylaxis. Splenic artery embolization (March 2019) did not increase neutrophils. Hydroxychloroquine stopped due to retinal pigment epithelial defects; cyclosporine A trial stopped after 10 days due to hypertension. Methotrexate started Aug 2019 (10 mg weekly) with inadequate control and continued steroid dependence. Etanercept initiated with improvement after 3 months (DAS28 < 3.2) and steroids discontinued, but after 8 months recurrent leukopenia/neutropenia and new thrombocytopenia (platelets 90–130 x 10^3/µl); platelet counts improved off etanercept and fell again on rechallenge, so etanercept discontinued. Rituximab started Dec 2020 with remission: no active arthritis, low inflammatory markers, leukocytes increased, neutrophils stabilized at 1–2 x 10^3/µl, platelets normalized (170–200 x 10^3/µl), no further glucocorticosteroids required.

60-year-old Vietnamese man with recurrent mouth and genital ulcers; long history of pulmonary artery aneurysm and erythema nodosum. Presents after 10 years lost to follow-up with low back and buttock pain and >60–90 minutes of morning stiffness. Plain film X-rays show bilateral sclerosis of the anterior inferior iliac portion of the sacroiliac joints bilaterally. Concurrent nongranulomatous panuveitis treated with corticosteroid eye drops. Contrast-enhanced chest CT shows no interstitial lung disease or adenopathy. Treated with infliximab 5 mg/kg with remission.

45-year-old man admitted (Dec 2016) with chronic, treatment-resistant diarrhea, fatigue, bilateral leg edema, and weight loss; history of difficult-to-treat diarrhea since 2000. Markedly low serum immunoglobulins (IgG 0.67 g/L, IgA 0.02 g/L, IgM 0.156 g/L). 2012 upper endoscopy: atrophic gastritis; chronic duodenitis with partial–subtotal villous atrophy (Marsh 3A–3B); celiac serology (IgA/IgG anti-transglutaminase) negative. Colonoscopy/ileoscopy: terminal ileum severe edema with nodular appearance; biopsy confirmed nodular lymphoid hyperplasia. Gluten-free diet led to resolution of diarrhea and weight gain. Past: central diabetes insipidus treated with desmopressin; right leg deep vein thrombosis treated with acenocoumarol for 3 years; episodes of severe/protracted infections (e.g., panaritium after minimal trauma requiring clindamycin). Exam: mildly impaired general condition, edema on shank. Labs: normal glucose, renal/liver function, electrolytes, ESR/CRP, WBC/platelets, thyroid and gonadal hormones, cortisol; negative HIV/HBV/HCV/EBV markers. Anemia with microcytosis/hypochromia and iron deficiency parameters; low vitamin B12; low total protein (46 g/L) and borderline-low albumin (35 g/L). Treated with RBC transfusion, vitamin B12 and iron. Immunoglobulin replacement started (IVIG escalating doses) with partial IgG rise; switched to SCIG with IgG increasing to ~10 g/L, with improvement in edema, reduced diuresis, diarrhea-free and weight stabilized. Immunophenotyping: low CD4 percentage with CD8 predominance, low B-cell percentage; later increased activation markers; functional T-cell responses normal (PHA and CD3/CD28), naive CD4 percentage ~14–19%. No other identified cause of hypogammaglobulinemia.

A 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, obesity, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertension was on insulin glargine 38 units nightly and metformin 1000 mg twice daily. Due to HbA1c 8.2% and desire for weight reduction, she previously used semaglutide for ~3–4 months without adverse reactions but stopped due to insurance/financial constraints. She then received her first dose of tirzepatide; within 10–15 minutes she developed sudden severe diffuse pruritus with generalized urticarial rash over arms, hands, back, and body (face/neck spared). She denied lip/tongue swelling, dysphagia, or shortness of breath. She took antihistamines and fully recovered without medical care. She stopped tirzepatide and had no recurrence while other medications remained unchanged. Two weeks prior she received influenza and COVID-19 vaccines without symptoms. No food intake or other medications immediately prior to the reaction. Past allergy: penicillin causing rash. Event was reported to pharmacovigilance.

15-year-old girl born at 36 weeks to non-consanguineous parents with normal birth weight/length. From age 2, progressive, disproportionate and asymmetric overgrowth over time with multisystem involvement (central nervous and circulatory systems, lung, skeleton/limbs, abdominal organs). Physical findings included dolichocephaly; focal skull hyperostosis in the right fronto-parietal region; facial asymmetry with right ptosis; depressed nasal bridge with wide anteverted nares; oligodontia with multiple caries; long neck; thin skin; adipose dysregulation with reduced subcutaneous fat; marked asymmetric limb/foot overgrowth (greater calcaneus/cuboid enlargement, especially left foot); severe kyphoscoliosis; limb length discrepancy; macrodactyly of the 3rd–4th fingers of the right hand. Additional manifestations included emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, a syringomyelic cavity (~2 cm) at C3–D4, and ovarian cystadenomas. Complications during follow-up: portal thrombosis at age 12 with portal/splenic/mesenteric hypertension and liver atrophy; transient ischemic attack at age 13. Brain MRI showed cortical dysplasia and progressive right fronto-temporal skull thickening/mass effect enlarging over 4 years (to 44 mm) causing midbrain/brain compression, cerebral edema, hydrocephalus, and right eye proptosis. Clinical course progressed to respiratory failure, coma, and death. Immunology: normal serum immunoglobulins and adequate vaccine responses; lymphopenia with reduced peripheral total T and B cell numbers but no significant infection history; T-cell subsets with normal naïve/RTE CD4 percentages, increased terminally differentiated CD4 cells, reduced CD8 T cells; B-cell subsets with reduced recent bone marrow emigrants and reduced IgM memory cells; NK subsets normal. In vitro stimulation showed normal T-cell activation to PHA; increased B-cell CD69 and CD86 up-regulation to CpG suggesting B-cell hyper-responsiveness. Genetic testing for AKT1 mutation not performed due to premature death.

A 48-year-old mildly asthmatic female presented with vomiting, weakness, and syncopal symptoms after a recent self-limited upper respiratory illness with anosmia and dysgeusia; she had a positive SARS-CoV-2 test two days before admission. She was hypotensive with mottled/purple extremities. Initial echocardiogram showed pericardial effusion with low-normal LV function, normal RV function, and no pulmonary hypertension; the effusion decreased by transfer and pericardial fluid sampling showed a nonspecific inflammatory profile. EKG was nonspecific. She received large-volume crystalloids (6 L then an additional 9 L) but had persistent shock with severe hemoconcentration, anuria, and very low central venous pressure (<5 cm H2O). Chest X-ray was clear and she had no respiratory symptoms. Inflammatory markers were low/near-normal (normal CRP and IL-6; minimally elevated ferritin and fibrinogen). Extensive evaluation (including tryptase, C1 esterase, serum electrophoresis) was unrevealing; all microbiologic cultures were negative. She required high-dose vasopressors and continuous renal replacement therapy; after high-dose IVIG she rapidly weaned off vasopressors within hours. She developed widespread deep venous thromboses treated with heparin. Transient hypoxemia occurred during recovery and improved with fluid removal. She recovered fully by discharge one week later.

A 43-year-old Caucasian male with myalgias and symmetric loss of muscle strength in the upper and lower limbs, predominantly proximal (shoulder and pelvic girdle). Creatinine phosphokinase (CK) elevated at 713 U/L (ref 10–172), aldolase elevated at 8.9 U/L (ref <7.6), and hepatic enzymes mildly elevated (AST 43 U/L, ALT 65 U/L; ref 10–37). Physical exam notable only for 4/5 strength in upper and lower limbs, predominantly proximal. No calcinosis, arthritis, heliotropic rash, Gottron's papules, cutaneous nodules, or erythema.

Caucasian female presented at 18 months with persistent daily vomiting and failure to thrive. Labs (CBC, liver function tests, viral serologies, serum amylase) normal. Anti–tissue transglutaminase antibody >200 RU/mL. Endoscopy showed mild gastric antral inflammation and scalloping of duodenal mucosa; gastric biopsy chronic antritis; duodenal biopsy with villous atrophy and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Started gluten-free diet with intermittent accidental gluten exposures causing occasional vomiting. At age 2, specific IgE to wheat was negative. Around age 7, accidental gluten exposure caused immediate mouth tingling for ~10 minutes followed by vomiting, without respiratory distress, urticaria, or angioedema; anti–tissue transglutaminase 7.9 RU/mL. At age 8, contact with airborne wheat flour on skin caused immediate urticarial lesions on exposed areas. Allergy evaluation: positive skin tests to wheat, oat, rye; serum specific IgE positive to wheat 42.5 kU/L, rye 33.9 kU/L, barley 11.3 kU/L, oat 11.3 kU/L; prescribed epinephrine autoinjector. Later that year, immediate coughing, shortness of breath, tingly mouth and possible wheeze after eating previously tolerated rice pasta; repeated immediate shortness of breath and chin pruritus with same batch; later tolerated a different batch of the same brand, suggesting prior wheat contamination. Subsequent accidental ingestion of wheat-flour pizza caused immediate mouth tingling and vomiting. Oral wheat challenge considered contraindicated due to recent reactions and need to avoid wheat.

39-year-old undereducated housewife with low social/financial status and a long history of repeated/prolonged hospitalizations and extensive negative/unchanged investigations, reporting multiple fluctuating physical complaints. Symptoms include bilateral hand/foot edema, dyspnea (worse at night), sore throat, heavy-headed feeling, oral ulcers, strong dependency on nasal oxygen with nasal mucosal dryness, recurrent severe epistaxis (including episodes during psychiatric admission), arthralgia/arthritis and photosensitivity, diffuse physical pains, insomnia (difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep), intense anxiety/panic with fear of death and fear of serious illness (e.g., cancer). Hyperventilation-type symptoms: asphyxia sensation, agitation, palpitations, dizziness, perioral/head/finger/toe paresthesias. Behavioral features: exhibitionism/area exposure when describing pain. Exam: no cyanosis; no nail/finger deformity; exophthalmos with normal thyroid tests; decreased libido, truncal/abdominal obesity, bradykinesia. Past history: ovarian cyst surgery at 23; thrombocytopenia (platelets ~59,000) with hemorrhage at 37; multiple reported food/antibiotic sensitivities. Multiple admissions across pulmonary, hematology, cardiology, psychiatry, rheumatology; repeated tests including echocardiograms, chest imaging, brain imaging. Imaging notes gallstones; renal cyst; hypoechoic renal mass. Echo: EF ~55%, mild valvular regurgitation, RVH/LVH. Cardiac perfusion scan reported chronic thrombo-emboli/vasculitis. Labs: anti-dsDNA elevated (1.2), ANA 0.7, antiphospholipid IgG normal; PFT shows obstruction/possible restriction; microcytic anemia indices (Hb 10.3, MCV 69.2) with CRP 3+ and prolonged PT (18.5).

A 28-year-old female with systemic autoimmune disease developed chest pain, fever, altered mental status, and headache over seven days. ECG suggested pericarditis. Exam showed tangential thought process, mildly slowed right fine finger movements, and brisker lower-extremity reflexes; strength, sensation, cranial nerves, and gait were otherwise normal. Labs: normocytic anemia (Hgb 9.3 g/dL), normal WBC/platelets, normal creatinine (0.75 mg/dL) with nephrotic-range proteinuria (urine protein/creatinine 9.8 g/day), low complements (C3 47 mg/dL, C4 4 mg/dL), ESR 94 mm/hr, CRP 1.18 mg/dL, hypergammaglobulinemia 3000 mg/dL. CT showed large pleural and pericardial effusions.

Brain MRI w/wo contrast showed a focal lesion with surrounding edema, weak enhancement, no mass effect, and reduced peripheral T2 signal; biopsy deemed too risky. Lumbar puncture: normal CSF WBC, mildly elevated protein (56 mg/dL), negative cultures. PET-CT showed low FDG uptake at the lesion and diffuse lymphadenopathy (axillary SUV up to 3.0); axillary node FNA showed reactive changes with negative flow cytometry/cultures. Treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotics and acyclovir; corticosteroids initially withheld due to concern for infection. Repeat brain MRI and MR venography 10 days later showed significant improvement in the apparent “mass” and patent venous sinuses/veins; serial blood/urine (including fungal and mycobacterial) cultures remained negative.

Pericardial and pleural effusions enlarged, requiring pericardiocentesis and thoracentesis; fluid cultures negative. On hospital day 16, she developed acute left facial droop and right arm weakness with markedly elevated D-dimer (17.02 mg/L). MR venography demonstrated a large hemorrhagic venous infarct in the left frontal/parietal lobes with abrupt cutoff of the vein of Trolard and superficial draining veins and 7 mm midline shift; MRI did not suggest an enhancing tumor and showed hemorrhage/hemosiderin on susceptibility imaging. She received IV solumedrol and mycophenolate for systemic disease activity after negative infectious evaluation and was anticoagulated (transitioned to warfarin), with neurologic improvement over subsequent weeks.

A 69-year-old female with a one-month history of recurrent gross hematuria with slight urgency and dysuria. No history of trauma or infection. Exam: ~5 cm × 4 cm fixed smooth palpable hypogastric mass without tenderness. Urine cytology: increased leukocytes, no atypical cells. CT: ill-defined solid mass in the anterior bladder wall. Cystoscopy: smooth bladder mucosa; bulge at bladder dome with normal overlying urothelium. Initial biopsy: chronic mucosal inflammation and lamina propria fibrous hyperplasia. TUR-BT: no mucosal abnormality; a mass deep in the muscle layer at the bladder dome; post-TUR biopsy again non-diagnostic. Proceeded to median laparotomy and bladder exploration; mass adherent to bladder apex, pubic symphysis, and peritoneum; completely resected with part of bladder and peritoneum. Gross pathology: bladder wall thickening replaced by gray-white tough woven scar-like lesion with diffuse infiltrative growth into perivesical soft tissue. Microscopy: urothelium/lamina propria unremarkable; spindle cell proliferation in muscularis propria and peripheral adipose tissue in fascicles with mild–moderate atypia and hyperchromatic nuclei; inflammatory cells superficially; deeper layers with abundant eosinophilic collagen and occasional bizarre hyperchromatic stromal cells; small foci of lipoma-like well-differentiated adipocytic component found on extensive sampling. Margins negative; peritoneum normal. FNCLCC grade 2; stage T1N0M0. Immunohistochemistry: positive MDM2, CDK4, p16, SMA, focal MSA; Ki-67 ~5%; negative Desmin, ALK-1, p63, CK7, PCK, S-100, CD34, EMA, beta-catenin. Molecular: MDM2 and CDK4 amplification by FISH in spindle cells and adipocytes; no FRS2 amplification, ALK rearrangement, or CTNNB1 mutation; WES showed TSPAN31 and JUN amplifications. Managed with surgical resection and surveillance only; no recurrence over 85 months.
diagnosis: Dedifferentiated liposarcoma of the urinary bladder

case_information: 29-day-old male infant born at 37 weeks (3528 g) with low Apgar scores (1/3/6) requiring NICU care for seizure-like activity and respiratory distress; blood cultures positive for E. coli; developed persistent pulmonary hypertension requiring inhaled nitric oxide, high-frequency oscillatory ventilation, epinephrine infusion, and then ECMO on day of life 5. Foley catheter placed per protocol. Abnormal renal function led to renal ultrasound showing moderate right and mild-moderate left renal pelvicaliectasis, bilateral echogenic kidneys, and small-volume ascites. After ECMO discontinuation on day of life 11, developed increasing abdominal distension and inability to void without Foley; ultrasound showed increased ascites and diffuse increased renal echogenicity. Peritoneal tap on day of life 25 with elevated RBCs, creatinine, LDH, and triglycerides. Persistent/worsening ascites and inability to wean Foley; serum/peritoneal/urine creatinine 39/53/442 µmol/L. Bedside voiding urethrocystogram demonstrated intraperitoneal urinary leak. Exploratory laparotomy found a 4–5 mm posterior bladder wall perforation; no posterior urethral valves or obstructive lesions noted; repaired and Foley left for drainage.

A 16-year-old boy presented to the ER after an injury to the genital region while cutting wood with an electric saw. He had profuse bleeding and a ragged, near-total transection of the penis distal to the symphysis pubis. During attempted urethral catheterization, the catheter emerged through the wound. He was resuscitated, a pressure dressing applied, and taken urgently to surgery. Intraoperatively, the corporal bodies were bleeding profusely with complete ragged transection of the right corporal body and near-total transection of the left; the urethra was catheterized and repaired with urine flow noted. Hemostasis and approximation of transected corporal edges were performed, and a suprapubic cystostomy was created for urinary diversion. Postoperative penile ultrasound/Doppler demonstrated preserved vascularity. Retrograde urethrogram and micturating cystourethrogram showed no contrast extravasation and normal caliber/outline of anterior and posterior urethra. Healing was satisfactory with superficial scarring; on follow-up at 6 months and 1 year, there was minimal scarring, preserved touch sensation, and the patient reported mild painful erection and curvature not bothersome.

An eight-month old tortoiseshell cat presented for sex identification. Physical examination showed small body size, female appearance, absence of a scrotum, and an underdeveloped penis without visible spines. Presented for neutering; surgery did not reveal gonads, though ductuli deferentes were identified, and histology confirmed normal organization of the ductuli deferentes.

Male patient had dry cough, fever, and sore throat; PCR test positive. No shortness of breath; self-isolated at home for 14 days and received treatment without a bronchodilator. Symptoms improved and repeat PCR became negative.

Two months later at follow-up: income decreased by 30%; stayed home about 14 hours/day due to lockdown. Resumed sexual activity about 30 days after the negative PCR. Partner reported being less active/responsive than before. Reported decreased intercourse frequency and worsening morning erection frequency/rigidity.

Sexual function assessed before vs after illness using IIEF-15: no erectile dysfunction before the illness; after recovery scores worsened, consistent with moderate erectile dysfunction, with declines across orgasmic function, sexual desire, intercourse satisfaction, and overall satisfaction compared with pre-illness.

Premature Ejaculation Diagnostic Tool (PEDT): shifted from no premature ejaculation before illness to definite premature ejaculation after recovery; described as acquired generalized type.

Depression assessed with BDI-II: increased from normal mood before illness to worse category after recovery.

Physical and genital exams unremarkable. Morning sex-hormone panel largely normal; prolactin elevated. Random blood sugar normal.

Seventy-three-year-old female with suspected pelvic malignancy recurrence causing bilateral ureteric compression and hydronephrosis underwent rigid cystoscopy with urgent bilateral ureteric stent insertion. Procedure was technically difficult and lasted ~90 minutes with continuous bladder irrigation using 1.5% glycine (total ~10 L) hung ~2 m high, infusion rate controlled by surgeon. Intraoperatively had rising peak airway pressures that improved with additional neuromuscular blockade and altered ventilation. Immediately after extubation developed agitation, diaphoresis, progressive central cyanosis and severe hypertension (SBP ~200 mmHg), requiring reintubation. Expanding abdominal girth noted; FAST ultrasound showed new free intraperitoneal fluid (not present on CT 24 hours earlier). ABG on 100% oxygen showed hypercapnia and hyponatraemia (pO2 184 mmHg, pCO2 54 mmHg, Na 126 mmol/L, HCO3 21 mmol/L). Irrigation was changed to normal saline and rate decreased; continuous irrigation later stopped. CT chest/abdomen and cystogram demonstrated intraperitoneal fluid extravasation related to the urinary tract. ICU course included prolonged ventilation, diuresis (8.5 L), careful electrolyte monitoring without hypertonic saline, pulmonary oedema on CXR with impaired gas exchange; sodium normalized over 7 days.

29-year-old female with intermittent right flank pain. Ultrasonography showed mild hydronephrosis. CT demonstrated ~12 mm calcifications at both ureterovesical junctions with mild right hydronephrosis; left kidney absent. Plain radiography did not show a corresponding ureteral stone in the same location. Past history: bilateral endoscopic injections of dextranomer/hyaluronic acid for vesicoureteral reflux 6 years prior; subsequent left nephrectomy 1 year later. Urinalysis normal and urine culture sterile. Because of solitary kidney, cystoscopy/ureteroscopy performed: volcanic cone-like mound caudal to both ureteral orifices on cystoscopy; no ureteral stones seen on ureteroscopy. Repeat CT at 3 months showed unchanged ureterovesical junction calcifications.

35-year-old male transferred for abdominal pain with a 3-month history of abnormal bowel movements and a 3-week history of an enlarging palpable abdominal mass. CT showed a 14 x 18 x 20 cm abdominopelvic mass causing ureteral obstruction and bilateral hydronephrosis, without retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Exam noted an undescended left testicle palpable in the left inguinal canal. Tumor markers: beta-hCG 10 mIU/mL (upper limit of normal), AFP normal, LDH >6x upper limit of normal. Percutaneous biopsy of the mass obtained. Underwent cystoscopy with bilateral ureteral stent placement and radical left inguinal orchiectomy; orchiectomy specimen contained no tumor. Right testicular ultrasound showed no lesions. Chest CT negative for metastatic disease. Treated with 4 cycles of BEP (bleomycin omitted in cycle 1 due to PFT abnormalities and omitted in final cycle due to rash during cycle 3). Follow-up imaging showed residual mass decreased to 5 x 3.4 x 5 cm and an incidental asymptomatic pulmonary embolism treated with therapeutic low molecular weight heparin for 3 months. PET showed avidity in residual mass; underwent surgical resection 5 months after chemotherapy completion. Surgical pathology showed no viable tumor but did contain testicular parenchymal tissue. No complications and no evidence of recurrence at 1- and 6-month follow-up.
diagnosis: Pure seminoma arising in a supernumerary testis

case_information: 36-year-old woman achieved pregnancy via single embryo transfer after ICSI. First-trimester screening showed low aneuploidy risk. Fetal ultrasound showed an anterior abdominal wall hypoechoic area; repeat scan at 16 weeks demonstrated an umbilical cord cyst (~1.7 cm) with vessels coursing around it, no gut within, and normal anterior abdominal wall and bladder wall. Amniocentesis showed normal 46,XX karyotype. The cord cyst enlarged progressively to ~4.9 cm by 35 weeks; cord became homogeneously echogenic with concern for increased Wharton’s jelly/edema and possible cord compression. Elective cesarean after maternal corticosteroids; cyst ruptured during delivery; cord noted thickened with Wharton’s jelly and elongated umbilical stump with overlying skin (~2 cm). On day 5, after cord clamp fell off, urine jetted from the umbilicus when the infant cried; this later ceased after treatment of a urinary tract infection. Postnatal ultrasound confirmed an abnormal connection between the bladder and umbilicus. Infant had a prominent umbilical stump with bulging during voiding. Laparoscopic surgery at 11 weeks showed the bladder dome continuous with the umbilicus; post-op cystourethrogram showed no vesicoureteral reflux; recovery and follow-up normal.

A 5-year-old boy underwent ICG-based intraoperative near-infrared laser angiography during a one-stage delayed bladder closure with radical soft-tissue mobilization (Kelly procedure). Serial ICG perfusion assessments (0.15 mg/kg; real-time visualization ~80 seconds post-infusion; re-dosing possible every 15 minutes) were performed after: mobilization of the bladder plate and exposure of corpora; full mobilization of the left corpus with periosteal incision/peeling of the left ischiopubic rami to mobilize the ipsilateral corpus and identify the neurovascular pedicle exiting Alcock’s canal; full mobilization of bladder and both corpora with detachment of the right corpus and associated striated muscular structures from bone (concern for reflex vasoconstriction/edema and ischemia, but no substantial blood-flow change); separation of an epispadic urethral plate from the corpora with penile disassembly and external rotation of corpora and complete mobilization of the urethral plate; completion of reconstruction including funnel-shaped cervicoplasty, tubularization of the urethral plate, wrapping mobilized muscular structures around the neo-urethra to promote continence, closure of bladder, re-approximation of corpora, suturing rectus muscles, and re-approximation of pubic bones with hip rotation/symphysis apposition (bladder plate perfusion remained stable, supporting a complete repair rather than staged approach); and after ventral transposition of the neo-urethra to a scrotal position for penile elongation with dorsal re-orientation of penile skin. Final assessments showed good tissue and penile perfusion without evidence of pudendal vessel injury or compression. Perioperative course was uneventful with excellent esthetic and functional outcomes at 1-month follow-up.

41-year-old individual admitted to urology for evaluation of a suspicious left testicular lesion seen on MRI and infertility. Past history of right inguinal cryptorchidism treated with orchiectomy. Known 46,XX genotype with male gender identity; prior karyogram and orchiectomy performed abroad with unavailable histology and unknown SRY status. Exam: scrotal hypospadias; elevated left testis, not remarkable on palpation. Labs: azoospermia with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (LH 31 IU/L, FSH 44 IU/L, testosterone 226 ng/dL). Tumor markers negative (hCG/beta-hCG 1.0 IU/L, AFP 7.1). Left orchiectomy performed; grossly a biphasic mass. Histology: solid tumor with eosinophilic granules and occasional Reinke crystalloids; immunopositive for inhibin, calretinin, and melanA; low mitotic activity, low Ki-67 (1–2%), p53 wild type. Residual compressed seminiferous tubules without spermatogonia. Germ cell neoplasia in situ excluded (morphology and Oct3/4). Second component showed ovarian-type stroma with corpora albicantia, without oocytes/follicles.

A 27-year-old man presented with hematospermia and painful ejaculation for 8 months, along with irritative lower urinary tract symptoms and primary infertility. DRE revealed a large bulge near the prostate. Physical exam showed normal bilateral testes and vas deferens. Semen analysis: ejaculate volume 1 mL with oligoasthenozoospermia (total sperm count 10,250,000; 99% nonmotile). Serum prolactin, LH, FSH, and testosterone were within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasound showed left renal agenesis with contralateral compensatory hypertrophy. Transrectal ultrasound demonstrated a large cystic mass in the left seminal vesicle region; the right seminal vesicle was not visible. Pelvic MRI (non-contrast) revealed a 5 x 3.5 cm cystic structure in the left seminal vesicle containing hemoglobin degradation products; the right seminal vesicle was hypoplastic; prostate and bladder were normal. Cystoscopy showed a normal right ureteral orifice but no left ureteral orifice; urethroscopy noted bulging on the prostatic urethra near the verumontanum. Medical therapy (antibiotic, alpha-blocker, anti-inflammatory) for several weeks gave no satisfactory response, so transurethral resection of the ejaculatory duct with cyst wall resection was performed using methylene blue injection via the left vas deferens to localize the ejaculatory duct. At 2-month follow-up, hematospermia and painful ejaculation resolved; ejaculate volume did not increase.

A 67-year-old female presented with right flank pain, fever, and vomiting. Labs showed leukocytosis (total leukocyte count 16,600/µL) and acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 3.1 mg/dL). Non-contrast CT demonstrated moderate hydronephrosis, a right upper ureteric calculus, and a well-circumscribed medial renal lesion. Percutaneous nephrostomy was performed due to impaired renal function, followed by percutaneous nephrolithotomy. After renal function improved (creatinine 1.47 mg/dL), contrast CT showed an enhancing medial renal mass (33 to 118 HU) with renal vein thrombosis and multiple paracaval lymph nodes; clinical stage recorded as T3aN2M0 and treated with laparoscopic radical nephrectomy. Gross specimen showed renal vein thrombus; histology revealed foamy macrophages admixed with inflammatory infiltrate, with no evidence of malignancy.

Infant female underwent laparotomy with operative findings of hydrometrocolpos, patent urachus, intestinal malrotation, internal cloaca (rectum, vagina, and urethra connected), imperforate anus, and a fistula between the uterus and colon. Ladd’s procedure performed with bowel repositioning; double-barrel colostomy created; catheterization of urachus and uterus with Foley catheter; hydrometrocolpos drained.

Postoperative course included recurrent admissions for upper urinary tract infection. At 11 weeks old presented with 1 day of yellowish vomiting, decreased stool output for 2 days, mild fever (38°C), and 2 days of abdominal distension; appeared ill and dehydrated. Underwent surgery for intestinal obstruction; found to have small bowel obstruction due to an adhesion band ~100 cm from the duodenojejunal junction and ~70 cm from the ileocecal valve with proximal dilation and distal collapse.

Labs: Hb 9.5 g/dL, PCV 31%, RBC 3.49×10^6, RDW 18.3%, platelets 539×10^3/µL. Urinalysis: turbid yellow urine, pH 5, nitrite positive, 10–12 pus cells and bacteria; no protein/ketones; 0–2 RBCs. Treated with metronidazole; discharged stable.

At 6 months, DMSA renal scan showed enlarged solitary left kidney with dilated pelvicalyceal system and mild hydronephrosis/possible malrotation with reduced cortical uptake (especially mid-cortex); right kidney not visualized (suggesting absent or nonfunctioning kidney). Poor prognosis noted.

A 27-year-old male referred to urology with mild recurrent lower abdominal pain associated with dysuria. No other lower urinary tract symptoms, no gross hematuria, no constitutional symptoms, and no family history of kidney disease. Physical examination unremarkable. Blood investigations and renal function tests within normal limits. Urinalysis showed red and white blood cells. Urine culture grew Escherichia coli. CT urogram with delayed images showed a congenital renal fusion anomaly with a unilateral left-sided single ureter. Screening found no other organ anomalies. Treated with oral antibiotics per culture/sensitivity and counseled on UTI prevention; planned one-year follow-up.

In March 2017, a 55-year-old was referred for intermediate-risk prostate malignancy and underwent open radical prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection after negative conventional imaging. Pathology showed pT3a with nodal involvement (2 positive pelvic nodes out of 9; along the left internal iliac artery and left obturator fossa), margins negative (R0), lymphatic invasion present (L1), venous invasion absent (V0), Gleason score 4+3, with postoperative undetectable PSA. In September 2017, he received salvage radiotherapy to the prostatic fossa including the pelvic lymphatic template for early PSA recurrence (0.1 ng/mL) with complete PSA response. Over the next three years PSA rose to 1.05 ng/mL. A PSMA PET scan demonstrated tracer uptake in a single left pararectal lymph node (SUVmax 14.7) with no local tumor and no distant metastases. In November 2020, after counseling, he underwent left pararectal and presacral PSMA-radioguided salvage lymph node dissection using 99mTc-labeled PSMA tracer with preoperative SPECT/CT; pathology found one positive left pararectal node out of 14 retrieved.

Age/Gender: 29-year-old male 
Occupation: Construction worker 
Medical History: Previously healthy, no chronic illnesses or prior surgeries 
Presenting Complaint: Brought to the emergency department after falling from scaffolding at a construction site, approximately 20 feet high, "cracked helmet found at site" Upon arrival, the patient is unconscious with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 6 (E1V2M3). Observable scalp laceration on the right parietal region. 
No other visible injuries or fractures identified during the initial examination. "right side arms/legs not moving" --> motor score M3 Vital Signs: Blood pressure 140/90 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 92% on room air. 
Neurological Examination: Unresponsive to verbal commands, withdrawal response to painful stimuli, pupils are equal but sluggishly reactive to light. 
Primary and Secondary Survey: Reveals no additional injuries. CT Scan of the Head: Shows a large right-sided epidural hematoma with midline shift and signs of uncal herniation. There is also a small subdural hematoma on the same side without significant mass effect.
Cervical Spine X-rays: No fractures or dislocations noted. --> trauma pan scan which is entire body
diagnosis: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) with right-sided epidural hematoma and uncal herniation, accompanied by a small subdural hematoma (but where is it the same side or the other side). Missing information - size of epidural.

case_information:
Age/Gender: 41-year-old female
Occupation: Environmental consultant
Medical History: Asthma managed with inhalers; otherwise, no significant medical history.
Presenting Complaint: Involved in a high-speed bicycle accident without wearing a helmet, resulting in a loss of consciousness for approximately 10 minutes. Regained consciousness but remains confused and disoriented. The patient was brought to the emergency department by paramedics, with visible head injuries and facial abrasions.
Vital Signs: BP 150/90 mmHg, HR 110 bpm, RR 20 bpm, SpO2 96% on room air. Physical Examination: Multiple lacerations on the scalp with a contusion over the right temporal area. GCS score of 13 (E3V4M6) upon arrival.
Neurological Examination: Pupil examination shows right pupil slightly dilated and less responsive to light compared to the left. Difficulty following commands and answering questions appropriately. No gross motor deficits observed, but assessment is challenging due to the patient's altered mental status. CT Scan of the Head: Reveals an acute subdural hematoma on the right side with a midline shift. No skull fractures detected.
MRI of the Brain: Confirms the presence of the subdural hematoma and identifies underlying contusions in the right temporal lobe.
diagnosis: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) with right-sided acute subdural hematoma and temporal lobe contusions.

case_information:
Age/Gender: 30-year-old male
Occupation: IT specialist
Medical History: No significant medical history; non-smoker, occasional alcohol use.
Presenting Complaint: Victim of a severe car crash, ejected from the vehicle after it rolled multiple times. Found unconscious at the scene and transported to the hospital by emergency services. The patient arrives at the emergency department in a comatose state with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 64 (E1V2M131).
Vital Signs: BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, RR mechanically ventilated, SpO2 100% on room air. Physical Examination: Multiple abrasions and contusions across the body; no external signs of head trauma other than superficial scalp lacerations.
Neurological Examination: Pupils are bilaterally equal but sluggishly reactive to light. No motor responses to painful stimuli, indicating a deep coma. CT Scan of the Head: No evidence of skull fractures or intracranial hemorrhages. Some subtle signs of brain swelling.
MRI of the Brain: Reveals diffuse axonal injury (DAI), characterized by multiple focal lesions in the white matter tracts of the brain, particularly in the corpus callosum and brainstem.
diagnosis: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) characterized by diffuse axonal injury due to high-velocity impact in a car crash.

case_information:
Age/Gender: 8-year-old male
Occupation: Elementary school student
Medical History: Generally healthy, with a history of asthma controlled with medication. No previous hospitalizations or surgeries.
Presenting Complaint: Fell from a climbing frame at the playground, landing on his head. Cried immediately after the fall but became drowsy and vomited once about an hour later. The patient is brought to the emergency department by his parents, appearing drowsy but arousable. He complains of a headache and says he feels "sick."
Vital Signs: BP 100/65 mmHg, HR 98 bpm, RR 20 bpm, SpO2 99% on room air. Physical Examination: A small contusion on the scalp with no apparent skull deformity. No other visible injuries.
Neurological Examination: The patient is oriented to time, place, and person. Exhibits mild irritability when questioned but follows commands and moves all limbs appropriately. Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light. CT Scan of the Head: Shows no evidence of skull fractures, intracranial hemorrhage, or significant brain swelling.
Observation: Given the mild symptoms and normal initial CT findings, the decision is made to observe the patient in the pediatric unit for 24 hours.
diagnosis: Pediatric mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) with concussion symptoms following a fall.

case_information:
Age/Gender: 49-year-old male
Occupation: Construction foreman
Medical History: Hypertension managed with medication, no history of previous head injuries.
Presenting Complaint: Struck on the head by a falling piece of equipment at the construction site. Found unconscious and transported to the hospital by coworkers. Upon arrival at the emergency department, the patient is unconscious with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 8 (E2V2M4).
Vital Signs: BP 145/90 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 14 bpm, SpO2 92% on room air. Physical Examination: Significant scalp hematoma over the right temporal area, no other visible injuries. Signs of respiratory distress.
Neurological Examination: Unresponsive to verbal commands, localized pain response, right pupil dilated and sluggish in response to light, indicating possible herniation. CT Scan of the Head: Reveals a large right-sided epidural hematoma with midline shift. No visible skull fractures.
MRI of the Brain (if stable for MRI): To assess for any underlying brain injuries, contusions, or additional intracranial hemorrhages. Goes straight into surgery.
diagnosis: Severe head trauma with right-sided epidural hematoma, leading to increased intracranial pressure and signs of herniation.

case_information:
Age/Gender: 65-year-old female
Occupation: Retired teacher
Medical History: History of mild cognitive impairment. On anticoagulant therapy for atrial fibrillation.
Presenting Complaint: Slipped and fell in her kitchen, hitting her head on the floor. Initially felt fine but developed a headache and confusion over the next 48 hours. The patient is brought to the emergency department by her family due to increasing confusion, lethargy, and difficulty speaking.
Vital Signs: BP 160/95 mmHg, HR 78 bpm irregular, RR 16 bpm, SpO2 97% on room air. Physical Examination: No external signs of head injury except for a small bruise on the forehead. Increasing drowsiness during the examination.
Neurological Examination: Oriented to person but not to time or place. Speech is slurred, and she is unable to follow complex commands. Weakness in the right arm and leg. CT Scan of the Head: Shows bilateral subdural hematomas, more extensive on the left side, with midline shift and signs of brain compression.
Blood Tests: Indicate prolonged INR due to anticoagulant therapy.
diagnosis: Acute on chronic bilateral subdural hematomas with cerebral compression, secondary to fall and exacerbated by anticoagulant therapy.

case_information:
Age/Gender: 4-year-old male
Occupation: Preschool student
Medical History: Generally healthy with a history of mild asthma. No previous hospitalizations or surgeries.
Presenting Complaint: Sustained a head injury from falling off playground equipment three weeks ago. Initially diagnosed with a minor concussion and a linear skull fracture. Recently, his parents have noticed a bulging area on his head where the injury occurred, accompanied by intermittent irritability and decreased appetite. The child is brought to the pediatric neurosurgery clinic by his parents due to concerns about the bulging area on his skull and changes in behavior.
Vital Signs: Within normal limits for age. Physical Examination: A palpable, pulsatile mass on the left parietal region of the skull. No signs of acute distress, but the child appears more irritable than usual.
